system.description:
The aboleth is an amphibious creature of underground lakes and caverns. It is intelligent, hates most land-dwelling life, and looks for ways to enslave or destroy the beings of the surface world. The race is extremely long-lived and has gathered much knowledge older than man; it is perhaps better that men do not learn these ancient secrets, which are rumored to be more horrible and foul than could be thought possible.

Appearance: a slime-covered, fish-like body with a large fluke-like tail that drives it through the water. It is a blue-green mottled gray with a pinkish tan belly, with blue-black slime-producing organs on either side. Three long, slit-like, purple-red eyes are set one above the other in its head, under protective ridges. Four 10-foot tentacles grow from the top of its head, and its toothless mouth is on the underside. On land it drags its obscene bulk along with its 4 tentacles.

  • Tentacles: 4 attacks for 1-6 points of damage each. A creature struck must save vs. spells or its skin turns into a clear, slimy membrane over 2-5 rounds. A cure disease spell cast on the victim stops the change. Once the change is complete, the membrane must be kept damp with cool water or the victim takes 1-12 points of damage each turn from intense pain. A cure serious wounds spell turns the membrane back into normal skin.
  • Illusions: by concentrating and doing nothing else, it can create very realistic illusions with sound and sight.
  • Enslave (3 times per day): against a single creature up to 30 feet away, which must save vs. spells or be filled with the desire to serve the aboleth. Enslaved creatures will not fight for it but try to follow its other telepathic commands. A slave more than a mile from the aboleth gets a new saving throw each day. The charm is broken by remove curse, dispel magic, or the death of the aboleth.
  • Mucus: in water it surrounds itself with a cloud of mucus 1 foot thick. A creature drawn into it must save vs. poison or inhale it and become unable to breathe air, suffocating in 2-12 rounds if it tries. The aboleth uses this mucus to let its slaves breathe water, as a potion of water breathing, for 1-3 hours. Soap or wine dissolves it.

There are reports of huge underwater cities built by aboleths and their slaves, but these reports, like the stories of their vast knowledge, have never been proven.

The afanc is dreaded for its ability to swim rapidly and create a whirlpool. It is generally found in shallow salt water, swimming lazily, and is then usually mistaken for some kind of whale.

  • Attacks: a bite (5-20) or 2 flipper strikes (1d12 each).
  • Whirlpool: its usual way of attacking surface prey. It swims in closing circles around the prey, starting 100 feet out and closing 20 feet per round to 40 feet, speeding up from its usual 15” to 30” or more. This makes a whirlpool strong enough to drag down a ship of small to small-medium size (up to 60 feet long) at 10 feet per round. It avoids larger ships.
  • Driving it off: making the whirlpool takes 5-8 rounds, and the afanc must stay at the surface to do it, so a concerted attack with spells and/or heavy missile fire might drive it off.
  • After: creatures dragged down can be attacked, since the afanc is 10% likely to submerge and either try another mode of attack or look for easier prey.
  • Small craft: rafts, boats, and similar craft 30 feet long or less are usually rammed and capsized, and the passengers eaten by the greedy beast.

Description: like a cross between a whale and a great fish: a whale-like body, a more fish-like head, and a vertical tail. Gray to blue-gray. Afancs are fish, though they breathe both air and water.

Agathia are kindly, helpful spirits. Multitudes of them live on the Upper Outer Planes, but on the Prime Material Plane usually only one is met. They are usually sent there by a deity, or perhaps a solar, to help creatures of good disposition confront and defeat evil.

Forms: an agathion takes material form as it wishes.

  • Human form (60%): it uses weapons typical of a cleric and has the spell powers and abilities of a 7th-level cleric. Its wisdom is 18, so it gets bonus spells. It may look young or old, male or female, handsome or plain, rustic or urbane.
  • Creature form (30%): the form of a kindly creature such as a lammasu, shedu, or unicorn. It has that creature’s attack forms and any spell abilities, and turns undead as a 14th-level cleric.
  • Housed in an object (10%): non-corporeal, contained in a ring, talisman, or perhaps a small vase or flask, etc. It can then give the item’s owner its 1st-level cleric spell ability and automatic detect evil, and let the owner affect undead as a 6th-level cleric.

Other powers: besides its cleric spells and turning undead, it can become ethereal at will, travel astrally, detect evil, and speak any language telepathically.

  • Defenses: struck only by +1 or better magic weapons. It saves as a 14th-level cleric in any form, and is immune to level draining, death spells, disintegration, and energy from the Positive Material Plane.
  • Psionics: clairaudience, clairvoyance, object reading, suspend animation, aura alteration, dimension walk, mind bar, and telempathic projection, at 14th level of mastery.

Leaving its form: if it leaves its form willingly, or is slain, it returns to its own plane. If it left willingly, it does not come back unless called; if slain, it cannot come back for 10-60 years while it regains its strength. Astral or ethereal travel in pursuit of its mission does not count as willingly leaving its form, except for an object-housed agathion travelling without the object’s owner.

Description: in its natural form, an elf-like creature with opalescent, luminous skin and eyes that actually shine. Males and females are equal in size and power. Its touch in natural form does 7-14 points of positive-energy damage to an opponent.

Annis are relatives of the night hags (q.v.) of the Lower Planes and look much like them, but they are larger and physically stronger, and live naturally on the Prime Material Plane. These giantesses are particularly fond of human flesh, but their appetite is so great that they will eat even so rank a beast as a stench kow. They usually live alone or in small groups, but sometimes cooperate with ogres, trolls, and evil giants for safety or better food, and mixed communities have been found.

  • Attacks: iron-like talons and teeth that inflict horrible wounds.
  • Grappling: with strength equal to a hill giant’s (19), an annis also tends to grapple. If she hits one creature with all 3 attacks in the same round, she automatically seizes it after doing damage and holds it fast. From the next round all her attacks hit automatically, unless the victim is stronger, the annis is slain, or the victim has some magical means of escape. Otherwise she keeps her grip, raking and gnawing, until the victim is dead.
  • Spell-like powers: fog cloud (to confuse resistance or delay a stronger foe) and change self (to appear as a large human, an ogre, etc.). Each is usable twice per day, one at a time, one per round, at 8th level for range, duration, etc.
  • Iron-hard skin: treat her as wearing plate mail for weapon vs. armor adjustments. Edged weapons also do −1 damage against her and blunt ones +1 (count flails and morning stars as blunt).
  • Senses: normal infravision, but superior hearing and sense of smell.
  • Languages: their own, Ogre, common Giant, and a smattering of Common. The most intelligent speak various humanoid languages and better Common.

Description: a deep blue color, much like a night hag in complexion and face. Hair, teeth, and nails are glossy black. The eyes are usually dull, greenish or yellow rather than the red of their night hag cousins. The tall body is thin, muscular, and wiry, with long, quick arms and legs. They dress much like peasant women, but usually more tattered and filthy.

Giant ant lions are huge insects of sandy and gravelly places where giant ants and similar large insects are common: typically desert fringes, badlands, and rocky terrain.

  • The pit: a tapering pit about 60 feet across, which looks like a cave or lair entrance 50% of the time. A creature entering it is 50% likely each round to slip down the loose sides to the bottom.
  • Attack: the ant lion lies buried at the bottom under loose sand, gravel, and stones, bursts out, and attacks with its huge mandibles. A hit means its jaws have closed, and it will not let go until it or its prey is dead; each round after the first hit it does 5-20 points of damage automatically.
  • Feeding: it eats one or more giant insects each day, carrying the remains away and hiding them, so one may be met outside its pit.

Lair: ant lions collect no treasure, but there is a 30% chance of 1-4 of the following in the lair from earlier kills:

1-610-40 gp
7-105-20 pp
11-13shield*
14-17metal weapon*
18-19jewelry*
20miscellaneous item*

* 10% chance that the item is magical. If so, roll on the appropriate table in the DMG or assign an item of fairly low value.

Ascomoids are huge puffball-like fungi with very thick, leathery skin. They move by rolling: slowly at first (3” for one round, 6” the next, then 9”, then 12”), but they can keep going for hours without tiring. Their surface is covered with pocks that serve as sense organs, and each pock can shoot a jet of spores.

  • Rolling: they attack by rolling into or over opponents. Small and medium-sized opponents are knocked down and must get up the next round or stay prone.
  • Spore jets: used against dangerous enemies; large opponents, and those who have damaged the ascomoid, are always attacked this way. The stream is about 1 foot across and 30 feet long, and puffs into a cloud 5-20 across where it strikes. Those attacked must save vs. poison or die of internal infection in 1-4 rounds. Even those who save are blinded and choked for 1-4 rounds before they can rejoin melee, and meanwhile are nearly helpless: all attacks on them are at +4, with no shield or dexterity bonus.

Weapons and magic:

  • Piercing weapons such as spears over 6 feet long do double damage; shorter stabbing weapons do damage as against a small opponent.
  • Blunt weapons do not harm it, and slashes and cuts from edged weapons do only 1 point of damage.
  • It saves against magical attacks such as magic missiles, fireballs, and lightning at +4, and takes only 50% damage. (Cold-based attacks are at normal chances.)
  • Having no mind by ordinary standards, it is unaffected by spells that affect the brain (charm, ESP, etc.) unless they are specific to plants.

Humans find aspis mysterious, and they are seldom met in populated lands except when raiding for food. They live in small groups, minding their own business and dealing with outsiders only now and then. Few people have ever met one, and larvae and cows are only rumored, though they must exist for the race to survive.

Cow: unlike other larvae, which change into drones, cows keep their larval form and become huge, bloated females 10-15 feet long, whose only purpose is to lay eggs for the nest. They are sluggish, but their size makes their bite dangerous. Their skin oozes a milky, acidic slime that eats through metal or wood in 1 round and burns exposed flesh for 1-8 points of damage each round until washed off.

Nest: underground, a set of sloping tunnels bored through soft rock or dirt, usually about 4 feet high and well defended by traps and guards. It holds 1-3 egg chambers, 2-4 granaries, 1-6 grub hatcheries with 1-10 larvae each, and a central chamber. Only 1 cow is found in any nest. There is a 10% chance that 10-100 giant ants share the nest.

Larvae: the offspring of the nest, 1½-3 feet long, looking like fat, white grubs. They are blind and deaf but locate and identify other creatures by vibration and scent. They are always hungry and need an almost constant supply of food, so they are usually found in hatcheries kept by the drones: pits of rotting matter in which they swim, burrow, and feed. Now and then the drones pick one larva and feed and treat it so that it becomes a cow instead of developing normally.

Drone: the adult males, who handle all dealings with the outside world. They lack individual identity, even personal names.

  • Combat: fierce warriors able to use all weapons except bows, and skilled at making what they need. They prefer to walk on all 6 legs, but in combat stand on their hind legs and use the other 4 to wield 2 weapons and 2 shields (making their armor class 2). They are fanatically loyal to a single cow and defend her to the death.
  • Defenses: immune to electrical and cold attacks; fire-based attacks do half damage.
  • Language: their own, and 5% speak Common. They have no written language as such but may communicate with subtle scents and perfumes.

Description: drones are 6 feet long and look like giant weevils, with an extremely long proboscis and many-faceted eyes. They eat plants and meat, and prefer blood as a drink.

The smallest of sprites, atomies live only in secluded glens, in great trees, grassy banks, and the like, where they build balconies in the branches, snug rooms in hollow trunks, underground halls, and so on. They come out at night to gather food, frolic, and pursue the usual activities of such folk. They are sometimes (20%) found with grigs (q.v.).

  • Speed: nimble and fast, they dart in to attack almost before an opponent knows it, gaining 1 on initiative die rolls.
  • Combat: they attack as 3rd-level fighters. Typical weapons: small crossbows (20%), 3” range, 1-3 points of damage; small spears (60%), 1-4 points thrust or thrown (double when used in a diving or charging flight); small swords (40%), equal to a knife, 1-3 points.
  • Spell-like powers (at will, one at a time, one per round, at 5th level): blink, invisibility, pass plant, speak with animals, summon insects.
  • Senses: 90% likely to surprise and only 10% likely to be surprised. Their hearing is twice the human norm, and they have infravision and ultravision at double normal range (120 feet).
  • Languages: their own (a dialect of Sprite), Pixie, and a smattering of Common.

Description: very thin, with long arms, legs, and fingers, long heads, and long, narrow ears. Their features are pointed but quite attractive compared to others of their kind, such as sprites, pixies, and grigs.

The aurumvorax, or golden gorger, is mean, vicious, and always hungry. It lives in open or lightly wooded areas. Though small and badger-like (1½ feet tall, 3 feet long), it weighs over 500 pounds, since its flesh is very dense.

  • Attack: it scuttles out of its burrow, locks its teeth into the victim, and brings 2-8 of its clawed legs into play. Attacking from a hidden den, it surprises 50% of the time.
  • Holding on: once its bite hits (2-8 points), it holds on. Each round after, it automatically does 8 points of biting damage and makes 2-8 more claw attacks of 1-6 points each. The opponent’s dexterity does not count toward armor class against these. Only death unlocks its jaws.
  • Defenses: its very dense hide and bones halve damage from blunt weapons. Small, normal fires do not harm it, and large, magical fires do half damage. Poisons and gases do not harm it at all.
  • Lair: prey dragged into the lair may have carried treasure, and typical items may be mixed in with bones and other remains.

Description: a golden coat, often as shining and bright as real gold. Its 8 legs end in copper-colored claws, and its teeth are coppery too. Its whiskers and mane guard hairs are tawny bronze, and its eyes are silvery with golden pupils.

(References in parentheses are to the Elemental Plane of Fire.)

The azer are a race of humanoids of the Elemental Plane of Fire. They are common there but never seen elsewhere unless summoned. They look much like dwarves with brass-colored skin and flames for hair. Their skin is metallic, which accounts for their high armor class. They wear only kilts or apron-like garments of beaten brass, copper, or bronze.

  • Sizes: common azer (2+1 hit dice) are the weakest, met 90% of the time; those of 3+2 hit dice are next most common (30%); larger azer are less likely (20%); and the strongest (5+4 hit dice) least likely (10%) (percentages as printed). Their gems rise in value with strength: base values 10 gp, 50 gp, 100 gp, and 500 gp respectively.
  • Weapons: broad-bladed javelins doing damage as a spear; in melee, mallet-like weapons equal in all ways to a footman’s mace.
  • Strength: their strength always adjusts hit probability and damage:
BonusBonus
Hit diceStrengthto hitto Damage
2+117+1+1
3+218+1+2
4+318/01-50+1+3
5+418/51-75+2+3
  • Heat: creatures not immune to fire take 2-5 points of damage from being grasped by any azer, and the heat of azer weapons adds +1 damage against them.
  • Cold: azer cannot survive temperatures below 200 degrees F. for more than an hour or so, and cold attacks do double damage to them.

Amaimon: the legendary king of the azer, the largest (9+8 hit dice), strongest (18/00 for +3/+6), and most intelligent of his kind. His 8-32 nobles are only slightly lesser (7+6 hit dice, 18/76-90 for +2/+4). Amaimon has 35% magic resistance and noble azer 25%. Their other powers are not yet known.

Homes: Amaimon’s people live in small groups, typically in a tower worked from the natural basalt of their realm using the plentiful flame nearby. With 20 or more in their home, there are also 2 of the largest normal size, a noble, and 40-70 non-combatant females and young. The defenses probably include air projectors (bellows-like devices) and even special containers to haul water and pour it on attackers.

Nature: unfriendly, taciturn, and lacking compassion. They are greedy, and for clear purple or red gems may agree to reasonable requests. Once given, an azer’s word is a solid bond.
system.hpNote: Printed odds: 2+1 90%, 3+2 30%, 5+4 10% (as printed; MMII p.12).

system.description:
Elephant-like baku are seldom seen in the wild, since most move invisibly among the communities of man. On the Prime Material Plane they prefer semi-tropical forests, where groups of 2-5 are sometimes met. Their true home is the Upper Outer Planes of Neutral. Baku hate evil, and abandon their usual timid, peaceful natures to fight malicious monsters; in this they secretly live among humankind and serve its interests.

  • Attacks: despite its size and bulk it moves quickly. It attacks with a goring butt and two forefoot stomps; the stomps are possible only against man-sized opponents (or four-legged ones under 6 feet tall). Its short, prehensile trunk can hold simple devices such as weapons or wands, so a baku often attacks with some magic weapon or device.
  • Movement: it can become invisible at will and stay so until some action breaks the dweomer, become ethereal and travel that way, and travel astrally.
  • Psionics: 12th-level animal telepathy; 6th-level body control and body equilibrium; 12th-level cell adjustment (printed “fighter cell adjustment”); 12th-level detection of good or evil; 12th-level reduction; and shape alteration.
  • Roar (once every 4 melee rounds): all evil creatures within a 4” radius take 1-8 points of damage and must save vs. paralyzation or flee in panic as from a fear spell cast by a 12th-level magic-user.

Description: an elephant-like head with a trunk only about 4 feet long, and a pair of tusks thrusting up from the lower jaw and curving slightly back. The forelegs are stout and rhino-like, the hind legs rather lion-like. The body is dragon-like, ending in a shortish tail, and the back is scaled with horny plates.

Banderlog are intelligent, baboon-like primates found only in tropical or subtropical forests, living in tribes. They usually live among palms.

  • Possessions: 95% of the time they have none, but now and then they find a piece of jewelry or some other valuable item and keep it.
  • Missiles: coconuts or retch-plant globes (q.v.); coconuts do 2-5 points of damage, with a 30-foot range.
  • Bite: at close quarters, their long canine teeth do 2-5 points of damage.
  • Leaders: always one or more large males with 6-8 hit points per die.

Description: green-skinned with brownish fur. They have a simple language of their own.

Of the many monsters living in the rifts of the Planes of Gehenna, the barghest is surely the most common and one of the most fearsome. Barghests live apart even from each other, each with its own stronghold and servants, ruling as a despot. Now and then a barghest spawns a litter of 6, which is sent to the Prime Material Plane to feed and grow; the survivors eventually return to Gehenna, but while young they must feed on the lives of men. Whelps on the Prime Material Plane are found alone or in pairs, usually near isolated human communities or with bands of goblins.

Forms: they can take the form of large war dogs or wild dogs at will, and are sometimes wrongly called devil-dogs. Their natural shape is much like a large goblin’s, and among goblins they keep it. Goblins recognize and worship them, but other races can hardly tell them from goblins. The goblins fear and serve them, going to great lengths to bring them human sacrifices; in return the barghests kill the goblins’ powerful enemies and generally add to their treasure.

Growth: whelps arriving on the Prime Material Plane are fairly weak, with only 6 (1d8) +6 hit dice.

  • For each energy level of human life they kill and devour they gain 1 hit point; 8 such levels in effect give them another hit die plus 1 more hit point per die. Zero-level humans count as only half an energy level, so exceptional people are better prey.
  • As they gain hit dice they grow stronger: armor class improves by 1 for each extra hit die, and strength grows from 18/00 up to 24, with damage, magic resistance, and intelligence rising to match.
  • At full growth and power a barghest can shift itself to Gehenna, where it seeks out its own reeking valley rift.

Treasure: what they gather in their strongholds on Gehenna is unknown, though rumored to be great. On the Prime Material Plane they own none themselves.

  • Spell-like powers at will (one per round): shape change to dog or goblin-like form, change self, levitation, misdirection, projected image.
  • Once per day each: charm (person or monster), dimension door, emotion.
  • Dog form: it moves at double its normal rate (30” maximum), can pass without trace, and is 75% likely to go unnoticed when still, so it surprises opponents 50% of the time (3 in 6).
  • Defenses: hit only by +1 or better magic weapons. Fire does no damage to them at all, but in dog form they must save against a magical fire attack such as a fireball, flame strike, or meteor swarm; failure hurls them back to their own plane. Weaker barghests returned this way are most likely slain or enslaved by stronger ones, and even if not, they cannot return to the Prime Material Plane without outside help.

Description: as whelps they look much like large goblins, but as they grow larger and stronger the skin darkens from yellow toward a bluish red; adult skin is blue. The eyes glow orange when excited but otherwise look like a goblin’s. In dog form they can look like any typical large dog and are almost (95%) impossible to tell from normal dogs, except that other dogs fear and hate them and attack at every chance.
system.hpNote: Whelps arrive with 6 hit dice +6 (printed “6 (1d8) +6”); every 8 energy levels of human life devoured add a hit die and 1 hit point per die (MMII p.13).

system.description:
Barkburrs: animated plants that arise spontaneously in a wood or forest to defend it. In build they are like limpets: a very hard, woody shell (armor class 0) over a soft, woody interior (armor class 8).

Lair: always met in the lair: one or more oddly shaped trees (the changed remains of past victims; see below), usually on paths through a wood where travellers are likely to pass. Clinging to a tree they are very hard to tell from ordinary burrs. Only druids and rangers have any chance of recognizing one (4% plus 1% per level).

Who they attack: they can sense, within 1 mile, any act against the interests of their forest (basically anything a druid would find abhorrent). They attack any humanoid that comes within 20 feet if it has done such an act within that mile and/or if its alignment has an evil part.

Attack: it leaps suddenly from its tree at a victim up to 20 feet away, always gaining surprise unless recognized. It tries to fix its soft underside to the victim and drive in a sharp, barbed tube (1 point of damage). This whole routine takes a single round and is treated as one attack by a 6 hit dice monster. If it misses, it falls to the ground, where it is nearly helpless (see below).

Lignification: after a successful attack it begins injecting a poison that turns wood-like, for up to 2 rounds plus 1 round per hit die of the barkburr. Each round the victim must save vs. poison or lignification sets in.

  • The victim quickly turns into a small tree: feet become roots, body and legs the trunk, head and arms the branches. The change takes 1 turn and, once started, does not stop even if the barkburr is killed or removed.
  • Most gear close to the body (clothes, armor, etc.) is enclosed in bark, but some (such as a sword, shield, or ring) may be left hanging from a branch or caught in the roots. Of the enclosed gear, everything except magic items, gold, silver, platinum, and gems is absorbed into the wood over 2-7 hours.
  • Once lignification has set in, the barkburr stops injecting and uses the victim as a platform to leap at any other eligible victim within 20 feet. It can inject poison for only 2 rounds plus 1 round per hit die in total each day, and the poison works only when a barkburr injects it.

Removing it (before or after lignification):

  • Killing it: attacks are made against its armor class 0 shell; a missed attack is rolled again against the victim’s armor class.
  • Fire: a cumulative 15% chance per round of dislodging it. Fire on the outer shell does it only 1 point of damage per round, and the victim takes fire damage unless protected.
  • Force: it cannot be pulled straight off, but pulling or pushing it sideways works if 5d10 rolls less than the total strength applied. Success does 1-10 points of damage to the victim as the barbed needle tears out. At most 3 people, including the victim, can work together this way.

On the ground: it cannot leap, crawls at only ½”, and is easily flipped over to show its armor class 8 underside; fire on the underside does normal damage.

Mindless: immune to spells such as charm monster or sleep.

The final change: once lignified, the victim begins a further change into a form that is safe for the wood. This takes as many days as it has levels or hit dice, during which it is a helpless tree (armor class 10, with its original hit points). Then it either stays a tree or quickly changes into a woodland creature or a druid. Roll percentile dice, adding 10 for a creature whose alignment had a neutral part, or 20 for a true neutral:

d%Final form
01-50Ordinary healthy tree (grows to full size within 3 months)
51-70Adult badger
71-80Adult giant weasel
81-90Treant (7 hit dice)
91+Druid (1st level; strength, intelligence, dexterity, and constitution as before; wisdom 14, charisma 16)

A creature taking any final form other than druid has no wish at all to leave the wood and resists attempts to make it.

Restoring a victim: once the change is complete, only a full wish restores the original form. While it is still under way, the victim can be restored by wish, limited wish, polymorph other, or turn wood or plant growth (cast backwards); neutralize poison has a 30% chance plus 5% per level of the caster. Any of these spells (including neutralize poison) cast within the first turn stops the initial lignification. Cure disease, remove curse, dispel magic, etc. have no effect. A restored creature has lost 1 level or hit die for each full day spent as a tree.

Growth: barkburrs grow by absorbing their victims’ energy levels and reproduce by budding. There is a 50% chance that a 6 hit dice barkburr has 1 or 2 offspring of 2 hit dice budding from it, which attack on their own.

Direburrs: unwholesome woods produce direburrs, which attack any humanoid coming within 20 feet whatever its past actions or alignment. Their attacks work like a barkburr’s, except that a lignified victim always ends as a dry, dead, leafless tree that nothing short of a full wish can restore. In all other ways they are identical to barkburrs.

Basidironds are many-stemmed fungus monsters with woody, leathery bodies of orange color. Their cone-shaped tops look much like upside-down umbrellas, sooty black inside.

  • Attack: they lash forward with their spore-ejecting caps. A hit does 2-8 points of damage, and the victim must save vs. poison or have spores clog its breathing passages; it smothers in 2-5 rounds unless cure disease (or the like) is cast.
  • Hallucinatory spores: released only when standing quietly. Each basidirond’s spores form an invisible cloud around it with a radius of 20-35” (as printed). Each creature in the cloud must save vs. poison each round or begin hallucinating, which lasts while it stays in the cloud and for 1-4 rounds after it leaves.
  • Mindless: all mental attacks, including charm monster, hold monster, and similar spells, have no effect.
  • Cold: does no damage, but slows it to 50% of normal movement and stops its spore attacks.

Typical hallucinations (d8):

d8The victim believesand so
1he is in a swampstrips off armor to keep from sinking
2spiders are attackingstrikes at the floor to kill them
3he has shrunkshouts for help to return to normal size
4the item he holds is a viperdrops it and leaps back to avoid its attack
5he is suffocatingruns gasping in random directions to breathe
6his companions are diseasedstays more than 10 feet from them
7he is meltingstands howling and “holding himself together”
8a leech is on his backtears off anything worn on his back and attacks it

The greater basilisk is a cousin of the more common reptilian horror, the ordinary basilisk. Both have 8 legs and move slowly. Its fearsome abilities make it a common guardian for treasure.

  • Attacks: it raises its forebody to strike with its sharp claws and bite with its toothy jaws. The claws carry a weak poison (saves at +4).
  • Breath: its foul breath is poisonous too: every creature within 5 feet of its mouth, even for a moment, must save vs. poison (at +2) or die. Check each round of exposure.
  • Gaze: worst of all, its gaze turns victims to stone, out to 50 feet. Its oddly shaped eyes are nearsighted, though, so it cannot see its own gaze beyond 10 feet: even with a polished reflector in good light, there is only a 10% chance of it being petrified unless the reflector is within 10 feet.
  • Sight: like its smaller cousin, it sees into the Astral and Ethereal Planes.

Its normal home is said to be the Elemental Plane of Earth. Its coloring is much the same as other basilisks’.

Mobat: rarely found, usually in warm climates where large caverns give shelter and food is plentiful. Mobats eat anything but prefer warm-blooded prey, which they bite to death with their fangs. They have a dim, evil intelligence and a liking for shiny objects.

  • Flight: with a wingspread of 12-16 feet they need a large area to take off, but once airborne their sonics let them fly through narrow places, even in total darkness. Their flight is fast and fairly silent, so they surprise prey 50% of the time.
  • Screech: a piercing screech, always used if the prey resists, so painful that victims within 20 feet try to cover their ears instead of fighting unless they save vs. paralysis.
  • Armor class: 2 when flying freely, since their reflexes and sonics let them dodge attacks; 7 in crowded flying conditions; 10 out of the air.

Ordinary bat: many kinds are included here. They attack only if cornered and forced to. Startled bats become frightened and confused, swarming and flying into things, which puts out torches, confuses spell casting, and so on. Their sonar lets them fly in total darkness. In good flying conditions their armor class improves from 8 to 4. Some large caverns may hold 1,000 or more bats.

In good flying conditions their armor class improves from 8 to 4. Some large caverns may hold 1,000 or more bats.

The fire bat comes from the Elemental Plane of Fire. Fairly common there, it seldom appears on the Prime Material Plane. Its bat-like body is about 2 feet long with a wingspan approaching 4 feet; its whole body is aflame and radiates a temperature of several hundred degrees. Its skin is tough and leathery, and even the fairly thin wings are hard to pierce.

  • Bite: its mouth is small but its fangs are razor-sharp; the burning hurts more than the blood drain (2-8 points of damage per round in all).
  • Attaching: fire bats swoop in, trying to attach themselves. Once attached they need no further attack rolls and automatically burn and bleed the victim for 3 rounds in all (the round they hit plus 2 more). Then the sated bat drops off and returns to its lair. If the victim dies sooner, unsated bats attack others to finish feeding, but never drain more than 3 rounds’ worth of blood, whether from 1, 2, or 3 victims.
  • Pack tactics: every member of the victim’s group is attacked by about the same number of bats. If 12 attack 4 victims, 3 attack each; if 12 attack 9, then 6 victims get 1 bat each and 3 unlucky ones (chosen at random) get 2 each.
  • Retreat: if their number falls below 25% of the starting force (from losses or sated bats returning), all withdraw at once and try to escape to the lair. Cornered in the lair, they fight ferociously to the death.
  • Senses: advanced sonar and infravision let them detect and attack invisible targets without penalty. Unlike ordinary bats, sunlight and other bright light do not harm them, and they see well within normal vision range.
  • Death: a burst of flame envelops a dying fire bat and carries its body back to the Elemental Plane of Fire, where it is reborn.
  • Allies: they are allies of fire elementals and never attack them.

Colonies: usually 1-2 dozen, lairing only in very hot places such as volcanoes, near hot springs, and on their own plane. How they reach the Prime Material Plane is a mystery; some sages think a few fire bats sometimes come along when fire elementals are summoned, and woe to the conjurer, for they are not under the mage’s control at all. They reproduce by splitting in two after gorging on blood, so even one escaping into this plane can start a colony and replace losses, but they instinctively limit their numbers to the food available.

Lair: rocky and cave-like, with many exits and maze-like passages but only one large, easily noticed entrance. Treasure is likely to be gems and jewelry, since they love sparkling stones and especially prize rubies, jacinths, and carnelians. If a hunting pack is destroyed, 1 or 2 young fire bats (under a year old) may be found in the lair, each with half the hit dice and damage per attack of an adult.

Movement: an awkward hop-walk on the ground, or (better) flight. They truly fly rather than glide, since hot internal gases make them very light. They can glide through hot liquids (lava and magma included) at flying speed.

Water: water frightens them. It takes at least 10 gallons of cool water to put out one fire bat’s flames, and it then needs 10 rounds to dry before it can ignite again. Meanwhile it cannot fly and does only 1-4 points of damage if it hits.

Like all bears, these dwellers of subarctic and temperate regions eat both plants and meat.

  • Hug: a paw hit of 18 or better means a hug, doing 3-18 points of extra damage.
  • Toughness: these aggressive animals keep fighting for 2-5 rounds after being brought to 0 to −12 hit points; greater damage kills them at once.

All kinds of giant bees are like their ordinary small cousins. Honeybees have hives; bumblebees have nests.

  • In the lair: a hive holds 20 times the workers rolled and 3-12 soldiers, plus a non-combatant queen and 2-5 non-combatant drones. A bumblebee burrow or nest holds 7-12 giant bumblebees and a fighting queen of 8+6 hit dice whose sting does 1-8 points of damage.
  • Poison: normal for workers; stronger for soldiers and bumblebees (−1 to save), and −2 for a queen bumblebee. A successful save vs. poison means 2-8 points of extra damage; failure means an extra 5-20, +1 for soldiers and bumblebees and +2 for queen bees.

Hive products: honey is found in proportional amounts. Bee “bread” is excellent food, equal to iron rations. “Royal jelly” is found only 20% of the time and equals 2-5 potions of extra-healing, each with the side effect of cure disease. It can also be made into 2-5 jars of unguent against aging, which keeps a youthful look for up to 1 year; charisma is unaffected by age while the unguent is used without a break. Rich and noble women prize it greatly, and each jar fetches 3,000-8,000 gp on the open market.

This monstrous insect of temperate regions is especially dreaded because it often disguises itself, from wearing the shells of other giant beetles to sticking rubbish to itself with a glue of earth and saliva. It is usually met outdoors, but giant death watch beetles have also invaded underground areas in search of food.

  • Bite: its normal attack, with its great mandibles.
  • Death click: before attacking it makes a clicking sound with its shell, like a drum or gong, whose vibrations are deadly. After 1 round, every creature within 30 feet must save vs. death magic or die; those who save take 5-20 points of damage. The sound seems to come from everywhere, so it is 90% unlikely that the beetle can be located by it. The effort is so great that it can click only once every 2-5 hours.
  • Treasure: it moves often in search of food, so it is unlikely to have treasure except perhaps an item stuck on its back as camouflage. Even if it stays in one place for a long time (10% chance), only the belongings of its victims will be in the area.

The slicer beetle is like a stag beetle (q.v.) without horns, with razor-sharp mandibles.

  • Severing: an attack roll of 19 or 20 means it has nipped off an opponent’s arm or leg.
  • Fleeing: if the fight goes against it, it grabs any food handy (such as lost limbs) and flees.
  • Lair: usually many bones and 1-6 kinds of normal weapons; possibly magic weapons (25% chance) or magic boots (10% chance).

Mismatched pairs: boots or gauntlets found in the lair are probably not a matched pair (only a 5% chance that they match). Trying to identify an unmatched pair gives standard (but false) results. The effects of mismatched items can be unpredictable and do not begin until the wearer is in an encounter, adventure, or other normal but possibly dangerous activity.

Each boot alone:

BootsEffect
Dancing1 foot taps and shuffles
Elvenkind1 foot tip-toes
Levitation1 side of the body tends to rise
Speed1 foot takes 2 steps to the other’s 1
Striding and springing1 foot either goose-steps or makes hops of 3-4 feet

Each gauntlet alone:

GauntletsEffect
Dexterity1 hand tends to attempt pocket-picking (base 50% chance of success)
Fumbling1 hand tends to drop things (50% chance)
Ogre power1 hand sloppily uses more force than intended; in combat, no strength modifiers apply
Swimming and climbing1 hand tends to wave about at random

Behemoths are huge relatives of the hippo, found only in deep rivers and lakes in tropical regions. They have huge mouths with great tushes like a hippopotamus’s, and tusks pointing outward from each side of the mouth, used to uproot water plants and roots.

  • Groups: a bull usually has 1-3 cows with him.
  • Damage: bulls do 6-24 points of damage, cows 4-16.
  • Temper: bulls are always aggressive; cows only if a calf is present (25% chance per cow). If a swimmer enters their territory, or a boat or canoe passes overhead, the aggressive animals move to attack. There is a 50% chance the bull rises under a boat or canoe and overturns it.
  • Movement: in water they sink and run along the bottom, and can stay under for up to 30 minutes.

The behir is a snake-like reptile with a dozen legs that let it move quite fast and climb well (at half speed). It can fold its legs against its long, narrow body and slither like a snake if it wishes. Its head is more like a crocodile’s than a snake’s.

  • Attacks: a bite, and looping its body around a victim to squeeze. If the squeeze succeeds, the victim takes 6 talon attacks the next round.
  • Lightning: once every 10 rounds it can discharge a 20-foot stroke of electricity that does 24 points of damage, or half if the victim saves vs. breath weapon.
  • Swallowing: on a 20 it swallows prey whole, with effects like a purple worm’s.
  • Treasure: since it sometimes swallows prey whole, there is a 10% chance of small valuables inside it: gems (10×Q, 60%), jewelry (1-8 pieces, 30%), and a small magic item of indigestible nature (10%).

Description: very hard, band-like scales, ultramarine to deep blue with gray-brown bands. The belly is pale blue.

The bloodthorn, or vampire vine, grows alone in forests. It has 5-12 tendrils 7-12 feet long that can lash out 5-7 feet to attack prey. Each tendril bears many sharp, hollow thorns.

  • Drain: any hit drains fluid equal to 25% of the victim’s total starting hit points.
  • Armor: tendrils armor class 4, stalk/trunk armor class 3.
  • Severing: each tendril takes 5-10 points of damage to cut off; this does not harm the main plant.

Attack data:

Hit diceSizeNo. of tendrilsRangeTendril valueAttacks as
5-16Average55’5-6 hp3 HD monster
17-25Large86’7-8 hp4 HD monster
26-30Large127’9-10 hp5 HD monster

Description: bloodthorns grow among hornwood trees and look very like them; only 10% are found among other kinds of plants. The trunk is smooth, yellowish to brown. The pointed, two-lobed leaves are smaller than a hornwood’s, and the vampire tendrils look much like the ordinary vines and creepers growing on other trees.
system.hpNote: Hit dice 5-16: 5 tendrils, attacks as 3 HD; 17-25: 8 tendrils, as 4 HD; 26-30: 12 tendrils, as 5 HD (MMII p.18). Set Attacks as HD to match.

system.description:
The boalisk is a tropical snake almost identical in every way to the constrictor snake (q.v.), but with a gaze attack. In tropical lands, constrictors may be accompanied by boalisks (25%), and vice versa. A boalisk cannot constrict more than 1 victim at a time.

  • Gaze: used each round besides its normal bite and constriction, and usually (75%) aimed at its opponent in melee, if any. Any creature that meets the gaze (shown by failing a saving throw vs. petrification) catches a rotting disease identical to that from a mummy’s touch (q.v.). With complete surprise (1-2 on d6), someone has met the gaze and gets no saving throw.
  • Looking away: a character who refuses to look at the boalisk avoids the gaze automatically, but is 20% easier to hit (4 penalty to armor class) while doing so.

A bodak is a human changed into a monster after venturing somewhere in the Abyssal Planes where mortals were not meant to go. The evil of the person’s nature and exposure to demonic substances set off a terrible change from man to bodak.

Bodaks are very rare, since they stay in the Abyssal Planes unless called into service by some evil or foolish magic-user; a few are found on the Prime Material Plane. A summoned bodak’s cunning lets it try to take control of the summoner, sometimes with a very high intelligence factor (roll d20 for the cunning it brings to bear; the factor for control can be as high as 20).

  • Weapons: it seldom uses one, though 90% have one, of a type the DM decides.
  • Death gaze: meeting its gaze, up to 30 feet away, causes death unless a save vs. death magic is made.
  • Defenses: struck only by +1 or better magic weapons or cold-wrought iron ones. Immune to spells such as charm, hold, sleep, and slow, and to poison; otherwise affected by attacks as demons are.
  • Sunlight: direct sunlight does 1 point of damage per round.
  • Senses and speech: ultravision and infravision. They speak the tongue of demons and demonic creatures well, but remember few words of human speech.

Description: sexless, with dark gray, pearly skin and a hairless, muscular body. The head is long, with oddly distorted features, and the eyes are large, milky-white, upright ovals.

A boggart is the young form of a will-o-wisp (q.v.). It can appear as a small demi-human, a humanoid, or a will-o-wisp as it wishes. It has more forms than the adult but can hold any one for only 10 or 12 rounds before losing control and shifting to another, though it can change on purpose whenever it likes.

Feeding: it needs both meat and life force to grow up, so it uses human-like forms to lure human-like adults and larger meat-eaters. Once the would-be predator is trapped or ambushed, it becomes the boggart’s prey: the boggart devours its life force and its body too, so no resurrection is possible.

  • Touch: 2-12 points of electrical damage.
  • Bolt: every other round it can discharge a bolt of the same energy up to 10 feet; a save vs. breath weapon halves the damage (1-6 points).
  • Confusion (once per day): its most devious attack. It makes noise (yelling, screaming, shouting, whistling, banging, pounding, or thumping) for 2 rounds in a row. All creatures within 30 feet that can hear it clearly must save vs. spell or be confused for 7-12 melee rounds; covering the ears does not help. Only a successful attack on the boggart stops the noise partway through. If several boggarts make the noise, all must be stopped, and saves are at −1 for each boggart that completes 2 rounds of noise.
  • Invisibility: up to 12 rounds, in any form. Noise does not end it, so an invisible boggart can make a horrible racket.
  • Defenses: as with a will-o-wisp, any weapon harms this young form, but all spells except magic missile, maze, and protection from evil are useless against it.
  • Escape: at 5 or fewer hit points it uses all its wits and devices to escape, usually by turning invisible and running, or floating in will-o-wisp form over ground its enemies cannot cross.
  • Other powers: a limited form of ESP lets it understand and speak all languages, though only in a very basic way. In glowing will-o-wisp form it can pass through solid non-living objects, even stone walls up to 2 feet thick, but not metals, which ground its electrical energy. In human-like form it has normal infravision.

Description: as a demi-human it usually looks like a small halfling or young gnome; as a humanoid, usually a goblin imp, young xvart, or norker neut. As a will-o-wisp it is smaller and brighter than an adult.

Boggles are vaguely humanoid creatures 3 feet tall, blackish-blue to dark gray. All have large, bulbous heads, but the rest of the body is out of proportion and differs from one to the next (large noses, arms of different lengths, spindly legs, and so on). Their society is loosely tribal. They whine and gibber a lot when dealing with others. Outside their lair they are rather cowardly and all tend to be thieves; in the lair they are aggressive and greedy.

  • Oil: they ooze a thick, non-flammable black oil from their pores. Anyone treading on it (except creatures adapted, like boggles, to climbing on slick surfaces) must roll their dexterity or lower on d20 or fall, and then spends an entire round getting up. Boggles try to steal from a fallen character, needing a successful roll vs. armor class 5 to steal any one item from a fallen or stunned character.
  • Body: a rubbery, partly elastic hide; they can stretch to twice their length or shrink to half their size. Their slippery, resilient hide reduces all weapon damage by 1 point per die.
  • Other powers: they resist fire naturally (as the ring) and can spider climb at will. They like to cling to ceilings and drop on unwary characters, getting 2 extra claw attacks (as cats do).
  • Dimension door: at will, up to 3”, through any complete frame such as a hole, a door frame, grillwork, between a character’s legs, and so on. They can reach through a hole and have their hands come out elsewhere, grabbing or striking a character from another side. Their lairs are often full of holes or look like grillwork, and the main nest can be reached only by dimension door or other magic.
  • Smell: exceptionally keen, even detecting invisible creatures. Other races use them as guards and watchers for this; when they sense intruders they set up a high-pitched keening wail to warn their masters.

The gigantic boobrie is like a smaller, marsh-dwelling relative of the roc. Besides the huge marsh catfish, its favorite foods are humans and sheep; if those are not available it eats snakes, lizards, and even spiders of enough size. Its long legs let it run fast and move easily through swampy ground, but its claws are fairly weak, and its flight is slow.

  • Attack: mainly with its long, hooked beak.
  • Poison: totally immune to all forms.
  • Surprise: gained by crouching in tall grass.
  • Pairs: 2 met together are either a mated pair of adults (at least 5 hit points per die) or a pair of young (4 or fewer points per die).

Description: like a huge heron with a beak between a heron’s and an eagle’s, with a row of small, sharp teeth along its edges.
system.hpNote: A pair met together are mated adults (at least 5 points per die) or young (4 or fewer) (MMII p.20).

system.description:
This small worm, only 1 inch long, is much feared by magic-users because it is drawn to paper in all forms. It can smell scrolls, maps, arcane tomes, and spell books 60 feet away. It is normally dull gray, but its chameleon-like ability lets it blend instinctively into any background. Its armor class comes from its speed and agility; motionless, it is AC 9.

  • Surprise: 95% at first, or 50% if the victim can see invisible things. These chances apply even to creatures normally hard to surprise (such as rangers and monks), because of its small size, speed (very great for its size), and harmless nature.
  • Being noticed: after gaining surprise it may be spotted (25%) on the outside of a victim’s leg or pack; otherwise it goes unnoticed unless the victim carrying the paper hears its noisy munching (base 50% chance per round).
  • Feeding: it is motionless while feeding until attacked. After any 1 attack it flees if it can, first jumping 10 feet and then crawling back to its lair at top speed.
  • Damage: it is always drawn to the largest amount of paper nearby. It burrows through dead wood or leather at 3 inches per round (as printed, “3 inch rate”), and through a leather scroll case or pack in 1 segment, but cannot digest living matter of any kind. It destroys spell books and scrolls at 1 spell level per round (5 rounds for a scroll of one 5th-level spell).
  • Lair: always a library or storeroom of some kind, in use or long forgotten. There is a 30% chance that undamaged paper items remain: a map (20%), scroll (30%), arcane work (of magic-user level 5-10, 20%), or normal spell book (of magic-user level 1-8, 10%). Spell books of either kind should suit the level rolled, but will be 0-90% destroyed by the worms (d10−1).

A bowler is a boulder-like creature of caves and similar places, where the rocks give it natural camouflage. It has no eyes but is extremely sensitive to sound, vibration, and smell.

  • Attack: sensing prey, it rolls toward it, gaining 1” of speed per round of combat up to a maximum of 15”, and rolls over its victims to crush them. The vibrations of its own movement let it detect and avoid walls, pits, and so on.
  • Stealth: it rolls quietly at first, so there is only a 50% chance that prey notices it before it is within 40 feet.
  • Weight: about 28 pounds per hit point.
  • Feeding: after crushing prey it rolls back onto the victim, and a mouth-like opening devours the flesh and bone, shell, etc.
  • Gem: each has at its core a single beryl worth a base of 10 gp.

Bowlers may be distant relatives of mimics (q.v.).

The buckawn are a race of woodland demi-humans of the brownie type, but less friendly and far trickier than their cousins. They shun humans and do not usually associate with brownies either. They are usually armed with small daggers and quivers of darts, which have been known to be drugged or poisoned when their targets had annoyed or offended them.

  • Spell-like powers at will (one at a time, one per round, at 6th level): audible glamer, change self, dancing lights, invisibility.
  • Once per day each (at 6th level): entangle, pass without trace, summon insects, trip.
  • Senses: very superior; never surprised. They see into the infrared and ultraviolet and detect invisible creatures with no difficulty. Their hearing is so keen that anyone’s chance to move silently near them is halved.
  • Stealth: in 1 turn they can hide in foliage or shadows, or move silently, with 80% probability.
  • Languages: the brownie tongue and a smattering of the languages of pixies, satyrs, and sprites.

Description: much like slender brownies with dusky skin, dressed in russets and greens.

Domestic and wild cats are closely related, and most kinds can interbreed. Domestic cats are found nearly everywhere in temperate to tropical lands, and some have “gone wild”. Wild cats range from subarctic to tropical regions.

  • Attacks: the smaller domestic cat has only 1 effective forepaw claw attack, the larger wild cat 2.
  • Rear claws: both gain rear claw rakes if their forepaw attacks hit: 1-2 points of damage from a domestic cat, 1-2/1-2 from a wild cat.
  • Surprise: both surprise prey on 3 in 6 and are surprised only on 1 in 6.
  • Climbing: both climb well and can move up and along tree limbs at half their normal rate.
  • Domestic cats do not normally attack medium or large creatures.

Domestic and wild cats are closely related, and most kinds can interbreed. Domestic cats are found nearly everywhere in temperate to tropical lands, and some have “gone wild”. Wild cats range from subarctic to tropical regions.

  • Attacks: the smaller domestic cat has only 1 effective forepaw claw attack, the larger wild cat 2.
  • Rear claws: both gain rear claw rakes if their forepaw attacks hit: 1-2 points of damage from a domestic cat, 1-2/1-2 from a wild cat.
  • Surprise: both surprise prey on 3 in 6 and are surprised only on 1 in 6.
  • Climbing: both climb well and can move up and along tree limbs at half their normal rate.
  • Domestic cats do not normally attack medium or large creatures.

system.psionicText: Nil (immune to psionics) Attack/Defense Modes: Nil/nil
system.description:
The cat lord, or master cat, rules all felines, from domestic cats through the giant lynx to the largest smilodons. Some believe him a minor deity; others claim he is a malign creature of evil. Those who truly understand cats know he is neither good nor evil, but concerned only with cat-things. He roams the Prime Material, Astral, and Ethereal Planes.

Abilities in human terms: strength 20, intelligence 19, wisdom 17, dexterity 23, constitution 16. Charisma varies: 25 to all felines, 22 to were-felines, 18 to partial felines and cat lovers, 13 to those indifferent to cats, and 7 to those who fear cats.

  • Movement: besides rapid movement, he can spring 30 feet forward, back, or up, and like most cats always lands on his feet, instantly ready for whatever comes next.
  • Feline form attacks: great forepaw claws and huge teeth, magically sharp, inflicting terrible wounds. His speed and ferocity mean he always has initiative in normal circumstances.
  • Spit: in feline form, his melee routine also includes a spit, used only before biting, every other round, at 1 opponent, with no to-hit roll. The target must save vs. spells or be blinded until cure blindness or dispel magic is cast on it. Like all his powers, it is at 19th level of ability (needed, for example, when casting dispel magic to remove the blindness).
  • Yowl: instead of a melee attack, a piercing howl that stuns all creatures within 19 feet, except other felines, unless they save vs. spells. Stunned creatures cannot move, attack, or defend for 1-4 rounds.
  • Human form: now and then he takes human form as either a 19th-level thief or a 13th-level monk, with all the abilities of the chosen profession (needing no tools), but with his movement rate (27”) and armor class (−9) unchanged.
  • Spell-like powers (one at a time, one per round): astral travel (1 per day), blur, detect evil/good, dimension door (9 per day), etherealness (2 per day), haste (2 per day; not in human monk form), hypnotism, improved invisibility, speed (as the potion), telepathy, teleport without error (1 per day).
  • Healing: he can lick his wounds 9 times per day, each lick restoring 2d4 points of damage.
  • Senses: hearing and vision 5 times human normal, ultravision of twice normal power, and infravision of 5 times normal (300 feet). He always moves with 99% silence.
  • Languages: all feline tongues; he can also talk with caterwauls, chimeras, displacer beasts, dragonnes, sea lions, kamadans, tabaxi, and weretigers of all sorts. In human form he speaks Common and the secret language of neutrals. He can communicate telepathically with nearly any creature if needed.

Summoning: he can summon felines at will. Summoned felines, even were-cats, are completely loyal and obey his every command. Any feline instantly recognizes him, even in human form.

Description: a black cat, a black panther, a pale human with dark hair, or a dark-skinned human. In human form he always wears black with gold and gems in feline colors. Other than cats, his only known friend is the deity Xan Yae.

Now and then a huge catfish survives to grow larger still into a giant of its kind. Catfish of all kinds live in fresh water in warm-temperate to tropical lands; giant ones only in very large rivers or the lakes they feed or drain. They are mainly bottom-feeding scavengers, but aggressive enough to attack any creature they see as food and small enough to swallow.

  • Swallowing: a 7 hit dice catfish can swallow a gnome or halfling whole, 8 HD a dwarf, 9 HD a small human or elf, and 10 HD a large human. Being swallowed does normal damage and traps the victim inside, where it takes 1 point of damage per round from digestive juices and has a 5% chance per round of suffocating.
  • Escape: only a victim with a sharp-edged or pointed weapon in hand when swallowed has any chance. Its attacks inside are handled normally; when the internal damage equals 50% of the fish’s total hit points, it has cut or stabbed its way out. Attacks that pierce the catfish from outside have a 20% chance of doing the same damage to a swallowed victim.
  • Feelers: many spiny, tentacle-like “whiskers” around the corners of the mouth secrete a strong poison. Besides biting, it lashes its head from side to side, attacking up to 2 other opponents with them. A creature hit takes 2-8 points of poison damage, or 1-4 if it saves vs. poison.

The giant cave cricket is basically harmless, usually just a noisy insect pest. It is like a normal cricket except for its size and its pale gray or white color, and eats plants, cloth, paper, and even fungi.

  • Chirping: anyone within 20 feet when it starts cannot hear speech, and there is a 2 in 6 chance of drawing every predator within hearing (about 90”).
  • Leaping: a frightened cricket has a 1 in 6 chance of leaping on a character within hopping distance, accidentally doing 1-4 points of damage.
  • Kicking: those that do not land on anyone may still accidentally kick someone within 10 feet with their powerful hind legs, at normal to-hit chances. Roll which character each one attacks, then roll for kick hits.

Cave fishers are hard-shelled, many-legged creatures that live by trapping animals in the underground world.

  • Filament: a super-strong, very sticky line 60 feet long, tipped with a powerful sticky sucker, shot from the proboscis with great speed and accuracy (striking as a 6 hit dice monster). It reels in prey at 15 feet per round with a complex natural winch housed in an armored bulge behind its head, and can pull in prey of up to 400 pounds (4,000 gp weight).
  • The adhesive: coats the whole filament. It is dissolved by liquids with a high alcohol content, or by a cave fisher’s blood, which is rich in alcohol. The filament can be cut only by a +1 or better edged weapon, and is so thin that there is only a 20% chance of noticing it within 10 feet, and none beyond.
  • Killing: 2 of its 8 legs end in powerful pincers, with which it kills and cuts up its prey into pieces it can eat. The other 6 cement it to the rock of its hiding place with the same adhesive.
  • Hunting: it hides on a ledge over a well-used path and strings filaments across good spots for catching small flying creatures. If something comes within range without blundering into a filament, it silently reels the filament in (1 round) and fires at the victim, trying again as long as the prey stays in range.

Lair: its ledge or niche is usually covered with its victims’ bones and belongings. If local animals learn to avoid it, it dissolves its bindings and crawls to a new area where prey is less wary.

These slug-like creatures live in colonies in caves, in cyst-like burrows in the stone walls. When prey passes they strike out, usually from both sides of the passage, at a range of 3-5 feet, and must pull back into the cyst to recoil for another strike.

  • Armor: the body is armor class 5, but it is so fast that there is only a 1 in 20 chance of hitting one while it is exposed.

Description: brownish-gray skin; knobby, splotched heads; dull brown, bulging eyes. They look like rock.

Huge centipedes: simply smaller versions of giant centipedes, like them in most ways, including a weak poison (+4 on saves). Being smaller, failure to save means the victim takes 4-16 points of damage rather than dying. Huge centipedes make their own saving throws at −2.

Megalo-centipedes: colossal cousins of giant centipedes with a deadly poison: saves against it are at normal chances. If the save succeeds, the poison only burns the skin instead of entering the blood, and the victim takes just 1-8 points of damage. Megalo-centipedes make normal saving throws themselves.

Huge centipedes: simply smaller versions of giant centipedes, like them in most ways, including a weak poison (+4 on saves). Being smaller, failure to save means the victim takes 4-16 points of damage rather than dying. Huge centipedes make their own saving throws at −2.

Megalo-centipedes: colossal cousins of giant centipedes with a deadly poison: saves against it are at normal chances. If the save succeeds, the poison only burns the skin instead of entering the blood, and the victim takes just 1-8 points of damage. Megalo-centipedes make normal saving throws themselves.

The cheetah lives on tropical plains and grasslands. It is the only cat with claws that do not retract, and, if taken young, the only large cat that can be trained and tamed to be trustworthy at all times. (Lion lovers say cheetahs are no more faithful than lions; the debate is unresolved.) Like all cats, cheetahs are meat-eaters that stalk and kill game to live.

  • Surprise: their camouflage coloring and hunting skill let them surprise on 3 in 6.
  • Sprint: they can burst into triple speed, a 45” sprint, for 3 rounds, then must rest 3 turns before sprinting again.
  • Leaping: 10 feet up or as much as 20 feet forward.
  • Rake: if both forepaws hit, it gets 2 extra raking attacks with its rear claws.
  • Lair: if only 1 or 2 are rolled, there are also 1-4 cubs, which have no effective attack. The parents will give their lives defending them, attacking at +2 to hit and damage (printed “2”).

The choke creeper, or strangler vine, seems to be a cousin of the hangman tree (q.v.). Its stem grows nearly as thick as a tree trunk and may be over 100 feet long, with a score or more of creeping, strangling vines.

  • Hit points: small choke creepers have only 1 point per hit die, and huge old ones 8 per die (200 points).
  • Vines: typically 8 strangler vines along each 10-foot section of the plant and twice that number at its end, usually fanning out to cover all directions. Each vine branch is 9-16 feet long and creeps 5 feet per round with flexible tendrils. Each takes 2-16 points of damage to cut off (the larger the plant, the hardier the vine), and damage to the vines does not affect the main plant.
  • Attack: the vines are drawn to light and movement. Since they look like normal plants, they can usually grab victims unawares. Held victims are squeezed for 1-4 points of damage per turn, and each turn of squeezing there is a 10% chance the vine uses a strangling grip, killing the victim at the end of the next round.
  • Fire: small, torch-sized fires do not affect it, but a hot fire, such as burning oil, does normal damage and makes the mobile vines move away.
  • Cold: 1 point of damage per damage die, and the struck sections are immobilized for 2-5 rounds.
  • Electricity: no damage, but the vines move at double speed for 2-5 rounds.
system.hpNote: Small choke creepers have only 1 point per hit die, huge old ones 8 per die (200 points) (MMII p.25). Vines are separate (2-16 points each to cut off).

system.description:
Cloakers are unearthly shadow-dwellers, normally met only in deep, dark caverns far below the earth. They are highly intelligent, but their thinking is alien to most races, and usually only magic-users can communicate with them.

Appearance: like a large semicircular cloak or blanket, with two claw-like limbs at the tips and a long, mace-like tail. Black eyespots cover its back like buttons on a cloak, and with the tail hidden it is almost impossible to tell from a real cloak. In the middle of its front are a large gaping mouth and 2 glowing red eyespots. All its eyes mean it cannot be surprised from behind. It is light and can fly at 15” or creep along walls with its claws at 1”.

  • Wrapping: it flies at a character and wraps the victim in its folds, pinning the arms so the victim cannot strike back. It can then bite the victim’s belly or back for 1-4 points plus the victim’s unadjusted armor class.
  • Tail: it can normally strike with its tail twice per round for 1-6 points each, often to fend off attackers while it kills the wrapped victim. The tail is armor class 1 and takes 16 points of damage to cut off.
  • Attacking it while wrapped: attacks on it while it is wrapped around a victim do half damage to the victim and half to the cloaker. Area attacks such as fire spells do full damage to both.

Moaning: cloakers constantly give off a subsonic moaning, blocked by stone. They cannot bite and moan at the same time. The moaning can be used at four levels of intensity, as the monster wishes; neutralize poison neutralizes its effects.

  1. Unease: causes nervousness and unease in all within 80 feet; those who listen for more than 6 turns in a row have their minds numbed and become zombie-like. Anyone within hearing fights at −2 to hit and damage.
  2. Fear: as a fear spell within 30 feet. Characters must save vs. spells or run in terror for 2 rounds.
  3. Nausea: nausea and weakness much like a stinking cloud, in a cone 30 feet long and 20 feet wide at the open end, lasting 2-5 rounds. Anyone in it must save vs. poison or be helpless with nausea.
  4. Hold: as a hold person spell on 1 target at a time, up to 30 feet, lasting 5 rounds.

Shadows: it can manipulate shadows to hide in or to obscure its opponent’s sight, raising its own armor class to 1. Its control is precise enough to make shadowy images, even shadow doubles of itself real enough to fool attackers (treat as a mirror image spell). A light spell blinds it and stops its shadow shifting.

The cooshee, or elven dog, is found only in woods or meadows frequented by elves, most often with sylvan elves. Elven dogs avoid other kinds of dogs. Their bark carries for a mile or more, but they bark only to warn their masters.

  • Speed: it moves quickly, and even faster (21”) when chasing something in a straight line.
  • Knockdown: it strikes with its huge forepaws to knock two-legged creatures of human size or smaller off their feet; this is resolved normally before its bite. Prone opponents are easier to bite (no dexterity bonus, +2 to hit).
  • Hiding: its coloring and silent movement let it hide easily in brush or woods (75% chance).

Description: the size of the largest common dog, with a greenish coat with brown spots. It typically weighs over 168 pounds and often reaches 310. Its huge paws have heavy claws, and its curled tail is held above the back.

Giant cranes live in the same places as ordinary cranes, herons, bitterns, and similar wading birds, hunting large fish in marshes and swamps, along riverbanks, and at lake edges. They are generally not aggressive, but protect their mates, young, and nesting areas.

  • Young: if more than 10 are met, each bird beyond 10 is 50% likely to be immature.
  • Flocks: if 20 are met, there is a 50% chance they are part of a great flock of 31-50 (1d20+30), of which 3-12 are half-grown fledglings.

The crysmal is a crystalline creature from the Elemental Plane of Earth, sometimes met on the Prime Material Plane, but only in underground places rich in the mineral formations it eats. It especially likes quartz, beryl, corundum, and carbon crystals, and will often attack to get them. Inside each crysmal are 4-32 undigested rough gems. Crysmals hate xorn (q.v.), which prey on them.

  • Armor: against edged and piercing weapons its effective armor class is −4; against blunt metal weapons only 0.
  • Movement: its build makes it slow; its 4-6 faceted walking limbs allow only stumping, jerky movement. It can move through solid rock or earth as a xorn (q.v.) does, taking 1 round to change its molecular structure; a phase door spell striking it while it changes kills it.
  • Attack: a sharp, rotating limb it pushes out from its top (3-12). If hard pressed, it can shoot this limb up to 2” for 9-16 (1d8+8) points of damage, but after that it has only a secondary limb, doing 2-8.
  • Defenses: fire and cold-based spells do not harm it; electrical attacks such as lightning bolt do one-quarter or no damage depending on the saving throw; poisons, gases, etc. do not harm it.
  • Spells that work: shatter does 3-18 points of damage, glassee blinds it for 2-5 rounds, and stone to flesh lowers its armor class to 6 against all weapons for 1 melee round.

Size: medium-sized crysmals have up to 16 hit points; large ones 17 or more. Those of over 28 hit points are about 2 feet wide, 14 feet long, and ½ foot thick.

Description: a truncated, prism-shaped heap of translucent crystals, each crysmal usually of one color, from pale amber through olive to deep violet.
system.hpNote: Medium-sized crysmals have up to 16 hit points, large ones 17 or more (MMII p.26).

system.description:
Crystal ooze is a kind of gray ooze (q.v.) adapted to life in water, where it is 75% invisible. Any dim or dark body of shallow water can be its home, and it can live out of water for several hours.

  • Attack: it flows over a victim and oozes a paralyzing poison, doing damage as shown above. Unless the victim saves vs. poison, it is paralyzed and soon consumed; prey reduced to −20 hit points has been totally consumed.
  • Defenses: acid, cold, heat, and fire do not harm it. Electricity and magic missiles do full damage. Weapon blows do only 1 point of damage per hit.
  • Wooden weapons: the corrosive poison attacks them; unless a save vs. acid is made for each hit, they are eaten away or break.

Cyclopskin are a humanoid race that prefers wilderness areas, favoring rocky places and living in caves. They live alone or in small bands and avoid other creatures whenever they can, unless those creatures are prey or slaves. Now and then a particularly powerful cyclopskin unites several bands to raid and pillage the lowlands; one such band is said to have numbered over 80.

  • Missiles: their poor depth perception gives them −2 to hit with missile weapons.
  • Strength: +2 to damage.
  • Arms: a large club (equal to a morning star) or a bladed, bardiche-like weapon, plus a huge sling and a heavy throwing spear.

Description: shaggy black or dull blue hair on the head and ruddy brown to muddy yellow skin, dressed in hides. The single eye is usually red.

The arcanadaemon looks like a robed human with the head of a fanged jackal or war dog and a pair of ivory white horns jutting from the top of the skull.

  • Attacks: horns (2-16), bite (1-6), and 2 claws (1-4 each). Besides clawing, it can use burning hands at will (as the spell), doing 13 points of damage to those within 3 feet of its claw attack, and can attack while doing so.
  • Flight: it can fly (as the spell) at the speed listed, for unlimited time.
  • Powers at will: shape change to any humanoid form, telekinesis of 3,250 gp weight, darkness in a 20’ radius, dimension door, and teleport (once per day).
  • Spells: as a magic-user of levels 11-18. It casts them without checking its magic resistance, and can also use scrolls and wands without checking it. All other magic devices must overcome its magic resistance to work.
  • Psionics: usually the minor sciences body equilibrium, detection of good/evil, and hypnosis, and the major sciences aura alteration and molecular manipulation, all at 10th level of mastery.

Society: a civilized breed of daemon. The race rules many petty baronies across the Lower Planes from red-iron forts, each with 1-4 lesser daemons as servants and 1-10 hordlings or diakka. The larger fortresses have portals to other planes, some said to reach the Prime Material, but magical signs and pentagrams bar entry.

Daemons: general (MMII)

Daemons live in the Lower Outer Planes of Gehenna, Tarterus, and the Glooms of Hades. There are many daemon races, each ruled by its strongest and most intelligent member. Weaker daemons are usually at the call of stronger ones of their race, and the strongest daemon of all, the oinodaemon, rules them all.

Relations: daemons are like both devils and demons, and will associate with either for their own ends. They do not like serving weaker beings, but given a strong, evil leader and enough reward they may enter an alliance, making themselves the senior partner.

Travel: they may move anywhere in the Lower Planes from the Nine Hells to the Abyss, and through the Astral and Ethereal Planes. They cannot enter the Prime Material Plane or the related Inner Planes without help, such as conjuration, summoning, or a gate.

Death: lesser daemons can be slain forever on any plane; their spirits reincarnate in a different form. Greater daemons can only truly be killed on the 3 planes they are native to. Slain elsewhere, a greater daemon’s essence returns to its home plane, and its body re-forms over a long time (1 year per hit die).

Names: every daemon has personal names by which it can be summoned and controlled. A lesser daemon has a single name; a greater daemon has many, all of which it tries to hide from the other powers of the Abyss and the Hells. A greater daemon has a 5% chance of hearing a mortal speak its name and coming to investigate. Whoever speaks such a name should be ready for a powerful daemon bent on returning the name to secrecy, usually by killing its betrayer. A pentagram protects the summoner from daemonkind.

Common powers: all daemons have infravision and ultravision, and these spell-like abilities: detect invisible, read magic, comprehend languages, invisibility, telepathy (with creatures of low intelligence or higher), and word of recall (once per day, back to their plane of origin).

Attack forms (unless noted otherwise):

AttackEffect on daemons
Acidhalf damage
Coldhalf
Electricity or lightningfull
Dragon or magical firehalf
Gasfull
Magic missilefull
Enchanted iron and silver weaponsfull damage
Poison, paralysis, and normal weaponsno damage

Magic resistance: the listed figure applies to 1st-level spells and drops by 5% for each spell level above 1st; it is still figured against an 11th-level caster. For example, a 12th-level magic-user casts a 5th-level spell at a daemon with 100% magic resistance: 100 − 20 (5th-level spell vs. 1st) − 5 (12th-level caster vs. 11th) = 75%. Charm and suggestion spells have no effect on daemons at all.

Using magic items: this resistance also affects magic items a daemon uses, treating the magic as a spell of similar level. A daemon using a wand of fireballs, for example, must fail its magic resistance roll (treating the wand as a 6th-level spell) for it to work. So daemons avoid most magic items, but will use magic shields and weapons, which keep their bonuses to hit or defend regardless of the daemon’s magic resistance.

name: Charon (The Boatman of the Lower Planes)

system.description:
The river Styx links the topmost layers of the Lower Planes, and its branches can be found anywhere from the Nine Hells to the Abyss. Where met, it is a deep, swift, unfordable torrent. Anyone who touches or drinks from it forgets his past life completely; if a saving throw is made, treat it as a forget spell cast by a 15th-level magic-user. The safest way across is Charon’s skiff.

  • Summoning: only on the banks of the Styx. Any of these spells attracts his attention: holy word or unholy word, conjure elemental, summoning an invisible stalker or aerial servant, or a symbol of any kind.
  • Passage: he appears with a large black skiff that holds 10, and if asked will ferry his passengers to the topmost layer of any Lower Plane. His price is a magic item, a silk bag of 100 pp, or two gems of 500+ gp value. He never keeps the payment but shares it among his servants, the charonadaemons (q.v.). He will not carry anyone who does not pay.
  • Gaze: causes fear (as the wand) in all he looks at.
  • Pole: 2-8 points of damage and paralysis for 2-8 turns (saving throw applies).
  • The river: he can call on the Styx itself to rise up and attack as a 16 hit dice water elemental. Each hit does 5-30 points of damage, and the target must save or lose its memory.
  • Servants: at any time he can summon 3-18 charonadaemons or 2-12 hydrodaemons, arriving in 1-3 rounds.
  • Psionics: the sciences body equilibrium, body weaponry, detection of good/evil, object reading, and sensitivity to psychic impressions, and the major sciences energy control and probability travel.
  • Death: his form can be destroyed, but he is never truly slain, being native to all 5 of the Lower Planes; his form vanishes from that plane for a single day and then returns.

Description: a skeletal man with a haggard face and glowing eyes, usually dressed in royal robes or ermine and silk.
