The Glooms of Hades hold many monsters, the most common being the diakka. Unlike hordlings (the next most common), diakka are more organized and dislike erratic behavior. They are not very bright, but do not attack stupidly: on first contact the flock’s strongest members size up those met for intent and weakness, and weakness puts an opponent in far more danger than hostility. Very powerful hostile creatures are attacked only if appeasement fails. No diakk wants to die, whether or not it would be eaten (as they often are by hordlings and other creatures of those planes); they even distrust other flocks. A diakk on the Prime Material Plane is always there by summoning. Night hags (q.v.) often use them as guards. They speak the hateful tongue common to Hades and their own language.

Kinds: the tall diakk (HD 6+6) and the broad diakk (HD 8+8). They are not separate races, and any group has an equal or nearly equal mix. A lair always holds 13-16.

  • Attacks: the tall diakk stabs viciously with its long, sharp bill; the broad diakk tears with its clawed arms.
  • Spell-like powers (both kinds, one at a time, one per round): weakness by touch in attack (1 per day), jump (2 per day), audible glamer (1 per day), and enfeeblement by group only (see below).
  • Group tactic: against obviously strong opponents, they try to force them into a tight group, surround them, and use audible glamer to sound like more diakka coming; the largest bound in and out of melee using jump and weakness. If at least 4 circle the opponents, hooting and croaking oddly, for 4 rounds in a row, the sound and rhythm of the dance cause a hypnotic enfeeblement over an area identical to the ray of enfeeblement spell. Each subject, regardless of magic resistance, must save vs. spell or be enfeebled as by a 13th-level magic-user (40% strength loss for 13 rounds). Then individual diakka use physical attacks and their remaining powers to kill the prey, and the whole flock feasts.

Description: tall diakka look like huge storks with bills on human-like heads and faces, and thin, human-like arms; they are very fast and give loon-like cries. Broad diakka look like huge, squat pelicans with short bills on human-like heads, and instead of wings have short, thick arms with huge, curving claws; they are rather slow and make gobbling croaks and caws while attacking. Their feathers come in sickening, wildly varied colors, such as pea green and rusty red-orange, purple and orange and pink, or dirty yellow. The heads are feathered but the faces brightly colored and bare. Legs, bills, feet, claws, etc. are usually black, dark brown, maroon, or deep green.

These two-legged plant-eaters feed upright or on all fours. If there is vegetation big enough nearby, they climb it to escape small predators. They are not aggressive, but their teeth are sharp enough to bite back at attackers.

Dinosaurs: general (MMII)

Dinosaurs are reptiles; the name comes from the Greek for “terrible lizard”. They are descended from a kind of reptile called thecodonts. All are extremely stupid and driven mainly by hunger.

  • Meat-eaters: both ferocious and greedy. Land meat-eaters pursue anything that looks or smells edible, stopping only when the prey has plainly escaped their reach. Marine kinds might overturn ships to get at the “food” aboard, or snatch unwary creatures from the decks of passing ships.
  • Plant-eaters: also insatiable eaters. They usually ignore anything inedible that does not seem threatening, or flee in panic from what they see as danger, though some defend themselves aggressively and are dangerous. Herds may stampede in almost any direction, as long as it is away from one of the big meat-eaters; any smaller, slower, weaker creature directly in the path is carried along or killed.

Several of the creatures listed are not “true” dinosaurs but are included because they fit the “lost world” surroundings these mighty reptiles share. See also the MM, “Dinosaur”.

These slow, exceptionally stupid creatures are easy prey for any hungry predator, usually too stupid to run until one of them is killed. A herd has small, medium, and large individuals.

  • Stampede: anyone caught in one must save vs. death ray or be crushed to death.

  • Meat-eaters: both ferocious and greedy. Land meat-eaters pursue anything that looks or smells edible, stopping only when the prey has plainly escaped their reach. Marine kinds might overturn ships to get at the “food” aboard, or snatch unwary creatures from the decks of passing ships.
  • Plant-eaters: also insatiable eaters. They usually ignore anything inedible that does not seem threatening, or flee in panic from what they see as danger, though some defend themselves aggressively and are dangerous. Herds may stampede in almost any direction, as long as it is away from one of the big meat-eaters; any smaller, slower, weaker creature directly in the path is carried along or killed.

Several of the creatures listed are not “true” dinosaurs but are included because they fit the “lost world” surroundings these mighty reptiles share. See also the MM, “Dinosaur”.

Its weak skull cannot anchor strong jaw muscles, so it uses its taloned hind feet, especially the spurs, to inflict horrible wounds, while its snaky neck strikes to bite. It prefers open areas to jungle and seldom goes where trees are thick. It often hunts with one or more of its kind, looking for a large dinosaur to kill for a feast.

  • Surprise attack: +2 to hit.
  • Dragging: a victim under 500 pounds is dragged into the water to be attacked further and eaten.

  • Tail: in a feeding frenzy it lashes with its powerful tail, damaging any creature behind it that is struck.

The dracolisk is said to be the offspring of a rogue black dragon and a basilisk of the largest size: a deep brown, dragon-like monster that moves fairly quickly and can fly, but only for short periods (a turn or two at most).

  • Attacks: this 6-legged horror attacks with its taloned forelegs and vicious bites.
  • Acid (3 times per day): a ½” wide stream spat up to 3”, doing 4-24 (4d6) points of damage on a hit, half if a save vs. breath weapon succeeds.
  • Gaze: petrifies any opponent within 20 feet who meets it. Its hooded eyes with nictitating membranes make it 90% safe from its own reflected gaze. Opponents in melee who try to avoid its gaze fight at −4 to hit. Like a basilisk’s (q.v.), its gaze reaches into the Astral and Ethereal Planes.
  • Other: dracolisks cannot use spells and speak only a very limited form of the black dragon language. A dracolisk is surprised only if asleep, and can never be subdued.

Chance of meeting a gaze (dracolisk or any large creature with a gaze weapon; add 1 if the creature is man-sized, such as a medusa, and 2 if small):

The character isChance
Completely surprised9 in 10
Surprised7 in 10
Viewing the monster5 in 10
Attacking normally3 in 10
Avoiding the gaze1 in 10

Cloud dragons are very solitary; 95% of encounters are with a lone individual, and 2 found together are a mated pair of adults (d4+4 for age category). They live in the sky: some in cloud-shrouded caves, but most (75%) on cloud islands, where they lair (compare “Cloud Giant”). They dislike intrusion and either avoid unwanted visitors or attack them.

  • Cloud form: they can take a cohesive gaseous form at will, and are then 75% unlikely to be told from a normal cloud. In this form their armor class is −3 and their only attacks are spells.
  • Solid form: needed to attack physically; armor class 0, and their natural magic resistance is lost. Attacks: claw/claw/bite/tail-lash, the tail useful only against opponents behind it.
  • Airblast (3 times per day): 3” wide, 3” deep, and 12-14” long (by the dragon’s hit dice).
    • Creatures weighing less than 10 pounds times the dragon’s hit points are blown about: an ancient cloud dragon of huge size, for example, affects creatures of 1,120 pounds or less. They take 1 point of tumbling and wind damage per hit point of the dragon, and are tumbled back along the blast for 1-6 feet per hit die of the dragon. Creatures not blown about take half damage from wind and wind-borne particles.
    • Creatures holding on to something secure add 10 pounds per strength point, plus any weight allowance (in pounds, not gold pieces), to their effective weight: a 200-pound human with 18/00 strength holding a tree counts as 680 pounds.
    • Paper and similar flimsy things are blown away, or shredded if held and torn free, and carried 20-200 feet beyond the blast. Loosely fastened clothing is torn off or tattered. Objects with large surfaces (shields, boxes, etc.) are torn away and battered or broken as by a crushing blow.
    • No saving throw is possible except at the edge of the blast, where it decides between full and half effect.
  • Spells (gained by age category; each usable twice per day, at a level equal to the dragon’s hit dice): 1 fog cloud, 2 precipitation, 3 stinking cloud, 4 cloudburst, 5 call lightning, 6 weather summoning, 7 control weather, 8 control winds.

Precipitation: a brief shower (12-14 segments) up to the dragon’s hit dice in inches away, in a cylinder 12” high and 3” across. It puts out small flames such as candles, makes small fires smoulder for 1 round, but does not affect large fires, and wets all but the most porous surfaces. Any very hot creature, such as a salamander, takes 1 point of damage per segment in the rain (saving throw applies).

Cloudburst: a cylinder 6” high and 3” across, up to the dragon’s hit dice in inches away. All the water in the air falls as huge drops, drenching everything and putting out all normal fires. Magical fires go out too: permanent ones relight in 1-2 rounds, and relightable flames stay out until rekindled. Spells such as burning hands and produce flame are negated, and a fireball or similar spell is put out, making a cloud of steam that does 1-3 points of damage (2-6 to cold-using creatures) to all within for 2-5 rounds.

Speech: their own dialect of dragon speech, which lets them talk with all other dragons, and halting Common.

Description: like fringed and frilled gold dragons. Their color depends on surroundings and mood: dark gray (angry), through pearly white (neutral), to golden or rose (satisfied or very pleased). In solid form they are translucent and opal-like, with specks of color showing mood.

Dragons: general (MMII)

Size: dragons come in 3 sizes: small, average, and huge. Roll d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge. The size sets the dragon’s number of hit dice.

Age: dragons pass through 8 ages. Roll d8 for the age, which also sets the hit points per die:

d8AgeHit points per die
1Very young (1-5 years)1
2Young (6-15 years)2
3Sub-adult (16-25 years)3
4Young adult (26-50 years)4
5Adult (51-100 years)5
6Old (101-200 years)6
7Very old (201-400 years)7
8Ancient (“40+ years” as printed)8
  • Senses: all dragons see equally well by day or in darkness (infravision, 60 feet), and have excellent sight, smell, and hearing, letting them detect hidden or invisible creatures within 1” per age level.
  • Fear aura: from adult age on, a dragon flying overhead or charging radiates a powerful aura causing fear:
    • All creatures under 1 hit die, and non-carnivorous creatures of any kind not trained for war or naturally fearless or aggressive, flee in panic at top speed for 4-24 turns.
    • Creatures with fewer than 3 hit dice must save vs. spell or be paralyzed with fear (50%) or flee in panic as above (50%).
    • Creatures of 3 or more hit dice fight at −1 to hit unless they also save vs. spell.
    • Creatures of 6 or more hit dice ignore the aura.
    • The aura of adult, old, and very old dragons is weaker than an ancient dragon’s, so saves against it are at +5, +3, and +1 respectively. A 2nd-level fighter, who normally needs 16 or better to save vs. spell (here, the aura), gets +5 against an adult dragon’s aura, so any roll of 11 or more avoids panic.
  • Speech and spells: many dragons speak one or more human languages besides their own, and a fair number of those can use spells; each species gives the chances, and the chance of being asleep. Attacking and subduing dragons are covered in the MM.
  • Treasure: very young dragons usually have none, but a 10% chance of one-quarter the listed treasure; young, 25% for one-quarter; sub-adults, 50% for one-half; young adults and old dragons, normal treasure; very old and ancient dragons are 50% and 75% likely to have 150% and 200% of it, respectively.
  • Saving throws: once a dragon has 5 or more hit points per die, it saves as total hit points ÷ 4 hit dice, more than it actually has, reflecting its magic resistance and toughness. Even a very young dragon saves by its actual hit dice, though it has only 1 hit point per die.
system.hpNote: Size (d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge) sets the hit dice; age (d8) sets the hit points per die (MMII p.55). At 5 or more hit points per die it saves as total hit points ÷ 4 hit dice (MMII p.56).

system.description:
Chance of: speaking 90%, magic use 100%, sleeping 40%.

This chaotic offshoot of the pseudo-dragon lives in peaceful, tangled forests in all climates, often with a group of sprites or pixies.

  • Invisibility: at will; it can attack and use magic or breath while invisible.
  • Bite: it attacks as a 4 hit dice monster, biting for 1-2 points.
  • Euphoria gas: much more likely than a bite. It breathes a 2-foot spherical cloud, just enough to give the target a good dose. A victim failing a save vs. breath weapon wanders about blissfully for 3-12 rounds, unable to attack and with armor class 10% worse than normal. Each round it can keep its mind on the situation only by rolling its intelligence or less on d20; once it fails, it loses all interest in the matter at hand, the gas having had its full effect.
  • Temper: it never attacks directly unless cornered or defending its lair, but uses its magic at every chance to make mischief for passers-by.
  • Magic: 65% use magic-user spells, 35% druid spells, at the level shown on the chart below. Spells are chosen only for their mischief potential; offensive or defensive spells are learned only if the dragon has thought up an exquisite prank using one. All learn water breathing and legend lore at the first chance. Many pranks are spur-of-the-moment, but months of preparation often go into a single grand practical joke.
  • Habits: they love swimming and diving, can hover, and are maneuverability class A. They eat fruit, roots, tubers, nuts, honey, and grains, and may go to great lengths for a fresh apple pie.
  • Speech: telepathy with one another up to 2 miles; their own language, their alignment tongue, and the languages of sprites, pixies, elves, and the local birds and animals. They often use forest creatures to help with their pranks.

Description: thin, miniature dragons with long prehensile tails, butterfly wings, and huge smiles. Their color runs through the spectrum from red (very young) to purple (ancient), as on the chart. Females’ hides shine with a bright golden tinge in sunlight; males’ with silver.

  • 3rd: fly, phantasmal force, slow, suggestion, water breathing
  • 4th: fire charm, fumble, hallucinatory terrain, polymorph other, polymorph self
  • 5th: distance distortion, faithful hound, telekinesis, transmute rock to mud, wall of force
  • 6th: control weather, legend lore, project image
  • 7th: limited wish, simulacrum
  • 8th: irresistible dance

Druid:

  • 1st: animal friendship, entangle, faerie fire, pass without trace, speak with animals

  • 3rd: plant growth, pyrotechnics, stone shape, water breathing
  • 4th: summon animal I, call woodland beings, control temperature within 10-foot radius, speak with plants
  • 5th: animal growth, control winds, transmute rock to mud
  • 6th: transport via plants, weather summoning

7Very old (201-400 years)7
8Ancient (“40+ years” as printed)8
  • Senses: all dragons see equally well by day or in darkness (infravision, 60 feet), and have excellent sight, smell, and hearing, letting them detect hidden or invisible creatures within 1” per age level.
  • Fear aura: from adult age on, a dragon flying overhead or charging radiates a powerful aura causing fear:
    • All creatures under 1 hit die, and non-carnivorous creatures of any kind not trained for war or naturally fearless or aggressive, flee in panic at top speed for 4-24 turns.
    • Creatures with fewer than 3 hit dice must save vs. spell or be paralyzed with fear (50%) or flee in panic as above (50%).
    • Creatures of 3 or more hit dice fight at −1 to hit unless they also save vs. spell.
    • Creatures of 6 or more hit dice ignore the aura.
    • The aura of adult, old, and very old dragons is weaker than an ancient dragon’s, so saves against it are at +5, +3, and +1 respectively. A 2nd-level fighter, who normally needs 16 or better to save vs. spell (here, the aura), gets +5 against an adult dragon’s aura, so any roll of 11 or more avoids panic.
  • Speech and spells: many dragons speak one or more human languages besides their own, and a fair number of those can use spells; each species gives the chances, and the chance of being asleep. Attacking and subduing dragons are covered in the MM.
  • Treasure: very young dragons usually have none, but a 10% chance of one-quarter the listed treasure; young, 25% for one-quarter; sub-adults, 50% for one-half; young adults and old dragons, normal treasure; very old and ancient dragons are 50% and 75% likely to have 150% and 200% of it, respectively.
  • Saving throws: once a dragon has 5 or more hit points per die, it saves as total hit points ÷ 4 hit dice, more than it actually has, reflecting its magic resistance and toughness. Even a very young dragon saves by its actual hit dice, though it has only 1 hit point per die.
system.hpNote: Hit points by age level (MMII p.57); it attacks as a 4 hit dice monster.

system.description:
Chance of sleeping: 20%.

Mist dragons are solitary; only 10% of encounters are with a mated pair, always adults or older (d4+4 for age category). They are found only near waterfalls, sea coasts, or where rain is heavy, such as rain forests. The lair is always some great natural cave, cavern, or similar place.

  • Mist form: their favorite state. They can take a cohesive gaseous form and look like mist, so at least 50% of the time they are not recognized for what they are unless they wish. In mist form they are armor class −2 with 30% magic resistance, and can only cast spells.
  • Solid form: taken if annoyed or threatened. Armor class 1, standard magic resistance. Attacks: 2 claws, a bite, and a lash with its jagged-scaled tail (effective only against opponents behind it).
  • Breath (3 times per day): a cloud of misty vapor 3” wide, 9” long, and 3” deep. All air-breathers in it are blinded for 1-4 rounds and must save vs. breath weapon or take 3-12 points of drowning damage each round they stay in it; those who save only cough and choke, taking 1-4 points per round. The mist lasts 5-8 rounds, depending on wind. It does not affect mist dragons.
  • Spells (gained by age category; each usable twice per day, at a level equal to the dragon’s hit dice): 1 precipitation (9-11 segments), 2 create water, 3 water breathing, 4 zephyr, 5 predict weather, 6 cloudburst, 7 gust of wind, 8 airy water. (See “Cloud Dragon” for precipitation and cloudburst.)
  • Speech: their own dialect of dragon speech, which lets them talk with nearly all other dragons; most know a smattering of Common.

Zephyr: a gentle draft of air flows from the caster in the direction faced, until it fills its area. It makes small flames waver and dance, and fans larger fires, making them hotter (+1 on damage dice, if any). It holds back moving vapors such as cloudkill for 1 round, halves the duration of vapors such as fog cloud and wall of fog, and pushes stagnant air, vapors, or even poison gas back 1”, also halving their duration and potency unless they are renewed from some source. Duration 1 segment; range 0; area of effect a 1” path, ½” long per level; casting time 2 segments.

Description: like gold dragons in build, but semi-transparent even in solid form, grayish-white to blue-white.

Dragons: general (MMII)

Size: dragons come in 3 sizes: small, average, and huge. Roll d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge. The size sets the dragon’s number of hit dice.

2Young (6-15 years)2
3Sub-adult (16-25 years)3
4Young adult (26-50 years)4
5Adult (51-100 years)5
6Old (101-200 years)6
7Very old (201-400 years)7
8Ancient (“40+ years” as printed)8

system.description:
Chance of: speaking 100%; magic use, see below; sleeping 50% in daylight, 5% otherwise.

The shadow dragon is nocturnal, lives underground, or is found on dim planes such as Shadowland. It is independent and solitary; only occasionally is a mated pair met. The female lays 5-8 eggs in a dark place, and the first to hatch quickly devours the others. They cannot stand very hot or arctic climates but thrive in cooler temperate regions. They prefer walking to flying, being poor flyers that tire in a few turns.

  • Size and hit points: size sets hit dice: 25% are small (all female), 50% average, and 25% large (all male). Age sets hit points per die as with all dragons, but a shadow dragon always has +1 per die: a very young hatchling has 2 per die and an ancient one 9.
  • Senses: their sight is poor in bright light but normal (at least human daylight standard) by starlight. They have ultravision and very superior infravision (180 feet).
  • Speech: all speak the tongue of all evil dragons and 1-4 more languages (intelligence 11-12, 1 language; 13-14, 2; etc.).
  • Spells: those of 17-18 intelligence can use illusionist spells, 2 per level, from adult age; the book says “of 3rd-4th levels”, but its examples give an adult 2 spells of 1st level and an ancient one of 18 intelligence 2 each of 1st-4th levels. They never use spells of light or fire.
  • Breath: a cloud of darkness 40 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 20 feet high, usually followed by claw and bite attacks. This tangible stuff blinds those inside, even those with infravision, and drains their life energy to 25% of their usual vitality (level or hit dice; 50% if a saving throw succeeds) for as many turns as the dragon has age categories. Spells lost this way are gone until relearned or regained normally. It does not affect shadow dragons.
  • Hiding: they hide in shadows as a 10th-level thief.
  • Defenses: harmed only by magic weapons; immune to all level loss. They cannot be subdued and sold.
  • Hoard: usually 10-80 opaque, dark gems, black preferred. It prizes items connected with shadow and darkness and tries to destroy magic dealing with fire and/or light.

Description: worm-like dragons of lighter and darker shadows, with semi-transparent bat-like wings and mostly semi-transparent bodies. The eyes, pools of feral gray opalescence, are the easiest part to spot, but by then it is usually too late.

Dragons: general (MMII)

Size: dragons come in 3 sizes: small, average, and huge. Roll d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge. The size sets the dragon’s number of hit dice.

3Sub-adult (16-25 years)3
4Young adult (26-50 years)4
5Adult (51-100 years)5
6Old (101-200 years)6
7Very old (201-400 years)7
8Ancient (“40+ years” as printed)8

system.description:
Unlike their small cousins, giant dragonflies are dangerous predators known to hunt humans. Fearless and greedy, they hunt not only all other such creatures but any warm-blooded creature. They range from subtropical to temperate regions; even larger ones live in tropical areas (statistics in parentheses).

  • Speed: their great speed, hovering, and darting give them +2 on initiative.
  • Hard to hit: if they have the initiative, hand-held weapons cannot be used against them effectively and missiles are at −4. Without the initiative they can be hit normally with hand-held weapons, but missiles are still at −2.
  • Skin: brilliant and glittering, and valuable. Preserved by magic, it brings up to 600 gp per square foot, used for clothing and decoration; only about 6 square feet can be taken from a normal specimen.

The sky-dwelling dragon horse is a relative of the ki-rin. They roam the open air above the Prime Material Plane or the Elemental Plane of Air, and are seldom (5%) met elsewhere. Usually only 1 is met; 2 or 3 are a stallion, mare, and foal (50%-75% grown: roll d6, 45% + 5% per pip). Free-roaming dragon horses have no interest in possessions or treasure. The presence of evil makes them want to go elsewhere.

  • Hooves: 2 blows; +2 damage per hit (3-10/3-10) when attacking while flying or rearing.
  • Breath (once per turn, at will): fog cloud, gust of wind, or a small, limited cone of cold (1” across at the base, 2” long, 4d8 damage). Other breath uses are at 8th level.
  • Senses: exceptionally keen, triple normal, infravision and ultravision included, so they are never surprised. Their sight includes aura detection, so they sense the alignment of creatures they meet; with a basic empathy, this makes it most unlikely that one is ever misled or enslaved by evil creatures.
  • Travel: they can travel the Astral and Ethereal Planes, but are known to do so only rarely, chiefly crossing the Ethereal to stay for a time on the Elemental Plane of Air.
  • Speech: a basic form of the ki-rin language, with much communication by shared empathy.
  • As steeds: much desired, but few succeed, since it must be a willing companion and no dragon horse likes being held to the ground for long. A foal raised lovingly and carefully and taken often into the sky might become a trusted companion and steed, as long as no ground-bound demands were made of it; but maturing takes 20 years, so this is nearly unknown.

Description: like a ki-rin without a horn. Pale azure to silvery blue coat, flowing manes and tails of pure white to silver, and deep sky blue to indigo hooves.

Dragonnels seem distantly related to both dragons and air dragons (pteranodons), though they are a separate species. As large as a small dragon, they have no breath weapon. They have a dim intelligence and have been known to do evil at times.

  • Attacks: vicious strikes with taloned forefeet, then a snapping bite of the toothy beak.

Range: dragonnels once lived in the World of Greyhawk from the Kron Hills and Gloriole to the Drachensgrab Mountains, but are now nearly extinct everywhere except the Pomarj. There they have been caught, tamed, and used as steeds by evil humans living among the humanoid hordes infesting the place. Luckily there are too few to threaten the surrounding states seriously, though rumor says several score dragonnel-mounted raiders have been sighted along the Wild Coast.

Description: a grayish underbelly fading to dusty red-violet along the sides and tail, maroon back spines, a gray beak, and white head frills.

system.psionicText: See below Attack/Defense Modes: See below
system.description:
Drelbs live on the Negative Material Plane, but evil-minded people sometimes call them to the Prime Material Plane to guard hidden wealth or secret places, so a drelb met here is always guarding something. The magic that brings one usually works only from sunset to sunrise, so, much like undead, drelbs appear only in twilight or darkness. A drelb looks so much like a wraith that the two cannot be told apart until it attacks.

  • Nether chill: its touch makes the victim fall shivering to the ground for the following round (no saving throw), at once dropping whatever it holds and unable to act until the chill passes.
  • Illusion trick: facing a cleric trying to turn it, or hesitant prey, it shrinks its form rapidly while gliding smoothly forward, 90% likely to make viewers think it is retreating while it is actually closing to attack.
  • Not undead: though it looks undead, it is not and cannot be turned.
  • Defenses: magic weapons are needed to harm it. Silver has no effect unless it is magical silver, which does double damage.
  • Psionics: it imitates or reflects psionic power: any power used within 30 feet of it, or any psionic attack aimed at it, is copied or reflected back on the user.
  • Speech: only its own strange language, though it understands simple phrases of Common.

The drider is a special creation of Lolth’s magic. When drow of promising ability reach 6th level or a little higher, Lolth summons them and puts them through a specially devised test; those that fail become driders.

Description: a cross between a giant spider and a drow: the torso, head, and arms of a pale, bloated drow on 8 spider legs. Their bloated shape makes it impossible to tell their sex, but 60% are female.

  • Magic: a drider keeps whatever drow abilities it had, so all have magic or cleric ability by sex: females are 6th or 7th-level clerics; males 6th, 7th, or 8th-level magic-users.
  • Drow spells (once per day each): dancing lights, darkness, detect magic, faerie fire, know alignment, and levitate; females also clairvoyance, detect lie, dispel magic, and suggestion.
  • Combat: all fight as 7 hit dice monsters, usually with swords or axes, and many carry bows on their backs. They can also bite (1-4 points); those bitten must save vs. poison at −2 or be paralyzed by the spittle for 1-2 turns.
  • Habits: outcasts from drow society, they bear the drow no love. They are seldom found in numbers, preferring to work alone, and are accompanied by 2-12 huge spiders 10% of the time. Usually living underground, they often stalk victims until the right moment to kill. They live mainly on their victims’ blood, having gained a spider’s tastes.

system.treasure: Individuals M, Q; Lair B (magic only), F
system.psionicText: 71-90 (2/level) Attack/Defense Modes: B, C, D/F, G, H
system.description:
The duergar are the seldom-met race of evil dwarves, also called gray dwarves or gray ones. Malicious in the extreme, they live in the underground depths where their evil need not face the light. Usually only a handful are found, but now and then a lair is discovered with hundreds of them.

  • Higher levels: for every 4 normal duergar, 1 has double hit dice (is 2nd level). If 9 are met outside the lair, an extra duergar of triple or quadruple hit dice (3rd or 4th level) leads them.
  • Arms: 1st-level duergar (75%) carry pick, hammer, spear, chain mail, and shield; 2nd-level ones (25%) pick, light crossbow, chain mail, and shield.

Additional weapons and armor (the first column is printed without a heading):

LevelArms
+1/163rdHammer, short sword, plate mail, and shield
+1/164thHammer, short sword, plate mail, and shield
+4-65thHammer, short sword, plate mail, and shield
+2-36thHammer, short sword, plate mail, and shield
+17th-9thHammer*, short sword*, plate mail*, and shield*
+4-63rd-6th/3rd-6th cleric/assassinsAny usable*/any usable*
+17th-9th/7th-9th cleric/assassinsAny usable*/any usable*

* 5% chance per level that the item is magical; for split levels, add half the lower to the higher to find the approximate actual level, rounding up.

  • Lair: always underground and extensive, with many passages, rooms, chambers, and secret areas. Non-combatant young equal to 10% of the normal fighters (21-30 young). There may (25%) be a monster kept as a guardian, and there is a 75% chance of 10-40 slaves. Roll d20 for the kind: 1-8 mountain dwarves or orcs; 9-12 dwarves or goblins; 13-16 gnomes or xvarts; 17-18 halflings (stout) or kobolds; 19 svirfneblin or norkers; 20 adventurers or others. Adventurers are typical; “others” are drow, grimlocks, and the like.
  • Neighbors: they have been known to live with derro (q.v.) and similar evil creatures, but such communities are rare.
  • Surprise: they surprise on 3 in 6 and are surprised only 1 in 10.
  • Defenses: like other dwarves, they save vs. magical attacks (death magic, polymorph, rods etc., and spell) at +4. Immune to paralysis and poison; illusion/phantasm spells do not affect them.
  • Psionics: all have expansion, invisibility, molecular attraction (as printed), and reduction, performed at their hit dice level.
  • Senses and speech: infravision to 12”. They speak the silent speech of underground creatures, their own tongue, and Dwarf; some speak other tongues too.

Description: emaciated, evil-faced dwarves with medium to dark gray skin, dressed in drab colors that blend into their surroundings. They live longer than normal dwarves, some reaching 500 or more years.
system.hpNote: For every 4, 1 has double hit dice (2nd level); a group of 9 outside the lair has a leader of triple or quadruple hit dice (MMII p.61). Roll those by hand.

system.description:
Dustdiggers live in dry areas of loose, sandy soil, such as desert dunes. They look like giant starfish with 5 arms around a central mouth. They travel above ground only at night, never for more than a few minutes, and often in groups.

  • Trap: it digs a hole, covers itself with sand, and inflates to fill the hole, leaving the ground level with its surroundings. When an animal walks on it, it deflates, making something very like a sinkhole; the sand shifting toward its mouth slows the prey’s escape. Fully deflated, it folds its arms up around the victim and tries to kill it before swallowing.
  • Folded: once it has folded, the prey is caught and cannot attack, so the best defense is to recognize a dustdigger before it folds.
  • Armor: back armor class 4, front only 7.
  • Illusion: 20% have an inborn talent for illusion, and usually project a pool of bubbling water in the sand when victims come within striking range.

There are several kinds of eagle, all fitting these statistics generally. Usually a single bird or mated pair is met, but there is a slight (5%) chance of meeting them in a rookery where 5-12 nest.

  • Nests: in the tallest trees, on cliffs, or in mountains, with 1-4 eggs and a 10% chance of some small, shiny item (a coin, gem, etc.).
  • Dive: they usually attack by diving from a great height. Diving from 100 feet or more they move at double speed and attack with 2 claws only, but at +2 to hit and double damage.
  • Eyesight: exceptional, so they are almost never surprised.
  • Prey: unless exceptionally hungry they do not attack even the smaller demi-humans, but a brownie, for instance, would be in real danger, since they attack prey of that size without hesitation.
  • Training: hard to train for hunting; only about 25% can be properly managed. Still, viable eggs or eaglets bring 60-100 gp on the open market.

Eblis, or storkmen, are seldom seen by humans, or perhaps few live to tell of it. These tall, evil birdmen live in marshes and swamps in subtropical and tropical lands. Each group is several mated pairs and their offspring; when a tribe outgrows its home, the younger ones form a new band and seek their own area.

  • Huts: pairs live in carefully built huts of reeds and grasses, 2-8 to a community, 90% unlikely to be found even by careful search. Inside are piles of rushes, sticks, etc., with an egg 30% of the time. Since they love shiny things, there is always some metal, glass, or similar item in a nest, and a 25% chance of one of these (d20): 1-2 scroll in a metal tube; 3-5 potion; 6 ring; 7 miscellaneous magic item (small only); 8-9 magic dagger or knife; 10-20 1-4 pieces of metal jewelry.
  • Combat: very fast at shifting and striking, hence their excellent armor class. Their snaky, sinewy necks are very powerful, and they attack by stabbing with the beak.
  • Illusionist: each community has 1 who uses illusionist magic through dance and song: 2-8 of the following spells (d8), each once per day at 3rd level: 1 audible glamer, 2 change self, 3 hypnotism, 4 spook, 5 wall of fog, 6 blur, 7 hypnotic pattern, 8 whispering wind.
  • Fire: they love water and are always damp, so they are less vulnerable to fire than their feathers suggest: saves vs. fire at +1 and damage −1 per die.

Description: giant gray-brown storks. Males have red-brown heads and black necks and legs.

Giant marine electric eels live only in warm, fairly shallow salt water, usually 30-150 feet deep. They move fairly slowly but strike fast, gaining +1 on initiative.

  • Shock (once every turn): all creatures within 5 feet of the eel take 6-36 points of damage, those 5-10 feet away 4-24, and those 10-15 feet away 2-12.
  • Stun: unless victims save vs. paralysis, they are stunned and helpless for as many rounds as the points of shock damage taken. Saves are at +1 at 5-10 feet and +2 at 10-15 feet. A successful save does not halve the damage; it only prevents stunning.

The grugach are “wild” elves related to sylvan elves, but smaller, thinner, and very fair. They are completely xenophobic, distrusting even other elves, and so are seldom if ever met outside their tribal bands. About 20% of encounters supposedly with wood elves are actually with grugach. Except as noted, they follow the rules for wood elves and elfkind in general.

  • Strength: despite their small size they have broad shoulders and great strength (+2 on the strength roll, treating 19 or 20 as 18).
  • Classes: they are not magic-users; dual-classed individuals are fighter/druids.
  • Animals: on good terms with all forest animals except evil ones; they often (70%) ride stags.
  • Traps: all adults can set traps, mainly pits and snares in and around their home territory, well hidden. Creatures passing near one are almost 90% likely to be caught; careful examination of a trapped area lowers this to 30%.
    • Pits: usually 10 feet deep and spiked: 1-4 points for the fall onto the earth floor, plus 1-6 per spike, plus poison (50% chance).
    • Snares: usually set to loop around creatures, jerk them off their feet, and hang them 5 feet or more above the ground.
    • Deadfalls: some snares drop a heavy log for 5d6-8d6 damage, pinning the victim as well.

(A stray footnote mark, “Possible in unusual character”, is printed with this entry.)

system.treasure: Individuals M, N; in lair G, S, T
system.description:
(A stray footnote is printed with this entry: “Possible in unusual characters”.)

Whether a separate race of elves or an offshoot of gray elves, the elves of the Valley of the Mage (valley elves) have distinct features and traits. As tall as most humans, they are thin, with sharp, pointed features. They are reclusive and resent intrusion. If anything, they are neutral in alignment.

  • Otherwise: they follow the traits of gray elves, but are not known to use any steeds except horses. For habitat, group make-up, weapons, and special abilities they follow the MM, “Elf” (q.v.).
  • Relations: all other elves, drow included, shun them, and they in turn dislike association with any race except perhaps gnomes, whom they tolerate, probably because gnomes also serve the Mage of the Valley.
  • Cooshee: used as guard animals; 75% of the time a wandering band has 1-4, and their lairs have a 90% chance of 2-8.
  • Greyhawk: in the WORLD OF GREYHAWK™ setting, valley elves are found only near the Valley of the Mage. Bands of them have raided into Bissel, Gran March, Ket, and the Grand Duchy of Geoff, probably at the bidding of their liege.

The elfin cat lives only in sylvan woodlands of temperate regions. It is usually taken for a wild cat or perhaps a lynx, because it does not wish to be noticed as unusual. It is about the size of an average dog, gray-brown with dark brown or black stripes.

  • Movement: fast; climbs very quickly, swims well, and leaps 20 feet or more with ease.
  • Lair: they are solitary, but in a lair there are 1 adult female, 1-4 kits, and 1 male within 1-4 rounds’ travel. Any treasure there was left for safekeeping by some friendly creature, such as an elf or gnome.
  • Combat: they can fight with claw and fang but prefer to avoid such fights, relying on magic to survive.
  • Spell-like powers (at 9th level): enlarge (1 per day; doubles its attack power), reduce (2 per day), pass without trace, tree (a limb, not a whole tree; 2 per day), and trip (1 per day). They roam field and wood in their small size, using enlarged form only to frighten possible enemies.
  • Stealth: they move 99.9% silently and hide in natural surroundings with 90% success. Their keen senses mean they are surprised only 1 in 20, and they surprise others 5 in 6.
  • ESP: a limited form lets them read nearby creatures’ thoughts to learn whether they are friendly or hostile.
  • Speech: their own language, a few words of Elf, and some speak Gnome, Brownie, etc.
  • Sentinels: one or more often live with a community of sylvan elves, woodland gnomes, brownies, sprites, etc. In return for food and protection they serve as sentinels, reporting any monsters or intruders in the area and what they intended.

The executioner’s hood is a small, bag-like monster with a unique way of catching prey. It looks almost exactly like a real executioner’s hood: dull black, about 1 inch thick, with 2 eye holes that can actually be seen through into or out of its cavity. It can also spread out into a disc and has been known to hunt as a lurker above (q.v.) does.

  • Attack: it crawls into a niche and waits. When prey comes in, it closes tight over the victim’s head (needing a to-hit roll), doing 1-4 points of damage at once and 1-4 more each round from strangling and suffocation until the prey or the hood is dead.
  • Hard to kill: wrapped around a head, it is very hard to slay, since its fibrous strands make the victim suffer whatever other spell effects the hood does. Sleep spells do not affect it at all.
  • Brandy: pouring strong brandy on it makes it lose 1 point of damage per round, and after 4 rounds (if a full quart is used) it falls off, drunk.

Falcons and hawks are common throughout the world, from tropical to subarctic regions, nesting in tall trees or on inaccessible cliffs. There is a 5% chance a nest holds some small, shiny item such as a coin or gem.

  • Dive: they usually attack with a plunging dive from 100 feet or higher: +2 to hit and double talon damage, but no beak attack.
  • Eyesight: exceptional; they are never surprised.
  • Training: taken young and trained by an expert, they can be taught to hunt, and can be set on opponents, attacking with claws and beak. Against an opponent with unprotected eyes, a beak hit has a 25% chance of blinding 1 eye.
  • Large falcons hunting in the wild have been known, very rarely, to attack small demi-humans.

system.specialDefenses: Immune to electrical and fire attacks
system.description:
The firefriend, or giant firefly, is well liked but rarely met, found in temperate lands. Its intelligence is low by human standards, but it is clever and avoids obvious enemies. It seeks out friendly humans and demi-humans as companions, loving to talk with them and hear fanciful stories.

  • Bite: small but sharp mandibles for self-defense.
  • Light beam (once every turn): its glowing abdomen, normally as bright as a torch, can be brightened and focused into a greenish beam about 3 inches across and up to 14 feet long. Flesh struck takes 5-20 points of damage, half if a save vs. wands succeeds.
  • Defenses: electricity and fire do not harm it.
  • Life: they hatch in spring, mature by age 2, live about 10 years, and learn to talk with humans by age 1 or 2. Most speak their own language and Common.

All giant flies shun fire; a hit with a torch burns their wings off, and they seem to know this by instinct. Prey that defends itself aggressively makes them jump away: a backward spring of 3” taking 1 segment, after which the fly is airborne 1” up. So a giant fly can land on or near a victim, bite, and jump away if it has initiative, though opponents able to attack at a distance can still do so.

Bluebottle: seldom attacks living prey, preferring carrion, offal, and the like, and is drawn to sweet things. It does attack creatures covered with blood or with open wounds. Each bite has a 10% chance of giving the victim some disease.

Horsefly: the largest giant fly, very aggressive, apt to land on any creature and attack for its blood. After biting, it does the same damage again the next round by drawing blood or fluids from the wound, unless driven off or killed.

Foo creatures are found in scattered parts of the Prime Material Plane and in some of the Upper Outer Planes. They can become ethereal, travel astrally or ethereally, and often travel the Astral Plane.

  • Attacks: 2 raking forepaw claws, then a bite.
  • Against evil: fighting evil opponents, foo dogs attack as 10 hit dice creatures and foo lions as 15. Against lawful evil opponents, especially devils, they also get +1 per attack to hit and damage. Evil opponents attack them at −1 to hit and damage.
  • Invisibility: at will.
  • Roar: their barking roar warns humans of danger and threatens evil creatures. If it goes on for 7 or more rounds, there is a 20% chance it brings 1-6 more foo dogs or 1-2 foo lions, arriving from the Astral Plane in 1-10 rounds.
  • Service: they can sometimes be persuaded to serve and guard very good humans, but never for long.
  • Speech: their own language; they understand human speech if they know the tongue.

Description: large, blunt heads with wide-set, bulging eyes and huge, fanged mouths; rather lion-like bodies with bushy-tipped tails, short for dogs and long for lions. The hind legs are quite dog-like, the forelegs more lion-like. Color runs from golden to black, and odd ones may be white or almost any other color. Foo lions have manes and larger mouths than foo dogs.

  • Speech: their own language; they understand human speech if they know the tongue.

The forester’s bane, or snapper-saw, is a low-growing shrub. Broad, tough leaves with sinewy ribs spread 5-7 feet from the central plant, whose bushy center hides 3-6 stalks with saw-toothed edges.

  • Trap: when a creature steps on or near the leaves, they snap shut around it, holding it fast, and the jagged stalks saw at it. Trapping is automatic, and the victim takes 3-6 attacks that round.
  • Escape: on later rounds, a 5% chance per point of strength to pull free and escape further attacks.
  • Damage: besides what the main plant can take, the leaves can take 9-16 points of damage and the stalks 17-24. Lost leaves and stalks grow back in 2-8 weeks unless the central plant is killed.

Description: green to dark green, with purple stalks. The bushy center grows large, plump, delicious-smelling berries of white, greenish, golden, or bright yellow, very nutritious and rich in protein.

Formians, the race of intelligent ant-men, are sometimes called centaur-ants. They live in cities built partly above and partly below ground. At first glance a formian city looks like a normal walled human city, but the buildings inside its smooth walls are truncated cones, cylinders, or hemispheres entered only at or near the top. Their chambers have sloping ramps or vertical shafts leading down to a complex of tunnels and chambers that forms the underground part of the city, always about 3 times larger than the upper part.

  • Encounters: 90% are with workers, 10% with warriors; check whether the encounter is within 1 mile of their city (“in lair”). Workers (10-40) are only 10% likely to have warriors with them, and if so the group is a raiding party, probably attacking another city or a giant termite nest.
  • Myrmarches: formian nobles, met only in their cities, each served by 2 warrior guards and 8 workers (in addition to the number rolled).
  • Royal chamber: each city also has 2-5 gymarches (males, equal to myrmarches but with 7+7 hit dice) and 1 non-combatant queen, in a special royal chamber complex on a level near the bottom of the city, attended by 1-4 myrmarches, 11-20 warriors, and 31-40 workers (all extra). Type A treasure is kept with them.
  • Extra city population: per level below ground, 10 warriors, 100 workers, and 200 slave workers; near the royal chambers, 10 eggs, 10 larvae, and 10 pupae. Slaves are formians of other colors; they will not attack, report, communicate with, support, or aid intruders, but merely exist there. Formians whose nursery is threatened fight fanatically to save it, or bargain to prevent its destruction.
  • Attacks: myrmarches use large mandibles and an abdominal sting whose poison does 4-16 points of damage (2-8 with a successful saving throw). Warriors use mandibles, 2 pincer-like foreleg claws, and a small sting (2-8 or 1-4). Workers use only their small mandibles.
  • Strength: all are strong: workers equal 22, warriors 23, and myrmarches 24.
  • Speech: they communicate silently (telepathically) by touching another with one or both antennae. Myrmarches and special formians are 75% likely to speak Common, with a limited vocabulary.

Description: workers are about the size of a large dog, warriors pony-sized, myrmarches horse-sized, gymarches as large as draft horses, and the queen half again as large. All are ant-like, but their waists are flexible, and they often go about on 4 legs with thorax and head raised, looking like centaur-ants. Their forelegs have wrists and 3 opposing claws: clumsy in workers, enlarged in warriors, but nearly as useful as human hands in the others. A formian’s color shows its city of origin, and each city constantly wars with any other nearby. Known colors: solid dark brown, striped brown and tan, tan, red, striped red and tan, red head with black body, black head with red body, black, striped black and gray, and dark gray.

Huge and weird, froghemoths live only in large swamps or fairly shallow (100 feet or less) bodies of fresh water holding large creatures to prey on. They are solitary except in the spring mating season.

  • Toughness: its 4 tentacles, each about 15 feet or more long, are very strong and covered in thick, leathery hide; each takes 19-22 hit points to sever or disable. The body is only slightly less well protected and can take a full 16 hit dice of damage (16-128 points) before the creature dies. The tongue is the most vulnerable part, taking only 12-16 hit points to sever. Injured parts heal or regrow in 2-5 weeks.
  • Ambush: it floats with its body under water, its retractable eye-stalk raised to its full 3 feet to just break the surface (the nostril stalks too), and its 4 tentacles thrust ahead, perhaps near shore, to seize unwary victims. Or it crouches behind screening plants, and when prey comes in range thrusts its head forward and lashes out its 10-foot barbed tongue (18/50 strength).
  • Tongue: the tongue snaps back at once, dragging the victim to the toothy mouth, where it is swallowed whole on 19 or 20 (14-20 if size S); otherwise it is bitten and chewed for 5-50 hit points.
  • Resisting the tongue: a seized victim not surprised (1 or 2) compares its d6 result (3-6) to a d8 rolled for the froghemoth’s speed and accuracy. If it equals or beats the froghemoth’s roll, it can try to grab some fixed object in reach to resist being drawn in, and succeeds in grabbing and holding on. Unless its strength exceeds 18/50, it must compare d6 against d8 again each round; any result lower than the d8 breaks its hold, and it is bitten or swallowed at once. A held creature cannot attack the tongue, but its companions can. Meanwhile the froghemoth uses its tentacles on the resisting prey and anyone helping it.
  • Swallowed: a creature swallowed whole takes 4-16 points of damage from digestive juices at once, and 4-16 more each round after. It can attack the stomach only with a dagger or similar short stabbing weapon (not a short sword), and falls unconscious after 2 rounds. At −10 hit points or less it is fully digested and gone, and no resurrection of any kind is then possible.
  • Tongue severed: it attacks for 2-5 rounds with its tentacles at double damage (10-16 hp each); if still opposed by active opponents after that, it withdraws under water to heal.
  • Fire: normal fire does not harm it; very large or very hot fires do half damage and drive it back for 1 round. Burning hands drives it back only if it does 10 or more points, but a fireball, flame strike, etc. do.
  • Electricity: only 1 point per die of damage, and it is slowed to half movement and attacks for 1 round.
  • Other attack forms do normal damage.

Movement: fairly fast in water, kicking with webbed hind feet. In marsh or swamp it lies on its belly and slides along, pushed by its hind legs and tentacles. On dry land it moves in short, vaulting hops, tentacles thrust well ahead and legs lifting the body forward and up.

Lair and treasure: the lair is usually a sunken mass of trees and debris. Most prey is killed and eaten away from it, so the only treasure is what hapless victims dropped.

Breeding: in late spring females lay only 10-100 eggs about 1 foot across, left in shallow water. About 90% of the hatched tadhemoths are eaten by earlier-hatched ones or other predators; the few survivors seek deeper water to grow up in, taking 3 years to reach adulthood. About 1-4% survive.

Tadhemoth stage: the young grows about 1 foot per month for 6 months, then 60% more slowly until maturity. At first it is fish-like, with 4 fins at the chest and 2 at the rear, and a vicious bite (2-8 hit points). After 6 months the chest fins begin lengthening into tentacles; the rear ones show no change until the last month or two, when they lengthen into thick, bowed legs with webbed toes. After the first growth its mouth enlarges a great deal, and its bite does 3-24, 4-32, or 5-40 depending on size. A tadhemoth is wholly aquatic, with gills, and swims at 16”.

Description: a yellow underbelly; pale yellowish undersides to the hind legs and tentacles; light green sides; and a mottled green back, upper legs, and tentacles. The eye-stalk and 2 nostril stalks are yellow-green. The eyeballs are amber with a greenish tinge, and the slit, upright pupils bright green edged with orange.
system.hpNote: The body takes 16 hit dice of damage; each of the 4 tentacles 19-22 and the tongue 12-16 to sever (MMII p.67).

system.description:
The galeb duhr is a curious boulder-like creature with limbs that serve as hands and feet. These intelligent beings are very large and slow. They live in rocky or mountainous areas, where they can feel the “earth power” and control the rocks around them.

  • Spells (as 20th-level magic-users, once per round): move earth, stone shape, passwall, transmute rock to mud, and wall of stone.
  • Animated boulders: they can animate 1-2 boulders within 6” (AC 0; MV 3”; HD 9; damage 4d6), as a treant controls trees.
  • Cold: double damage, and saves against it at −4.
  • Fire and lightning: lightning and normal fire do not harm them; magical fire does full damage, but they save against fire attacks at +4.

Fomorians are the most hideous, deformed, and wicked of all giants. They tend to live alone in forlorn places such as mountain caves or abandoned mines.

  • Armor: their thick, hairy hides plus the pelts and odd bits of metal they wear give an effective armor class of 3. The strongest sometimes have crude shields and better armor, so armor class 2 or even 1 is possible.
  • Stealth: they move slowly for their size but very quietly, gaining +1 to +3 on surprise depending on terrain.
  • Never surprised: their deformities keep them from hurling rocks but help in another way: oddly placed eyes, huge ears, and/or large noses let them detect any normal approach, so they cannot be surprised under normal circumstances.
  • Weapons: anything from huge clubs to chains with heavy metal balls.
  • Lair: a 25% chance of 1-2 females per male, and 1-3 young per female. Females equal males but get no bonus points on their hit dice. Young (roll d6 for size):
Size (d6)Hit diceDamage
Small (1)7d42-8
Half-grown (2-3)13d44-16
Near-adult (4-6)13d64-24

Description: each has terrible deformities, such as an arm in the wrong place, huge feet on short legs, eyes on the sides like a fish’s or one in the back of the head, a humped back, a long pointed head, flapping ears, a gaping or tiny mouth, a huge nose or snout, and so on. They have scattered patches of hair as tough as wire.

Giants: general (MMII)

Giants are huge humanoids. There are 6 major races of giants, described in the MM, plus the minor races listed here and in the FF. Each race has some things in common with the others and many differences; the common traits are in the MM, “Giant”.
system.hpNote: Young: roll d6 for size (1 small, 2-3 half-grown, 4-6 near-adult) (MMII p.68).

system.treasure: Individuals M (x10), Q; in lair E, Y
system.description:
The firbolg is the most powerful of the minor races of giants. They are cautious, crafty, and have considerable magic power. They have learned to distrust (and fear) humans and are found only in remote, wild places. 90% of encounters are with small groups or a lone wanderer; 10% are with a gathering of several groups meeting for some purpose. These human-looking giants do not always greet strangers warmly, but usually do not try to kill them (unless provoked, of course). They do enjoy appearing as little people and cheating humans out of their treasure.

  • Weapons: they prefer two-handed swords and great halberds. All their weapons are very large: they use their preferred human-made weapons one-handed and their own with 1 or 2 hands. Their double-sized clubs, axes, spears, etc. do double normal damage used two-handed.
  • Batting missiles: with 1 hand free, a firbolg can bat away missiles such as arrows, bolts, bullets, darts, and stones, or catch projectiles such as javelins, spears, and boulders, twice per round, succeeding on 6 or better on d20 (75%).
  • Spell-like powers: besides magic resistance, each has these powers (by hit dice, whatever its age), usable at will, 1 per round, when not engaged in melee, each once per day: detect magic, diminution (as the potion, with double effect and double maximum duration), fool’s gold, forget, and alter self.
  • Shamans: a 5% chance per firbolg met that one of the group is a shaman. Besides the standard shaman spells, firbolg shamans use 2 1st-level illusionist spells per level, chosen at random, and at 6th and 7th levels gain 2nd-level illusionist spells, also random. So a 7th-level shaman has 10 1st-level and 4 2nd-level illusionist spells, on top of all its other spells and powers.

Giants: general (MMII)

Giants are huge humanoids. There are 6 major races of giants, described in the MM, plus the minor races listed here and in the FF. Each race has some things in common with the others and many differences; the common traits are in the MM, “Giant”.

system.treasure: Individuals K, L, M (x6); in lair B (but 25% for magic)
system.description:
Verbeeg, or human behemoths, are a race of human giants living in the same areas as hill giants and ogres (q.v.).

  • Encounters: 30% likely to be with hill giants (40%) or ogres (60%); 50% with 1-6 wanderers; 30% in the lair, with 5-30 verbeeg in all; and 20% with 1-2+ others (percentages as printed). Being intelligent, verbeeg usually command any hill giants or ogres they live with.
  • Armor: if they have them, they wear protective materials to improve their armor class: hides and furs, odd pieces of metal such as shields, and so on.
  • Weapons: usually clubs and spears, but those who can get better weapons do.
  • Strength: 18/51 to 18/00 (roll d10):
d10StrengthDamage bonusAdded throwing range
1-218/51-75+33”
3-618/76-90+44”
7-918/91-99+55”
018/00+66”
  • Spears: thrown spears have normal range plus the 3”-6” bonus, so a verbeeg with 18/00 strength hurls a spear up to 9” for 7-12 points of damage. Each has at least 3 spears.
  • Lair: always a leader with 18/00 strength and at least 40 hit points; 2 females for the leader and 1 for each other male; and young making up about 50% of the population over 9. Females equal males in combat; young fight as bugbears (50%) or goblins (50%). Guards: 2-8 wolves (75%) or 1-4 worgs (25%), or in arctic lands 1-3 winter wolves (25%) or 1-2 polar bears (75%).
  • Shamans: 2% chance per verbeeg met of a shaman of either sex, up to 7th level.
  • Magic: the group is 90% unlikely to have any magic item it cannot understand or use.

Description: unusually thin for their great height, otherwise human-looking. Some have deformities that only add to their fearsome look. Notable verbeeg are usually rogues who stalk humans (Jimmy Squarefoot and Jack-in-Irons are but two).
