system.description:
A muckdweller is a two-legged amphibian monster that lurks in swamps, marshes, or still, mud-bottomed waters. It eats plants, insects, aquatic animals, or even carrion, but prefers fresh warm-blooded meat.

  • Ambush: packs lie in wait for careless victims. When one comes near, several squirt jets of muddy water up to 10 feet at its eyes (save vs. wands negates; no save if surprised) while others climb out to bite with their small, sharp teeth.
  • Blinded victims: cannot act that round, and all attacks against them are at +2 (with no dexterity bonus to armor class).
  • Lair: always underwater, but with a muddy area above water for resting and eating where they pile up their hoards of shiny things. If 16 or more are met in their lair, there is double the listed type Q treasure.
  • Allies: on rare occasions they associate with lizard men, and some are reported serving kuo-toan masters.
  • Language: their own croaking, hissing tongue, and possibly that of lizard men.

Description: a mottled gray and brown back and a pale, yellowish belly. The short tail is used for swimming and walking on land. The toes of the front feet can grasp but are weak; the rear feet are partly webbed.

system.specialDefenses: Need magical weapons to hit; immune to certain spells (see below)
system.description:
Mud-men form in pools of mud where enchanted waters (even mildly enchanted ones, such as a stream wearing away a magical structure) gather, evaporate, and concentrate the dweomer. They are animated mud that takes a stocky humanoid form when roused. Slow and unable to leave their pool, they have one aim: to kill any creature entering the pool that moves better than they do, which means almost every creature and certainly all humans and demi-humans.

  • Dormant: they lie under the surface, their substance spread through the pool, feeding on the dweomer. In this state weapons (magical or not) cannot harm them, but spells can (see below).
  • Rising: they sense anything entering the pool at once, take 1 round to gather themselves and stand, and attack the next round. Once fully formed and standing, they can be harmed by magic weapons only.
  • Mud blobs: they attack by throwing mud, treating opponents as AC 10 (adjusted for dexterity). The mud hardens on impact. At first they throw blobs (range up to 6"), each hit slowing the victim’s movement by 1", while moving toward their opponents at full speed.
  • Hurling themselves: within 1" they literally throw themselves. A hit kills the mud-man but slows the victim’s movement by 4". A miss means it spends the next round re-forming before attacking again.
  • Suffocation: at zero movement the victim cannot move and starts to suffocate, taking 1-8 points of damage per round until the mouth and/or nose is cleared, and dies after 5 rounds unless rescued. Breaking away the hardened mud restores movement at 1" per 5 rounds.
  • Limits: they cannot sense creatures outside their pool and will not attack them. When no living opponents remain in the pool, they sink back under the surface, rising again if someone re-enters.

Spells:

  • All spells that directly damage living creatures affect them (e.g., cause light wounds, magic missile, fireball, flame strike).
  • Dispel magic and dig act as fireballs cast by a magic-user of the caster’s level.
  • Transmute mud to rock kills all mud-men it can affect, with no saving throw.
  • They are immune to poison, magical (e.g., cloudkill, poison) or not, and unaffected by spells that affect the mind (e.g., charm, sleep) and by psionics.
  • Until they are fully formed, damage from spells cast on them has no area of effect (e.g., magic missile) and is divided among them (fractions rounded down), since their bodies are spread evenly through the mud.

system.sizeText: S to L (2' per hit die)
system.description:
Myconids, or fungus men, look like walking toadstools in humanoid form. Their flesh is bloated and spongy, purple to gray. Each pudgy hand has 2 stubby fingers and a thumb on either side. They live deep underground where conditions suit fungi, never go to the surface, and fear direct sunlight terribly. (The exact effects of sunlight on them are unknown, but they must be harmful or the fungus men would not fear it so.)

  • Poison skin: except on the hands, their skin oozes a substance poisonous to animal flesh. Touching a myconid in most places does 1-4 points of damage to whoever touches it.
  • Size and damage: they grow 2 feet taller with each hit die: a 1-hit die myconid is 2 feet tall, the 6-hit dice king 12 feet. They fight by clubbing with clasped hands for 1d4 per hit die (1 hit die: 1-4; 2 hit dice: 2-8; and so on up to the king’s 6-24).

Circles: their society is built on "circles", very close groups bound by shared work and melding. A circle usually has 20 members, 4 of each size from 1 to 5 hit dice. Each day is rigidly set: 8 hours of rest, 8 hours farming fungus or other needed work, and 8 hours of melding. Melding is entertainment, worship, and social life in one: they gather in a tight circle, the elders release rapport and hallucinator spores, and the whole group shares a telepathic hallucination for 8 hours. Myconids consider melding the reason for existence; only distress spores bring a circle out of it early.

Spores: each time a myconid grows a size, it gains another kind of spore, and it can use each kind it has a number of times per day equal to its hit dice (at 3 hit dice: 3 kinds, 3 times each per day). In the order gained:

  • Distress (1 hit die): alerts other myconids to danger or a need for help. The cloud spreads 40 feet per round, to 120 feet at most, and gets the attention of all myconids around.
  • Reproducer (2 hit dice): released only at the right time to grow new myconids, keeping the population controlled. A dying myconid releases them automatically.
  • Rapport (3 hit dice): used mostly in melding, but also to talk with other species, since fungus men do not speak. A small puff at 1 creature: if it fails a save vs. poison, it can speak mind-to-mind with myconids normally. A willing creature may choose to fail the save. Lasts a number of turns equal to the originator’s hit dice.
  • Pacifier (4 hit dice): a single creature that fails a save vs. poison becomes totally passive, able only to watch and taking no action even if attacked, for rounds equal to the spewer’s hit dice.
  • Hallucinator (5 hit dice): used mostly in melding, but also works on others. A single creature that fails a save vs. poison has violent hallucinations for turns equal to the myconid’s hit dice, reacting as follows (1d20):
d20Reaction
1-10Cower whimpering
11-15Stare into nothingness
16-18Flee shrieking in a random direction
19-20Attack closest creature to kill
  • Animator (6 hit dice, the king only): the king infects a dead person or animal. A purple fungus covers the corpse, takes over its body systems, and puts them back to work, so it resembles a zombie (AC 10, MV 9", HD 1, hp 4, #AT 2, D bony claws for 1-3/1-3). It is not undead and cannot be turned by a cleric. Animated bodies are slower than in life and always strike last in a melee round. The body keeps rotting while the fungus slowly replaces missing parts, until the decay goes too far and the body stops, at rest at last. Animation starts 1-4 days after infection and lasts 2-5 weeks. Animated creatures follow simple orders (given by the animator with rapport spores) as well as they can, putting orders ahead of self-preservation.

The king: always the largest member of the colony, the only one of 6 hit dice, and the only myconid not in a circle. Other myconids regard separation from a circle with horror and pity the lonely king; leadership is seen as a very unpleasant duty, almost a sentence. When the old king dies, the strongest 5 hit dice myconid always becomes the new king. The king stays outside circle affairs to remain objective and attend to leading: it animates guardians so the others need not commit violence, sets the work schedule, watches outside events that could affect the colony, and practices fungal alchemy, brewing special potions that may help in times of trouble.

Outlook: myconids are generally peaceful, wanting only to work and meld. In combat they avoid killing if they can, since violence spoils their meld hallucinations. Still, fungoids and humanoids have never come to terms: each sees the other as a disgusting threat, and crowding in the limited underworld inevitably causes conflict.

Nereids come from the Elemental Plane of Water. Their name means "the honeyed ones". Out of the water they can take human form, always beautiful and mostly female: young and slim, with long golden hair, pale white skin, and lovely voices. They may be dressed in white and gold but are often unclothed. Each has a white shawl, carried in the hands or draped over head and shoulders. In water a nereid is transparent and 95% undetectable, except as golden angel seaweed.

Where found: the sea, rivers, wells, mountain and cavern springs, and the Elemental Plane of Water. Like their waters they are chaotic and capricious; whether good, neutral, or evil depends on the individual. Most are chaotic neutral, but some are very good and some diabolically evil. All are shy and flighty, and their antics are playful.

  • Spittle: her only physical attack (range 20 feet). A hit may blind the target for 2-12 rounds; water washes it away. A blinded victim attacks at −4, and his or her saves and armor class are 4 worse.
  • Water control (3" radius around her lair): she can make the water heave in great waves that slow movement to one-fourth of normal, or boil and froth, adding 10% to the chance of drowning. She can make waves crash so loudly that characters within 6" may be deafened for 3-12 rounds unless they take precautions. She can also form watery shapes, from pleasant entertainment to real defense: a watery serpent or fist that strikes as a 4 hit dice monster for 1-4 points of damage, 1 such attack per round.
  • Charm over men: any male who looks at her cannot bring himself to harm her, and her actions seem like casual flirting. Men have sat watching a nereid all day, and many have tried to take one as a wife or chase her for her embrace, with disastrous results: her kiss can bring sweet bliss, or a watery doom.
  • Capture: if caught she may save vs. poison; if she succeeds, she flows away like water. If a kiss is forced from her (she hates to give them), the character must save vs. breath weapons at −2 or drown instantly; otherwise ecstasy is his.
  • The shawl: her great weakness, since it holds her soul. If it is destroyed, she dissolves into formless water. A character who gets her shawl can command her, and she obeys out of fear, but she will lie and try almost anything short of hostile acts to get it back.
  • Pets: 85% likely to have one. Roll 1d8:
d8Pet
1Eel, giant
2Otter, giant
3Snake, giant (poisonous)
4Octopus, giant
5Squid, giant
6Dolphin
7Leech, giant
8Ray, sting

Narwhales, the "unicorns of the ocean", are common in cool to cold waters. They are large marine mammals, about 20-40+ feet long, not counting the spiral "horn" of 6-12 feet. They are basically non-aggressive, but defend themselves with the great horn if seriously threatened or actually attacked. Communities of dolphins use them as pets and guards, and aquatic elves sometimes train and use them.

This evil black moss can magically steal memories.

  • Stealing: an intelligent creature within 60 feet must save vs. spells or lose all its memories of the last 24 hours, including memorized spells. The moss tries 1 creature per round until it succeeds, then does not attack again for 24 hours.
  • Mossling: if attacked while holding stolen memories, in 1 round it forms part of itself into a tiny moss copy of the creature it stole from. This mossling stays attached to the parent and can defend itself only by casting any stolen spells.
  • Getting memories back: the only way is to eat the living moss, which takes 1 round. With a successful save vs. poison the eater gains all the stolen memories, spells included; on a failure the eater is very ill for 3-18 turns. Someone else’s memories can be gained this way too, and anyone who gains spells by eating it can cast them. Memories gained this way fade in 24 hours.

The aquatic ogre is usually faster, tougher, and fiercer than its land kin.

  • Attack: usually a swimming charge with a piercing spear (2-12 points) "at 1 to hit" (as printed), followed by melee with talons and teeth.
  • Hiding: its green coloring lets it hide (in effect invisible 10-80% of the time, depending on terrain) and attack from cover, surprising 4 in 6.
  • Habitat: fairly shallow water 50-250 feet deep, lairing in caves, often with scrags. It can survive out of water up to 2 hours, so it sometimes raids the land.
  • Stronger ogres: among 7-12, 1 has 31-36 hit points; among 13-18, 2 do; among 19-24, 3 do.
  • Language: Ogre and their own dialect.

In the lair:

  • 1 chief, AC 3, 6+6 hit dice, +2 on damage;
  • 2 sub-chiefs, AC 3, 5+5 hit dice, +1 on damage;
  • 2-24 females, AC 5, 3+3 hit dice, 1-2/1-2/1-6 damage;
  • 1-12 young, AC 6, 2+2 hit dice, 1-2/1-2/1-4 damage;
  • 1 shaman, normal male or female.

Description: greenish and scaly with sloping shoulders, a long and very thick neck, a huge mouth and undershot jaw, and webbed hands and feet.
system.hpNote: Among 7-12 merrow 1 has 31-36 hit points; among 13-18, 2; among 19-24, 3 (MMII p.96).

system.description:
The oliphant is probably a modern-day relative of the Pleistocene mastodon. Its hairy hide lets it live in cooler temperate or subarctic climates. It is solitary and avoids inhabited areas, and can be captured and trained if young enough.

  • Attack: down-curving tusks and heavy forelegs; the trunk is too short to be a useful weapon. It can fight 4 man-sized opponents at once, 2 ogre-sized, or 1 giant-sized.
  • War beasts: properly trained, they become engines of destruction, especially the large males. Fed and cared for, they can grow 10 feet or more in size (10+5 hit dice) and bulk, far bigger than wild ones. For war they are armored with leather or scale and plate, given spikes on the head and forelegs, and carry castle-like howdahs of archers and pikemen. Elephants are armed this way in warm climates, but those less intelligent beasts lack a trained oliphant’s ferocity.
  • Temper: it does not fear fire unless directly threatened, and tends to remove threats rather than flee.
  • Ivory: each tusk is worth 100-400 gp, the ivory about 4 gp per pound.
  • Groups: if 3 or more are met, check each one beyond the first 2: 25% a calf, 75% half-grown. Young are evenly split between male and female. Single oliphants are always male, and a group of 2 or more has only 1 mature male.

Ophidians, or snakemen, usually live in tropical jungles. Unlike nagas, they have human-like arms and hands and can use weapons, shields, and the kinds of magic items fighters can use.

  • Attack: first a weapon, then a fanged bite.
  • Affliction: a bitten victim must save vs. poison or suffer a lycanthropy-like affliction. It starts in 2-5 days and lasts 8-16 days, ending by turning the victim into an ophidian if human or humanoid, or killing it otherwise. A cure disease spell prevents it.
  • Masters: they rarely form groups of their own; usually they serve spirit nagas or similar creatures.

Description: short-tailed, thick-bodied snakes with human-like arms sticking out about 2 feet below the neck, ending in 4-fingered hands. Colors range from gray-black to black and from dark brownish green to pale blue-green.

Opinicus are desert creatures of good will, usually found in old ruins such as a deserted city, palace, or temple, and now and then elsewhere, usually on some good errand. They are known for kind acts and friendliness, but also love teasing and jokes. That makes them less popular, but good creatures very rarely turn down their help. Creatures of Evil certainly dread them.

  • Attacks: 2 claws (1-3/1-3) and rakes with the rear claws.
  • Spells: as 7th-level clerics, and they can turn undead.
  • Powers: holy word once per day, dimension door twice per day, and heal 3 times per day.
  • Sun sparkles: a glowing gaze in a ½" × 1" × 2" cone, usable once every 10 rounds, affecting undead and creatures of the Lower Outer Planes (Acheron, the Nine Hells, Gehenna, Hades, Tartarus, the Abyss, and Pandemonium). It does 2-16 points of damage, half if a save vs. spells succeeds.
  • Senses: never surprised; they surprise 5 in 6 in their home and 3 in 6 elsewhere.
  • Travel: astrally and ethereally.
  • Psionics: 3-5 minor and 1-2 major disciplines, often used for pranks.

Description: they look like a mix of monkey, camel, lion, and eagle, though they are a creature in their own right. Color runs from light buff to golden brown, the wings slightly darker than the body. The forepaws can grasp.

Otters are water-dwelling relatives of the weasel and its kin, found in rivers, ponds, and lakes. The sea otter, the largest ordinary otter, lives along shallow coastal waters; its differences are in parentheses above. Otters are fast and playful, attack only if cornered, and their pelts are valued as fur.

Owls of various kinds live in every climate. Some are smaller than those these statistics cover, but most encounters are with the large ones.

  • Attack: talons and beak. Diving from 50 feet or higher, it gets +2 to hit and does double damage, but cannot use its beak.
  • Senses: double normal ultravision and four times normal hearing, and they fly in total silence.
  • Surprise: they surprise prey 5 in 6 and are never surprised at dusk or in darkness. From twilight to daylight they see just under the human standard, so despite their hearing they are surprised 3 in 6 if discovered in their hidden daytime roost.
  • Taming: they cannot be trained to hunt, but can be partly tamed if taken young and used to people.
  • Decoys: daytime birds (crows, ravens, etc., normally prey of night-hunting owls) flock to attack an owl found by day, and in their anger and determination to kill it they lose all caution, so hunters sometimes use owls as decoys.

The Para-elemental Plane of Cold (Ice) lies where the Elemental Planes of Air and Water meet. Para-elementals from that wintry land look like tall, see-through white humanoids coated with frost. They have a loose organization with no set leader, though there are rumors of several powerful ice-lords on their plane.

  • Cold aura: anyone within 10 feet takes 1-4 points of damage per round from the intense cold around it.
  • Freezing touch: it can freeze water, or liquids that are mostly water, up to 100 square feet per round to a depth of 6 inches.
  • Healing: in contact with ice, snow, or sleet it can heal itself at 1-8 hit points per round, taking no further damage while healing.
  • Vulnerabilities: cold does half damage; fire-based attacks do double damage. Its attacks against cold-using opponents are at −1 on the damage dice.

Para-Elementals: general (MMII)

Para-elementals live on the para-elemental planes, Ice, Ooze, Magma, and Smoke, which lie between the major planes of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.

  • Summoning: they are summoned like normal elementals, except that there is a chance of getting an elemental from one of the 2 major elemental planes next to it instead. The chance is 100% minus 5% per level of the summoner.
  • Strength: like major elementals, conjured ones come in 3 hit dice strengths: 16 HD by spell, 12 HD by summoning device, and 8 HD by staff.
  • Defenses: weapons of less than +1 enchantment cannot harm them, nor can creatures of 4 hit dice or less without magical ability.
  • Control: as with ordinary elementals, control must be kept at all times, or it turns on its summoner.
  • Material components (besides a large amount of the element): a lens of clear crystal or glass for ice; a damp cloth for ooze; volcanic glass for magma; dry ash for smoke.
system.hpNote: Conjured by staff 8 HD, by summoning device 12 HD, by spell 16 HD (MMII p.98).

system.description:
The Para-elemental Plane of Smoke is a dry, empty place with few long-term residents. Smoke para-elementals have no king, but several exceptional ones rule small pockets of the others and usually feud for control of the plane.

  • Movement: drifting along the ground as black ash, or flying as a concentrated blast of black fog. The fog form has maneuverability class E but does double damage when it hits. Forming or dissolving the fog form takes a full turn.
  • Attacks: it can engage every target within 10 feet. All within 10 feet must save vs. poison or be −2 to hit from the blinding smoke.
  • Air attacks: all air-based attacks on it, including those of air elementals, are −1 on the damage dice.

Para-elementals live on the para-elemental planes, Ice, Ooze, Magma, and Smoke, which lie between the major planes of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.

system.description:
Magma para-elementals, often called heat para-elementals, come from the Para-elemental Plane of Magma, a rocky, volcanic place at the edges of the Elemental Planes of Fire and Earth: a lonely plain spotted with volcanoes. Its natives do their tasks in packs with no set leader, though there may be exceptional ones with magical power. Summoned ones are humanoid from the waist up, their legs and torsos molten rock, their eyes and mouths glowing reddish from the fire inside.

  • Heat: works like the druid spell heat metal on everything within 20 feet. Round 1: metal grows hot. Round 2: metal armor and weapons do 1-4 points of damage to their users. Round 3 and later: characters using metal take 2-8 points, others 1-4.
  • Leaving the area: damage drops 1 step at once and is gone the round after.
  • Fire: wood and other flammable things touching the para-elemental, or metal it has heated, burst into flame.

system.description:
The ooze para-elemental, also called the mud elemental, looks like a liquid mass of dark, writhing tendrils. The Elemental Plane of Ooze is a cloudy, gray plane at the borders of the Elemental Planes of Water and Earth, and both water and earth creatures can be found there. Ooze para-elementals have no fixed leader, but several slime-barons compete for control.

  • Constriction: a hit means it has wrapped a tendril around its opponent, squeezing for 2-16 points of damage per round until the para-elemental is dispelled or defeated, or lets go on its summoner’s command.
  • Several victims: it can constrict any number of opponents, but can attack and catch only 1 at a time. A captured character can still attack, but may be swept off his feet and carried off.
  • Shape: its form can change, so it slips into tight cracks and under doors with ease.

Para-Elementals: general (MMII)

system.description:
No one knows what pech really are, or whether they come from the Prime Material Plane or the Plane of Earth. These spindly creatures live in dark places and work stone, and their flesh is nearly as hard as granite. They are basically good and want to be left alone. They hate bright light and open sky, and have both infravision and ultravision.

  • Lair: several larger pech, as many females as males, and young equal to 20-50% of the females. Also 50-100 gems, plus dishes and ornaments of ornamental stone and raw metal (5-30 pieces of jewelry of lowest base value, average weight 150 gp each).
  • Weapons: picks and peat hammers (treat as war hammers) for work and fighting, usually in equal numbers.
  • Spells: each can cast stone shape and stone tell 4 times per day. Four together can cast wall of stone as 16th-level magic-users; eight together can cast stone to flesh. Each group spell can be cast only once per day by any group.
  • Stone: immune to petrification. Against stony monsters such as a stone golem, their knowledge of stone lets them attack normally and knock it to rubble.

Description: thin, with long arms and legs and broad hands and feet, excellent for bracing and using tools on stone. Pale yellowish skin, red or red-brown hair, and large eyes without pupils.

Pedipalps, commonly called whip scorpions, live in almost any climate except arctic or tundra. They look like a cross between a spider and a scorpion, in various colors, browns and tans being most common.

Large pedipalp: the smallest, the schizomidae, have no obvious whips, but do have 2 grasping arms and fearsome mandibles. They cannot hold prey larger than themselves.

Huge pedipalp: the amblypygi have 2 whip-like limbs in place of 1 pair of legs, and another pair of legs ending in spiny pincers, used to attack. They also bite. After a hit, a huge pedipalp grips and automatically does crushing damage (the same as 2 pincer hits; 2-12) every round after. The chance of breaking free is the same as opening doors.

Giant pedipalp: the largest, the uropygi, have whip-like tails and forelegs ending in large pincers. The tail looks dangerous but is not used to attack.

  • Attacks: 2 pincers and a bite. After a hit it grips, automatically bites (2-8 points) and crushes (the same as 2 pincer hits; 2-16) every round after.
  • Breaking the grip: only by killing it or cutting off the pincer, which needs a roll 3 higher than the normal to-hit number.
  • Vapor: in combat it gives off a harmful vapor, 3 times per day, in a 20-foot radius. Non-pedipalp creatures there who fail a save vs. poison fight at −3 to hit for 1-6 rounds.

  • Breaking the grip: only by killing it or cutting off the pincer, which needs a roll 3 higher than the normal to-hit number.

Phantoms are soulless shells left behind by an especially strong death trauma, like a three-dimensional moving picture recorded at the time and place of a character’s death. A phantom often shows the death itself, or whatever was foremost in the character’s mind at the end. It has no intelligence and is neither alive nor undead.

  • Harm: phantoms are only images: they cannot cause harm directly and cannot be harmed.
  • Fear: because of the superstitious awe they inspire, anyone who looks at a phantom’s see-through form must save vs. spells at −2 or panic and run away at once, as from a fear spell.
  • Dispelling: often mistaken for ghosts, haunts, or groaning spirits, but they cannot be turned as undead. The clerical spell exorcism dispels one.
system.hpNote: A phantom is only an image and cannot be harmed (MMII p.100).

system.psionicText: See below Attack/Defense Modes: See below
system.description:
The phoenix, very rarely seen on the Prime Material Plane, comes from Elysium in the Upper Outer Planes. Cold, heat, and similar conditions do not harm it, so it could live in almost any climate or even the void, but it prefers beauty and sylvan peace and on the Prime Material Plane is usually found only in such places. Sadly, its feathers sell for an average of 50 gp each, its gem-like beak, talons, and eyes for a hundred times that, and alchemists prize its body for certain potions, so the rare phoenix is rarer still.

  • Attacks: in flight, its diamond-hard talons; on the ground, a single attack with its long, sharp beak. Being intelligent and magical, it usually prefers better means of attack and defense.
  • Whistle: its piercing whistle affects opponents within 30 feet so that it gets +3 on its initiative die, letting it act first in melee.

Spell-like powers (one at a time, 1 per melee round, at 20th level):

  • At will: affect normal fires, audible glamer, blink, blindness, blur, control temperature in a 10-foot radius, continual light, dancing lights, find traps, fire charm, fire shield, improved invisibility, misdirection, produce fire, pyrotechnics, remove curse, remove fear in a 10-foot radius, and snake charm.
  • 3 times per day: color spray, heat metal, polymorph self.
  • Once per day: call woodland beings, duo-dimension, find the path, fire quench, fire seeds, fire storm, neutralize poison, reincarnate, veil, wall of fire.
  • Once per week: incendiary cloud.
  • Wings and call: spreading its wings and calling acts as dispel illusion or dispel magic at 40th level.
  • Dance: acts as a double-strength (40th level) exorcise spell, working against all but the greatest evil magic, such as that of an artifact or relic.
  • Senses: automatically detects charms, evil, and magic. Never surprised. Infravision to 120 feet and double normal ultravision.
  • Protection: radiates protection from evil in a 10-foot radius. Hit only by +3 or better weapons.
  • Travel: it can become ethereal and travel astrally or ethereally.
  • Healing: a touch of its wing equals cure light wounds, 2 touches per person per day per phoenix. A touch of its comb equals cure disease, limited as a staff of curing is.
  • Blood: when hard-pressed, spilled drops of its blood act as holly-berry fire seeds, 1 for every 5 points of damage it takes.
  • Last resort: in extremity it creates a double-strength (40th level) combined fire storm (2" high × 5" wide × 8" deep) and incendiary cloud, even if it has already used those powers. This destroys the adult phoenix but leaves a gem-like egg from which a new phoenix rises in 20 days.
  • Communication: its own language and speech with all birds; otherwise limited telepathy, or limited empathy and telempathy.
  • Psionics: it cannot attack or be attacked by psionic means, but has these disciplines: cell adjustment (cleric class) once per day at 20th level; energy control 3 times per day; molecular agitation 3 times per day at 20th level; probability travel once per week at 10th level.

Description: like a peacock but far larger, with a proportionally longer beak. Its plumage has bright violet, scarlet, crimson, and flaming orange areas; beak and claws are blue-violet; the eyes are a deep, glowing ruby.

Phycomids are algae-like fungoid monsters that look like fibrous blobs of rotting, milky matter with capped fungi growing from them. Their sense organs for heat, sound, and vibration sit in several clusters.

  • Attack: it pushes out a tube and fires small globules of highly alkaline fluid, range 7-12 feet.
  • Infection: besides the alkaline damage, a victim who fails a save vs. poison becomes a host for new growth. In 5-8 rounds mushroom-like growths sprout in the infected area, doing 5-8 points of damage. The growths then spread through the body, killing it in 5-8 turns and turning it into a new phycomid. A cure disease spell stops the spread.
  • Immunities: all mental attacks, including charms, holds, etc.
  • Fire: it saves against fire-based attacks at +4, taking half damage or none.

A planetar is one of a powerful group of spirits, numbering at least 100, who serve the deities of good alignment. One or more usually serve as the right hand of a minor deity, while a major deity has many in attendance. They live on the Upper Outer Planes of Good but can travel at will to any plane except the lowest (the Hells, Gehenna, Hades, Tarterus, the Abyss), and if their deity commands, even into those. Only a solar (q.v.) is more powerful in the cause of Good.

A planetar may be of any good alignment (lawful, neutral, or chaotic), set by the master it serves.

  • Attacks: 3 per round, usually with a bastard sword (usable only by planetars) equal to a +4 weapon with both defender (q.v.) and wounding (q.v.) qualities, the wounding working only against creatures of Evil. For attacks, treat it as having dexterity 21 and 17th-level fighting ability.
  • Spells: spell-like abilities equal to a 7th-level cleric and a 7th-level druid, with bonuses for wisdom 21.
  • Protection: it radiates a globe of protection from evil, from its own size up to a full 40-foot radius as it wishes, kept up automatically.
  • Always: it can commune when needed; cure blindness, deafness, disease, or light wounds by touch; automatically detect evil, illusion, invisibility, lie, magic, and traps; and has know alignment working at all times. It communicates by ESP or tongues and can read any language. Infravision to 12" and ultravision at double normal range.
  • Gate (once per day): the listed number (1-3, 1-4, or 1-6) of the right kind of deva (q.v.): astral, monadic, or movanic.
  • Summon (once per day): lawful good, 1-4 couatl; neutral good, 1-2 baku; chaotic good, 1-2 androsphinx.

Spell-like abilities (one at a time, 1 per round, at will):

  • At will: continual light up to 10" radius, etherealness, polymorph object, improved invisibility up to 10-foot radius, polymorph self, read magic, remove curse, remove fear, resist cold (double effect), resist fire (double effect), speak with dead, teleport without error.
  • 7 times per day: dispel illusion, wind walk.
  • 3 times per day: blade barrier, dispel evil, dispel magic, flame strike, heal, raise dead, true seeing.
  • Once per day: animate object, control weather, earthquake, feeblemind, limited wish (listed twice, as printed), fire storm, holy word, insect plague, restoration, shape change, symbol (any), weather summoning.

Defenses:

  • Affected by the attack forms given for devas (q.v.). Only +4 or better weapons affect it.
  • Never surprised. Immune to all life level loss, from undead or magic, and to death spells. It cannot be beguiled, charmed, confused, dominated, or feebleminded, and its soul cannot be imprisoned or trapped.
  • Regenerates 4 points per round.
  • Unless met on the Upper Outer Planes, only its material body can be harmed; its spirit returns to its own plane to re-form and become solid again, which takes 4 decades.
  • Charisma effect is 21.

Psionics: animal telepathy (14th level), aura alteration, body control, body equilibrium, body weaponry (9th level), mass domination (17th level), molecular agitation, precognition, reduction, telekinesis (17th level), and telepathic projection.

Description: a tall, powerful humanoid. In material form the skin is opaline, the head hairless, the eyes glowing blue, and the double wings also opaline.

system.xp: Treat as human fighters (except pseudoghast, as below)
system.description:
Pseudo-undead are humanoids who thrive because they look like certain undead: ghouls, ghasts, wights, wraiths, spectres, and vampires. Each looks and smells exactly like its double, appears in the same numbers, and has the same armor class, movement rate, hit dice, number of attacks, and damage, so they can be fairly dangerous.

  • No special attacks: they lack the undead’s special attacks (paralysis, level drain, etc.), but have normal (6") infravision.
  • Pseudo-ghasts: their stench has the same effect as a ghast’s.
  • Pseudo-wraiths and pseudo-spectres: cannot fly, but walk so lightly they leave no trace and, unless closely watched, seem to float above the ground (an illusion).
  • Pseudo-vampires: red eyes and menacing behavior, but no special abilities. They are the most nearly human and have been known to interbreed. Several bandit (q.v.) clans came about this way, their members ranging from normal bandits (though pale and menacing) to leaders and spell casters with full pseudo-vampire status plus their bandit abilities. Other mixes of man and pseudo-vampire may be possible.
  • Not undead: clerics cannot turn them, and they have no link to the Negative Material Plane. They avoid sunlight but are not harmed by it, are never found with or near true undead, and normal attacks affect them.
system.hpNote: Same hit dice as the undead it imitates (MMII p.102): roll those.

system.sizeText: S to L (3' d. to 8' d.)
system.description:
Each of these deadly puddings is a variety of the better-known black (deadly) pudding.

  • All deadly puddings: acid, cold, and poison have no effect. Lightning bolts or weapon blows split them into smaller, living creatures. Fire and magic missiles do normal damage. See "Black Pudding" for how they move.
  • Brown pudding: lives mainly in marshes. It has tougher skin but a weaker attack than the others. It does not dissolve metal, but destroys leather or wood in a single round, whatever its magical pluses.
  • Dun pudding: adapted to dry regions, it scavenges barrens and deserts and feeds on silicates when no animal or vegetable matter is available. It dissolves leather as a brown pudding does, and eats metal at half a black pudding’s rate (chain mail in 2 rounds, plate in 4). Otherwise it is like a brown pudding.
  • White pudding: lives in cold places and is 50% likely to be mistaken for snow and ice even under the best conditions. It haunts polar or icy regions looking for prey, though it can live on any animal or vegetable material, and even ice gives it enough to survive. It does not affect metal, but dissolves animal or vegetable material in a single round, damaging flesh at an astounding rate. Attack forms affect it as they do all deadly puddings.

Pudding, Deadly: general (MMII)

Brown, dun, and white puddings: what they share, and how each differs, is given in the brown pudding description.

This monster is almost identical to the cockatrice (q.v.), but a close look shows 1 red feather in its tail and a reddish tint to its gray wings. Like its cousin, it lives in temperate to tropical regions. Its mortal enemy is the phoenix, which is also immune to fire and hates Evil.

  • Beak: a minor attack.
  • Gaze: anyone who meets it bursts into flame from within, dying at once if a save vs. petrification fails, or taking 2-13 points of damage otherwise. A creature naturally or magically fire-resistant (by spell, ring, or other effect) is immune, and a victim who saves is immune to that pyrolisk’s gaze from then on.
  • Fireworks: at will, once per round, just for the joy of the flames, it can make any fire source within 30 feet explode in fireworks, the same as the druid spell pyrotechnics (q.v.). The effect covers 10 times the fire source’s area, lasts a full round, and temporarily blinds everyone in it.
  • Immunity: all fire-based attacks, magical and normal.
system.hpNote: Hit dice are printed as “43” (MMII p.103), with no other figure given. Set hit points by hand.

system.description:
Lightning quasi-elementals live on the Elemental Plane of Air and the Positive Material Plane, and are rare even there. In a great lightning storm on the Material Plane, large numbers sometimes gather to feed and reproduce. They have no known social organization. They generally cannot be conjured, though powerful magic-users have been known to do it.

  • Arcing: besides normal movement, it can "arc", leaping up to 6" to any grounded or metal object of more than 50 gp mass, at the beginning or end of its movement.
  • Sizes: 3 hit dice categories. On the Prime Material Plane the small 6-hit-die kind is most common (60%), the 9-hit-die kind less so (30%), and the 12 (or more)-hit-die kind rarest (10%). On the Elemental Plane these are reversed: smallest 10%, medium 30%, largest 60%.
  • Attacks: an electrical discharge by touch. Each round it can also release 1 small globe of ball lightning, for 6, 9, or 12 rounds (by hit dice). The globe floats near it until a creature of large mass (2000 gp or more) or carrying much conductive metal comes within 5 feet, then moves to it and discharges for 1-4, 1-6, or 1-8 points of damage, by the size of the quasi-elemental that made it.
  • Weapons: only +1 or better magic weapons harm it. A wielder whose weapon is conductive takes 1-4 points of electrical damage each time it hits.
  • Other attacks: lightning and electricity do no damage. Fire and acid do half damage; cold does full damage. Water does 1-8 points per gallon, or double full normal damage (an ice storm does 6-60). Falling water such as rain does 2 points for each 1/10th of an inch that falls on it.
system.hpNote: On the Prime Material Plane: 6 HD 60%, 9 HD 30%, 12 (or more) HD 10%; reversed on the Elemental Plane (MMII p.103).

system.description:
These small, slender, extremely fast creatures are said to be brownies who meddled with magic and mysteries better left alone; legend says they were changed into evil creatures with great malice toward humans, demi-humans, and other little folk. They live in dark woodlands and wild, evil places.

  • Leaders: any group has 1 of 3 hit dice. If more than 10 are met, 2 have 3 hit dice and 1 is a leader of 4½ hit dice. Leaders are 75% likely to have a poison: after each dagger hit the victim must save vs. poison or fall into a drugged sleep.
  • Speed: their amazing speed gives them an excellent armor class and 3 attacks per round with their needle-like daggers.
  • Powers (once per day each, one at a time, at will): ventriloquism, forget, levitate, shatter, dig, and fire charm.
  • Seeing them: 90% likely to be visible when moving because of their speed (as printed). Motionless in natural cover they are totally invisible; when attacking they are only a blur.
  • Saves: their speed and dexterity (18) let them save against all attack forms as 19th-level clerics. They cannot be surprised.
  • Languages: their own, Brownie, Pixie, and Halfling. Most know many words of Common, but speak it too high and too fast to be easily understood.
  • Lifespan: short, because they live so fast. They mature at about 1 or 2 years and die between 12 and 15.
system.hpNote: The book gives no method for half a hit die; 1d4 for the half die is one way, not a printed rule. Groups have 1 of 3 HD; over 10, 2 of 3 HD and a 4½ HD leader (MMII p.103).

system.description:
Some say the quickwood grows only through the magic of a great wizard (or perhaps druid) who planted a mandragora root after casting mighty spells on it; others say these weird trees are plant life naturally advancing toward something like man. Either way, the quickwood is certainly intelligent, unlike most plants. It looks like an oak, but a close look reveals a face-like set of sense organs resembling a twisted human face. The "face" is 90% unlikely to be noticed unless the observer is within 30 feet (10 feet if the tree is hiding by not using its sense organs). It grows anywhere normal oaks do, including warmer lands with live oaks.

  • Roots: moving its huge trunk is very hard, so it stays still if it can. It sends out thick roots that move 3" per round through loose topsoil, range 30 yards, and can seize and hold still any creature under 1000 pounds. They are too strong to break and blunt weapons do not damage them, but edged weapons can cut one off (treat roots as large, 10 hit points each; root damage does not count toward killing the tree). After 6 roots are cut it pulls its other 7-12 to safety. The roots themselves do no damage.
  • Bite: its limbs are too stiff to attack with, but a mouth-like opening can clamp shut for 3-12 points of damage. This is only a danger to a victim touching the trunk or forced into reach by a root.
  • Senses: lesser roots spread out to sense approaching creatures, and its leaves detect air movement and pressure changes. Its eyes, ears, and nose (like large human ones) are slightly better than human, with infravision to 120 feet.
  • Host trees: a mature spy tree can possess 2-8 normal oaks, which then look like quickwoods, with faces and sense organs through which the master controls them and gathers information, up to 36" away.
  • Defenses: plant-affecting spells work on it, but most others do not. It can sweat, drenching itself so fire does not harm it. Lightning is channeled off harmlessly. Poisons and gases do not harm it, and mind-affecting spells do not affect it. Disintegrate certainly destroys one.
  • Spell energy: when attacked by a spell, it uses the spell’s energy to radiate fear in a radius of 10 feet per spell level. If the caster fails a saving throw, all the energy goes into the fear; otherwise the fear is just a side effect and the spell works normally.
  • Service: quickwoods are sometimes charmed or persuaded to hold treasure or guard an area. Treasure (typical of whoever put it there) is always kept inside the trunk opening. As a guardian it watches for intruders and, on seeing them, makes a hollow drumming sound heard a mile or more away.

Rams live in subarctic to temperate lands, preferring rocky, hilly grasslands and avoiding heavy woods.

  • Numbers: 25% of encounters are with a lone animal; others are with 1-6 rams plus 3-18 ewes and half as many lambs.
  • Attack: rams attack threats to the herd only if the herd cannot run away. A charge of 20 feet more (as printed) adds +1 to hit and doubles damage.
  • Ewes and lambs: ewes only butt and do not charge; lambs do not fight.

Rats of every size and color live everywhere from wild forest to city sewers. They are cowardly, but a trapped or cornered rat fights fiercely, and starving packs attack anything alive to feed.

  • Disease: like giant rats, their filthy bite has a 5% chance of causing a serious disease unless a save vs. poison succeeds.
  • Fire: normal rats fear fire, but hunger sometimes drives them to brave it.

Vapor rats look like nothing more than large, gray giant rats, but they also live in and on the solid cloud islands that are often home to cloud giants.

  • Gaseous form: they can change their bodies into gas, looking like wisps of cloud or similar vapor. In that state they steer like a ship before the wind, drifting from cloud to cloud.
  • Solid form: they move very fast, swim well, and burrow quickly through loose soil or cloud-island material.
  • Attack: if angry, hungry, or cornered, they scurry in and bite.
  • Death puff: whenever one is killed or badly wounded, it gives off a small puff of noxious fumes equal to a stinking cloud spell (q.v.), affecting only 1 individual within 5-8 feet. The rat always aims it at its opponent, and the gas thins out beyond that distance. So killing them from afar is safe, but up close they are especially dangerous.
  • Escape: wounded or seriously threatened, they always turn to gas. Then only attacks that destroy their vapors can harm them: very hot or magical fire, lightning, and exceptionally strong winds.
  • Treasure: like all rats they are omnivores who love garbage and carrion. They do not seek treasure, but the remains of meals may hold valuables. In the lair there is a 25% chance for each of: J (1-4), K (1-4), L (1-4), M (1-4), N (1-2), and type C for gems, jewelry, and magic.

Ravens (or rooks) and crows live from cold-temperate to tropical climates. They are mainly scavengers, but as omnivores they raid crops, nests, and unguarded food stores.

  • Scouts: they travel in flocks, though a few may seem to be alone; these are scouts. When a threatening creature is spotted, the scouts cry a warning, hide themselves, and keep a safe distance while tracking it and reporting to the flock by harsh calls and perhaps movements. So they can never be surprised in daylight.
  • Eye attack: being intelligent, they are 10% likely to go for an eye: whenever a to-hit roll hits, there is a 1 in 10 chance the eye is attacked and lost.
  • Speech: they have their own limited language. Some ravens, including some huge and most giant ones, can speak as many as 100 words of Common in meaningful phrases.
  • Huge ravens: tend to be malicious and serve evil masters when they can.
  • Giant ravens: combative and easily trained if raised from fledglings, so often used as guards and messengers. Their nests may hold type Q treasure (1 in 6 chance per nest, base gem value 10 gp).
  • Shiny things: all love glittering objects, so nests are 25% likely to hold several small metal objects, gems, and the like.

The retch plant, or globe palm, grows only in warm climates. It is an ordinary palm tree except that it always has 5-8 globe-like, coconut-sized fruits at its top. Each globe is a tight membrane, blue, violet, or lilac in color.

  • Bursting: a globe bursts on striking, splashing a nauseating fluid over a 5-foot radius (25% chance of splash at 5-9 feet). Creatures splashed vomit and retch for the next 3 rounds, then are at 50% of normal strength for 6 turns (1 hour). No saving throw.
  • Smell: unless washed in alcohol (wine, beer, brandy, etc. will do), the splashed are much more likely to attract nearby carnivores: check at double the normal frequency, with double the chance of an encounter. The odor carries 50 feet and lasts 1-4 hours.
  • Falling fruit: walking under one gives a 20% chance a globe falls. Solid contact with the trunk (banging against it, running into it, or climbing it) brings down 2-5 globes.

This weird lizard has a lumpy, warty hide and can change color like a chameleon, so it lies in wait in rocky places looking like nothing more than a pile of rubble. It prefers darkness but will come out by day if hungry enough.

  • Rush: its first rush is at double speed, surprising prey 3 in 6.
  • Treasure: since it drags prey to its lair, there may be bits of treasure there: 25% each for types J, K, L, and M, plus types Q, S × ¼, and T × ½. If 2 are met, they have double metal and gems only.

hpOptions.label: 5 HD (then add 1 hit point per foot of length)

system.hpNote: Printed “5+1 hp/1 foot of length”: add 1 hit point for each foot of the reptile’s length by hand.

system.specialDefenses: Immune to sleep, hold, charm and other mind influencing spells
system.description:
A sandling looks like a shapeless mass of moving, sliding sand. Adults are solitary and live in lonely sandy places such as empty deserts, sandy caverns, and deserted beaches. They seem to be silicon-based, and some sages believe they came from the Elemental Plane of Earth.

  • Territory: fiercely territorial, they attack any trespasser, slashing and cutting with a coarse, gritty pseudopod.
  • Armor: their flexible, shifting form is hard to damage physically (hence AC 3).
  • Water: 10 gallons or more of water or other liquid poured on one acts as a slow spell, and it strikes for only half damage (1-8).
  • Growth: it grows to full size (10 feet across) and then buds. The tiny ones grow to about 2 inches before splitting from the parent, so an adult’s territory often swarms with thousands of young, none larger than 1/2 foot across. One that grows past this is seen as a threat and killed by the parent. When the parent dies, the largest young grows to replace it, killing all rivals if it can.
  • Tripping: a group of young together forms an uneven surface that may trip the unwary.
  • Senses: heat, sound, and moisture. They dislike wet and burrow underground to avoid rain or water unless already defending their territory.
  • Infravision: always the same temperature as their surroundings, so infravision cannot see them.

There are unconfirmed reports of huge sandlings 3 times the size of normal adults.

Large scorpions, often found in dungeons and wilderness, are just smaller versions of the giant scorpion. Each attacks with pincers and a tail stinger. A victim struck by the stinger must save vs. poison or die instantly, but the large scorpion’s poison is weaker than normal (+2 on the saving throw).

Large scorpions, often found in dungeons and wilderness, are just smaller versions of the giant scorpion. Each attacks with pincers and a tail stinger. A victim struck by the stinger must save vs. poison or die instantly, but the large scorpion’s poison is weaker than normal (+2 on the saving throw).

Scum creepers are small, slug-like things that live underground or in gloomy swamps with little light. They eat plant growth and anything else their small mouths can manage, including rotting cloth, wood, or flesh. Countless tiny hooked legs and sucking belly segments let them move freely on walls and ceilings.

  • Attack: it tries to fasten onto its prey. A hit means it is attached (1 in 20 lands on the face, blinding the victim until it is removed). Every round after, it does 1 point of damage automatically, until it is killed or the victim dies. Its small, sucker-like mouth has very sharp shearing plates of horn.
  • Rock salt: rubbed on its soft flesh, it does 2 points of damage per round for 1-4 rounds. More salt has no effect until the first dose is finished.

Description: a fat, slimy gray body with a pale yellow head and a sickly white belly. Its eyes are only vestigial; its sense organs are a cluster of cilia on the head, and its mouth is on the underside of the head.

The selkie is a seal-like creature that can take human form for a few days, a sort of sealwere. It usually does so to visit a human community to trade for or buy supplies its group needs. Selkies live in the sea, from cold-temperate to subarctic waters, lairing in large caverns or grottoes with both air and water areas, because their young must breathe air until half-grown (about 1 year old). They eat fish, shellfish, crustaceans, and seaweeds, and can eat human food too; they love wine.

  • Weapons: in human form a selkie carries some weapon, but in seal form it cannot carry one and still swim fast. So selkies met underwater are 90% likely to be unarmed and usually bite. Any weapon they have is used if needed, especially to defend the home.
  • Community: males and females, usually slightly more females; the sexes are equal. The leader is an old selkie with these powers: augury, cure light wounds, cure disease, weather summoning, control weather. Each is usable 1 per round, once per day, except the weather spells, which need 1 week of rest between castings and are used only in dire need, for revenge.
  • Treasure: gathered from ships lost at sea and from sea creatures, so they likely have many pearls. Money is kept mainly for trade. Magic from sunken ships is used to help and protect the community.

Description: in human form, very attractive and fine-looking, with especially bright eyes. In true form they look almost exactly like seals, but a close look shows arms with slightly webbed hands instead of front flippers, and legs instead of a tapering body with rear flippers.

system.psionicText: As original creature Attack/Defense Modes: As original creature
system.description:
All knowledgeable authorities agree that shades are, or were, normal humans who through arcane magic or dark sciences traded their souls or spirits for the essence of shadowstuff. They keep the shape and abilities of their original species but have grown in power by joining with it. What a true native shade is remains unknown, and no one knows if shades are connected with the shadow (q.v.) or some power or substance of the Plane of Shadow. The method of changing a living being into a shade has been lost.

  • Who can become one: any human or demi-human, if the method is found again. Dwarves, elves, gnomes, half-elves, halflings, humans, and an occasional half-orc are known to have given up goodness for shadowstuff. Becoming a shade does not change species limits on ability, class, or level (except as noted below).
  • Long life: unless killed or met with an accident, they do not die. Disease has no effect once they enter shadow; they regrow lost body parts (except the head) in 1-4 weeks and regain 1 hit point per turn.
  • Home: because light on the Prime Material Plane changes, they live on the Plane of Shadow when they can (where they are rare), and leave only with good reason, such as treasure, forced service, or revenge.

Power and light: shades are powerful in shadow, but as shadows lessen, whether from more light or more darkness, so does their power. They are weakest in total light and total darkness.

Total darknessPitch black, overcast night sky; unlit, interior room or cavern; a darkness spell
  • Ability scores: bonuses may exceed normal species maximums, except for strength. Each +1 adds 10% to 18 strength, and scores over 18/00 count as 19. Penalties lower strength by a full point (18/00 drops to 17 at −1 and 16 at −2).
  • Magic resistance: check the shade’s base ability against the light. It never exceeds 60% (a 13th-level shade fighter in twilight has 60%, not 65%). In bright light a shade has standard magic resistance and makes all saves at −4 on the die because of its weakness.
  • Hit points: penalties and bonuses are per hit die; no die may be less than 1 point.
  • Shadow-walk: it gathers shadows around itself to carry itself to the Plane of Shadow, taking 1 full round.
  • Shadow images: it forms 2-5 exact duplicates of itself out of shadow that act as if alive, under its control while within 30 feet. Only changing the light around the shade dispels them. They have no substance (so their attacks do no damage), and the shade must draw on surrounding shadow to make them.
  • Hiding: all shades hide in shadows as a thief of the same level in twilight, shadowy light, and night/dark. Shades with thief ability gain 2% per level in shadowy conditions and 5% per level in night/dark.
  • Psionics: becoming a shade does not change the individual’s basic nature. Existing psionic powers may be enhanced, but psionics cannot be gained this way. Psionic shades lose all mastery of invisibility and etherealness, but gain 2 levels in dimension walking when in shadows, and usually gain shape alteration if they lack it (10% chance per year as a shade). Psionic strength changes because ability scores change. New powers and disciplines gained this way work only on the Plane of Shadow.

Description: a shade is almost impossible to detect, since it looks much as it did in life. Its eyes show no white, only a dark gray or purple iris and pupil, and its skin becomes dusky and gray. Shades prefer gray or black clothes and rarely wear bright colors. The change has some evil in it: shades become gloomy and brooding, and so are usually solitary, unable to trust other shades or deal with normal creatures without dominating or using them.
system.hpNote: As original class and level; light changes hit points per die (MMII p.108).

system.description:
Greater shedu are close allies of their lesser cousins and usually rule, very kindly, any group of 6 or more normal shedu. Like all lammasu and shedu they prefer warm, dry lands, but they tend to roam the Prime Material, Astral, and Ethereal Planes to help and aid creatures of good alignment and fight Evil.

  • Attack: powerful blows of the forehooves.
  • Protection: they radiate protection from evil in a 10-foot radius.
  • At will: become ethereal and invisible.
  • Psionics: 7 minor and 4 major disciplines at 14th level of mastery. Usual minor: clairaudience or clairvoyance, detection of evil or detection of magic, domination or hypnosis, molecular agitation, object reading or sensitivity to psychic impressions, and precognition. Usual major: body control or energy control, mass domination or mind bar, molecular manipulation or telekinesis (3150 gp weight), and shape alteration.
  • Free disciplines: dimension walk, probability travel, and teleportation cost them no strength at all.
  • Languages: lawful good, lammasu, shedu, Common, and root languages. They can speak telepathically with most animals and monsters, and even communicate with plants in a simple way.

system.treasure: Individual: L, M, N, Q; In lair: X
system.description:
Sirines are beautiful human-like females equally at home above or under salt or fresh water. Usually only 1 is met, always in lonely, uninhabited places. They breathe air or water equally well, have infravision and ultravision, and speak their own language and Common.

  • Armor: AC 3, from the race’s high dexterity (18) and magical nature.
  • Weapons: usually small (short) swords and daggers; 30% also have 3 javelins (40%) or a sling (60%). Check each weapon for a base 10% chance of being magic: +1, or a javelin of lightning.
  • Powers (once per day each, one at a time, at will): song, which will "charm person at 3" range all subject creatures of hostile nature within hearing suggestion" (as printed); polymorph self; fog cloud; and improved invisibility.
  • Touch: any intelligent creature she touches in melee must save vs. poison or become an idiot (intelligence 2). She can remove this at will with a touch; otherwise dispel magic restores intelligence.
  • Defenses: immune to all gases. All saves are made as an 11th-level magic-user, with +2 vs. poison.
  • Groups: more than 1 (30% chance) is always met in their home area. A lone sirine always has 6 or 7 hit dice. Among 2-8, at least 1 has 6 or 7 hit dice; the rest have an equal chance of 4, 5, 6, or 7. A group always shares the same good, evil, or absolute neutral alignment, but may mix lawful, neutral, and chaotic (an evil group, for example).
system.hpNote: A lone sirine has 6 or 7 hit dice; in a group at least 1 has 6 or 7 and the rest 4, 5, 6 or 7 (MMII p.109).

system.description:
Animal skeletons are animated from small animals with backbones by an animate dead spell, at 1-½ per experience level of the caster. Usually they range from the size of a house cat to that of a large dog (nothing larger than a human can be animated by the spell). They are typically made as minor guardians, so they usually have no treasure nearby except what is left from past encounters.

  • Attacks: no special attack forms.
  • Immunities: charm, cold, death magic, hold, and sleep.
  • Weapons: blunt weapons do normal damage; edged weapons do only half.
  • Turning: as normal skeletons but at +1 in the cleric’s favor, and 1d6+6 are turned or destroyed.

Skunks live in most temperate and subtropical regions, in lightly settled or uninhabited areas. They bite if cornered, but their main attack and defense is musk.

  • Musk: it backs toward a threatening creature and releases a 1" × 1" × 1" cloud of stinking musk. All inside must save vs. poison. Those who succeed must leave the cloud at once or count as having failed. Those who fail are nauseated for 1-4 rounds and must retreat and retch, and must save vs. poison again or also be blinded for 1-4 rounds.
  • The smell: ordinary clothing smells so bad it must be buried or burned. Flesh, leather, metal, etc. must be washed repeatedly for several days to remove the odor (vinegar removes it in only 2 or 3 washings).

Slime creatures are hosts changed by olive slime (q.v.) into new plant creatures that live in partnership with the slime. Whatever they once were, and whatever their general shape, they are only small, medium, or large; hence the variable hit dice and damage. They gather together to help each other feed and defend themselves, and can be identified only by close examination.

  • Habitat: from busy underground places to damp forests, swamps, etc., equally at home on land or in warmish, shallow water.
  • Infection: each hit has a 10% chance of infecting the opponent with olive slime.
  • Harmed by: acid, freezing cold, fire (only magical fire if they live in water), and magic missile spells. Magic that affects plants also affects them. All other attack forms have no effect.
  • Cunning: their plant intelligence is animal-like, but they learn from experience and can set traps.
  • Telepathy: limited telepathy with their own kind, up to 20" radius.

Olive slime is a monstrous plant growth related to green slime (q.v.), but contact with it is worse in most ways. It prefers to grow underground, feeding on animal, vegetable, and metal substances. The vibrations of a passing creature are enough to make it let go and drop.

  • Numbing: on contact it oozes a numbing poison. The victim must save vs. poison or not notice it has attached. Others nearby might (50%) notice; check once for the group, not each person, with no adjustment except for magic.
  • Spreading: it spreads over the victim’s body, sending tendrils in to feed on the host’s fluids, usually along the spine in humans.
  • Control: its secretions change the host’s mind so its main concern is to feed, protect, and help the slime grow. The host must eat double or waste away (10% of hit points per day).
  • Metamorphosis: after 7-12 days the host starts to change into a plant creature. The slime gradually replaces skin and muscle and links to the brain. The new creature has no interest in its old form or companions; it is a new species closer to plants than anything else, feeding by photosynthesis, as a parasite, or both. When it dies, it produces a new patch of olive slime. See "Slime Creature".
  • Harming it: only acid, freezing cold, fire, or a cure disease spell. Magic that affects plants also works. Other attacks, spells included, do not harm it. Green slime and olive slime attack and cancel each other.

Snakes of all sorts live in regions from cold-temperate to tropical. Larger kinds (constrictors) are usually found only in subtropical climates.

Constrictor: these snakes usually lie in wait for prey, preferring woods or swamps. They attack by biting and coiling. A successful coil means automatic constriction damage every round after. A humanoid can escape by strength: roll to open doors, penalized by +1 to the roll (compare "Snake, Giant Constrictor").

Poisonous: there are many kinds of poisonous snakes. Use this table for the strength and effect of the poison; length, color, habitat, etc. vary.

A solar is the most powerful of spirits, usually serving a greater deity of good alignment directly, often as marshal, steward, etc., and on rare occasions a lesser deity. There are at least 24 solars. They can go anywhere, but do so only in service to their deities. Like devas (q.v.) and planetars (q.v.), they may be of any good alignment (lawful, neutral, or chaotic), and are totally faithful and unswerving in alignment and loyalty.

  • Attacks: 4 per melee round. Each has a huge composite bow (36" range) with various arrows of slaying, and a sword equal to a 2-handed weapon (usable only by solars) equal to +5, with the qualities of dancing (q.v.) and sharpness (q.v.), the sharpness working without severing. For attacks, treat it as dexterity 24 and a 17th+ level fighter.
  • Spells: spell-like abilities equal to a 12th-level cleric, druid, magic-user, and illusionist.

Spell-like powers (one at a time, 1 per round, at will):

  • Globe: it can cast a globe of protection from evil (150% normal effect, for +3/−3) from its own size up to a full 70-foot radius, the size chosen at will and kept up automatically. It also acts as protection from normal missiles and a minor globe of invulnerability.
  • Always: it can commune as needed; cure (any sort) by touch; detect (any sort, automatically); and dispel (any sort) by gaze. It automatically knows alignment, communicates by ESP or tongues, and can read and understand any language.
  • Adaptation: by laying on hands it can give a creature perfect adaptation to any environment for up to a century.
  • Senses: infravision to 24", ultravision at triple normal range, hearing and normal vision double human.
  • Charisma effect: 24.
  • Summons (once every hour): lawful good service, 1-2 ki-rin; neutral good, 1-2 phoenix; chaotic good, 1-2 greater titans.
  • Gate (once per day): either a planetar or double the listed number of the right sort of devas, as the solar chooses.

Defenses:

  • Affected by the attack forms given for devas (q.v.), except that acid does not harm them. Only +5 or better weapons affect them.
  • Never surprised; always strike first against opponents with less than 22 dexterity.
  • Immune to life level loss from undead or magic, and to death spells and death magic. Cannot be beguiled, charmed, held, confused, dominated, feebleminded, paralyzed, or petrified; their souls cannot be imprisoned or trapped.
  • Regenerates 7 hit points per round.
  • Except on its own plane of service, only its material form can be destroyed; its spirit returns at once to its own plane to form a new body, which takes a full 7 decades.

Psionics: animal telepathy (4th level), aura alteration, body equilibrium, body weaponry (12th level), mass domination (24th level), mind bar (24th level), molecular rearrangement (16th level), object reading, precognition, reduction (24th level), telekinesis (24th level), telepathic projection (24th level).

Description: skin the color of molten copper, bronze hair, and glowing topaz eyes. Its form is beautiful and muscular, its deep, resonant voice commanding, and its double wings coppery-gold.

Solifugids, also called false spiders, camel spiders, or sun spiders, are arachnids with powerful hooked beaks and 10 legs, the first pair ending in sucker-like clamps. They live in warm deserts, eat anything, and when hungry attack anything that moves.

  • Grip: in combat it attacks with each of its 2 front legs. A hit does no damage but catches the character in its grip.
  • Beak: each round after, its beak gets +3 to hit for as long as the character is held. Only the beak does damage (the amount listed).
  • Breaking free: only by cutting off a limb, which needs a roll 3 or more above the normal number needed to hit.
  • Nocturnal kind: outdoors there is a 60% chance they are the nocturnal kind, usually coming out only at night. These flee from light brighter than a torch or lantern and attack at −2 in daylight.

  • Nocturnal kind: outdoors there is a 60% chance they are the nocturnal kind, usually coming out only at night. These flee from light brighter than a torch or lantern and attack at −2 in daylight.
