  • Nocturnal kind: outdoors there is a 60% chance they are the nocturnal kind, usually coming out only at night. These flee from light brighter than a torch or lantern and attack at −2 in daylight.

The spectator is a guardian of places and treasures. Once given a task, it guards for up to 101 years and lets no one use, borrow, or examine the item or treasure. The guarded treasure is 90% likely to be a magic item or worth at least 15,000 gp.

Incidental treasure: treasure the spectator picks up while on duty does not trouble its conscience and may be taken freely:

  • 40%: 3-300 coins of mixed types (1-20 platinum, 2-40 gold, 4-80 electrum, the rest, if any, silver);
  • 30%: 1-6 gems of base value 50 gp;
  • 20%: 1-4 potions;
  • 15%: a +1 piece of armor;
  • 15%: a +1 weapon;
  • 5%: a miscellaneous magic item worth under 10,000 gp.

Summoning and service: spectators are summoned from Nirvana by monster summoning V and the sacrifice of 3 (or more) small eyes from a beholder. A spectator can be ordered only to guard treasure; it does no other duty, and if ordered otherwise it returns to Nirvana at once. If its charge is destroyed or successfully stolen, it is freed and may return to Nirvana. The summoner can of course take the item himself and so release it.

  • Body: a large central eye and 4 smaller eyestalks on top of a round body. The tough hide is AC 4. Any general blow is 70% likely to hit the body, which holds all its hit points. Hits on the eyestalks (AC 7) or central eye (also AC 7) happen 30% of the time (20% eyestalks, 10% central eye), and any such hit destroys that eye.
  • Blinded: blinded in every eye, it cannot defend its treasure and teleports to Nirvana; this is the only reason it leaves its post. Its eyes regenerate in 1 day and it returns, unless the treasure is gone, in which case it goes back to Nirvana.
  • Magic resistance: 5% in general.
  • Spell reflection: while the central eye is unharmed it can reflect 1 spell per round back at the caster, if it makes a save vs. spells. Touch spells cannot be reflected. For example, against a lightning bolt it first saves to reflect; if that fails it rolls its magic resistance; if that also fails, the bolt does damage. The caster gets a normal saving throw against a reflected spell, and only he or she can be harmed by it (even a familiar on the caster’s shoulder is safe); if the caster saves, there is no damage at all. Reflection works only if the caster stands in front of the central eye within a 60 degree arc. Range does not matter, only that the spell reaches the spectator. Only 1 spell per round is reflected, even if 2 arrive in the same segment.
  • Small eyes: these work by glance and so are very fast:
EyePower
Central eyeSpell reflection (see above)
Eye 1Create food and water. Obviously not an attack.
Eye 2Cause serious wounds: 2d8+3 damage to a single figure at 60 feet; a successful save vs. spells halves it.
Eye 3Paralyzation ray: range 90 feet, one target only, lasts 5-20 rounds. The spectator never attacks a paralyzed character or eats it, and may let it go its way if it is willing to leave in peace.
Eye 4Telepathy: range 120 feet, 1 target only. It can communicate this way, and implant a suggestion if the target fails a saving throw. The suggestion is always to leave in peace.
  • Initiative: always rolled on 1d8 instead of 1d6. All three "attack eyes" can be used. Causing wounds, paralyzing, or the suggestion take 1 segment each; communication takes 2 segments; creating food and water for a large meal (up to 6 persons) takes 1 full round.
  • Senses: it senses psionic disciplines, powers, and spell-like effects at 240 feet, even through wood but not metal or stone, so it is surprised only on a 1 on 1d12.
  • Bite: in close combat it bites for 2-5 points of damage.
  • Manner: basically passive, it tries to communicate and implant its suggestion first unless attacked at once. Approached properly it can be quite friendly, telling a party early on exactly what it guards so there is no argument. If its charge is not threatened, it can be quite pleasant and even talkative by telepathy.
  • Movement: very fast levitation in any direction. Asleep (20% likely when met), it drifts aimlessly, never touching the ground.

Giant marine spiders live in shallow seas and ocean waters in semitropical and tropical areas. Like their freshwater cousins, they build huge air-filled nests under water from webs and plants. They hide in seaweed, rush out to grab prey, paralyze it with a poisonous bite, and carry it back to the nest. In all other ways they are like giant water spiders (q.v.).

These ugly, sullen cousins of gnomes live near isolated communities or in uninhabited areas, in burrows or ruins. They hate only gnomes more than humankind and associate only with their own kind. They can grow to giant size (with the statistics in parentheses above) to terrorize, rob, and do other vile deeds. In small form they are basically thieves; in large form, giant bandits. A group may mix both sizes if it helps their wicked ends.

  • Spell-like powers (at will, one at a time, 1 per round): affect normal fires, assume giant size, scare (at −2 on saving throws because of their ugliness), and shatter.
  • Giant form: no other magic can be used, but it can return to small size at will.
  • Thief abilities (small form only): as an 8th-level gnome thief with 18 dexterity:
SkillChance
Pick pockets75%
Open locks78%
Find/remove traps70%
Move silently77%
Hide in shadows64%
Hear noise35%
Climb walls81%
Read languages40%
  • Back stab: triple dagger damage, only in small form.
system.hpNote: The book does not say how hit points carry over when a spriggan changes size.

system.description:
Squealers live only in temperate to tropical forests. They are usually solitary, but there is a 10% chance of meeting a mated pair (with up to 2 young). Young have 1-2 hit points per die and only bite, for 1-4 points of damage.

  • Luring: it imitates many sounds perfectly, using the distress calls, death shrieks, mating calls, etc. of other creatures to draw prey. It is voracious and attacks any other carnivore or herbivore.
  • Ambush: it usually crouches on a low branch. When a victim comes near, it grips the branch with 3 limbs and swings down head-first to bite and claw.
  • Grabbing: if both claw attacks hit, it has grabbed and held the victim, and next round drops on it for 5-8 points of crushing damage plus 2 more claw attacks.
  • Attacks: bite, claw, claw, claw, claw (7-12/1-3 x4). It has 18/00 strength and weighs 400 pounds or more.
  • Hiding: among foliage its bulk is 75% invisible thanks to its coloring, stillness, and careful concealment. It is 50% likely to surprise a victim, and attacking by surprise adds +2 to hit and to damage on each attack.
  • Treasure: it cares nothing for treasure, but drags most prey near its lair to eat, so valuables may be there.

Description: very fierce; full grown it is about the size of a large gorilla and a match for almost anything. Long fur in alternating yellow and green splotches, hunched shoulders, and a jutting, pig-like head about 2 feet long that is mostly mouth full of sharp tushes. The arm-like forelimbs grow from the hunched back and the rear limbs from high on the hindquarters; the forelimbs are nearly 4 feet long and the rear ones 3 feet. A 5th limb, 4 feet long, grows from the middle of the back and can turn forward or back. All limbs end in 3 clawed digits; those of the forelimbs and back limb can grasp.

Giant black squirrels live only in old, dark forests held by Evil. They are malicious and attack weak or helpless creatures. Given the chance, they steal small, shiny objects (coins, rings, jewelry, flasks, etc.) from careless people to hide in their nests, which are always in tree hollows 20 feet or more above the ground. Treasure is incidental only. Common gray or red squirrels bite only in self-defense.

Giant black squirrels live only in old, dark forests held by Evil. They are malicious and attack weak or helpless creatures. Given the chance, they steal small, shiny objects (coins, rings, jewelry, flasks, etc.) from careless people to hide in their nests, which are always in tree hollows 20 feet or more above the ground. Treasure is incidental only. Common gray or red squirrels bite only in self-defense.

Flying squirrels "fly" using loose folds of skin on the inside of their front and rear legs. In fact they can only glide and cannot gain height once they jump.

  • Gliding range: 5 feet for every foot of height they jump from (usually a tree).
  • Attack: if they gain surprise with a flying attack, the first attack is made as a 2 hit dice monster. They attack only at odds of 2 to 1 or better.
  • Treasure: incidental only. Their treetop nests may hold gems, jewelry, and other small, bright, shiny things, so never armor, shields, most weapons, potions, etc.

Stegocentipedes probably developed on some distant parallel world, or were made by some insane breeder of creatures. Either way, luckily, they are rarely met. They adapt to temperate and tropical conditions and find almost any habitat suitable. They tend to be sterile.

  • Armor: the plates along its spine give it AC 3 in most (75%) combat situations. Its greater weight and legless tail make it somewhat slower than others of its kind.
  • Bite: it hunts constantly, rushing prey and seizing it in its huge mandibles. Each bite injects poison; saving throws apply.
  • Tail: its rear ends in a thinner, scorpion-like tail, heavily armored at the tip to form a ball-like club that lashes 6 feet in any direction. It is also poisonous: a victim struck must save vs. poison or die, and otherwise takes 3-12 points of damage.
  • Spine defense: it raises its spine plates and moves quickly. The spiked front plates mean anyone attacking its head is subject to what is in effect a horn attack (normal to-hit roll), doing 1-6 hit points of damage. Up to 3 attackers can be hit this way because of its quick defensive motions.

Description: about 2 feet high, with back spines adding 1 to 2 feet when raised. The plates are in double rows that lie flat along its back when not fighting. Color is light brown to gray-brown; green ones have been reported. Each body segment has a pair of legs except the long, specialized tail segment.

Stench kine are the cattle of the Nine Hells. They roam the reeking plains, fiery fields, and even the wintry wastes of the lower hells, and some reach Acheron, Gehenna, and even Hades. Like ordinary herd animals they form great herds, grazing on the noxious, poisonous plants of those vile lands.

  • Young: a herd has 5-30 young, which do not attack.
  • Bulls: 1 in every 5 is a bull. Bulls have at least 6 points per hit die, never do less than 5 points of damage, and are treated as monsters of 6 hit dice.
  • Charge: a charging kow that hits does double damage (at least 10 points for a bull), and makes another to-hit roll to trample, for 2-12 points of damage. Charging needs at least a 1" move. Usually only bulls charge unless the herd is cornered.
  • Immunities: all forms (including magical) of cold, fire, poison, and poison gas.
  • Stench: up close, their breath and bodies smell so foul that everyone must save vs. poison or be affected as by a stinking cloud spell. Those not affected must check again every 3 rounds of exposure.

Description: huge, misshapen bison. Bulls have large humps over the shoulders, cows smaller ones. Long, downward-curving horns; huge heads with pug features, large round eyes, and lolling tongues. Dull orange in color with greenish, matted manes.

hpOptions.label: Bull (at least 6 per die; treated as 6 HD)

system.description:
The stone guardian is a special golem-like figure.

  • Making one: it is made somewhat like a golem or a figurine of wondrous power, using enchant an item, transmute mud to rock, magic mouth, detect invisibility, and limited wish or wish. (Detect invisibility is optional, but no other detection spell may replace it.) A figure of a creature from man- to ogre-size (no smaller or larger) is made of mud and given a heart of stone. Enchant an item is cast on the heart, the mud is transmuted to rock, and the wish is cast. Magic mouth is needed so it can be activated under exact conditions.
  • Going wrong: each activation has a 20% chance that the exact instructions are ignored, and then it attacks anything!
  • Ring: a special ring of protection from stone guardians can be made at the same time. It makes the wearer and everyone within 10 feet immune to the guardian’s attack, but works only for the guardian(s) made with it.
  • Damage: edged weapons do only one-quarter damage, and normal missiles cannot harm it at all. Cold, fire, and electrical spells do half damage.
  • Immunities: having no mind and no living body, it cannot be poisoned, held, charmed, paralyzed, or frightened. It attacks until destroyed.
  • Destroying it: stone to flesh, transmute rock to mud, stone shape, or dig kills it instantly, with no saving throw.
  • Senses: the wish lets it see and hear, but it can detect invisibility only if that spell was used in making it.

The storoper (from "stone roper", also called "tar roper") is about 5 feet high and 2 feet across and looks like a small statue of a roper: a cigar-shaped creature with 6 tentacles and a gaping mouth, weighing about 500 pounds. Its body is silicon-based and rock-like. It senses movement up to 200 feet away and goes perfectly still, like a statue.

  • Attack: when anything comes within 50 feet, it suddenly shoots out its tentacles, preferring to attack 2 victims at once with 3 tentacles each.
  • Venom: the first 2 victims hit are injected through the tentacles (no saving throw) and seem to turn to stone! One round later they recover, but now drugged, they fight for the storoper as well as they can. If it is killed, they stop and wander aimlessly until the venom wears off, which takes 10 turns. It can inject only twice per day.
  • Like a roper: after that its attacks are like a normal roper’s. Each tentacle hit causes weakness (50% loss of strength in 1-3 rounds), and each round the victim(s) are dragged 10 feet closer to its mouth. The chance to break these strong tentacles is double the character’s bend bars/lift gates chance (a character with 15 strength has 14%).
  • Defenses: normal missiles cannot hurt its stony body, but magic missiles and normal or magic hand-held weapons can. All spells, including lightning, cold, and fire, do normal damage.
  • Treasure: once dead, it can be pried open with a chisel or iron spike; its gizzard may hold a few coins and possibly a few gems.

Unlike its small cousin, this plant is nearly intelligent, slightly aware of its surroundings. It prefers shady, cool places and grows only hair-like roots to anchor itself lightly; it can pull these up at will and drag itself along the ground with its sticky tendrils. It lives mainly on the prey it catches.

  • Attack: it senses moving creatures by vibration and lashes out at anything moving within 5 feet. Its lumpy body is covered in hundreds of tendrils, and up to 6 may attack each creature in range each round. They end in sticky globs of sap.
  • Sticky sap: for every 3 tendrils that hit, the victim is −1 on later to-hit rolls; this is cumulative, so 6 hits give −2.
  • Smothering: a to-hit roll of 20 means that tendril struck across the mouth and nose, clogging them with sap. The character suffocates in 2-4 rounds unless the sap is removed. Soaking the sap with vinegar or alcohol (such as wine) dissolves it harmlessly; this is the only non-magical way to prevent suffocation.
  • Acid: the sap is also a mild enzyme acid doing 1 point of damage per tendril each round until the tendril is broken. Each character’s chance to break a tendril is the same as opening doors; check each tendril separately.
  • Defenses: its sticky outside means missile and fire-based attacks do only half damage.

Description: 3-4 foot high mounds of gray-green tarry ropes or rags. Places where they grow are often thick with flies, and the air often has a heavy smell like sweet syrup.

Swans live where similar waterfowl do: rivers, ponds, lakes, and marshes.

  • Numbers: a single swan is always a male (cob). Only 25% of encounters are with a lone swan; otherwise they are with mated pairs of cobs and pens (females) and their young but full-grown cygnets, 1-2 per pair.
  • Attack: if their territory is invaded or they are attacked, both cob and pen threaten or attack as needed: a flying leap, a strong bill strike, and blows with both wings. This is 50% likely to blind and confuse an opponent so it cannot strike back that round.
  • Senses: like geese they have exceptional senses and notice approaching danger 90% of the time.
  • Nest: if there are eggs, there are 1-3. With no eggs or nestlings, swans escape severe danger by swimming or flying.

system.damage: As swan or by weapon type
system.description:
A swanmay is a human woman with the magical power to change into a swan. The power comes from the dweomer of an item, but no man is known ever to have used a captured one successfully. It is usually held in a feather token or feathered garment (both become part of the swan’s feathers), or possibly a signet ring (which becomes a band on the swan’s leg).

  • Swan form: harmed only by +1 or better magic weapons, with magic resistance of 2% per hit die.
  • Human form: all swanmays are rangers, with all the traits and abilities of that subclass. Roll 2d6 for level, from 1st (2) to 11th (12): 3 means a 2nd level swanmay/ranger, 4 a 3rd level, etc. They attract no followers and may have psionics as a normal human.
  • Gear: when met, she has light armor and gear, bow and arrows, sword, and dagger carefully hidden nearby, usually not magical.
  • Outlook: though rangers, they are mainly devoted to solitude, nature, and the company of their adopted kind. They may help good people in need, but otherwise avoid humanity and civilization, and hate underground places even more than enclosed places above ground.
  • Friends and foes: usually friendly with the little folk of the woods, such as sylvan elves, dryads, and similar creatures. They dislike noisy, brash creatures, ferocious beasts, and all Evil. Only druids are known to associate with them regularly, and then because swanmays want druid help against some evil.
system.hpNote: A swanmay is a ranger of level 2d6 − 1 (1st-11th); roll hit points as for a ranger of that level (MMII p.116).

system.description: These hardy fish are common in salt water. They are fast and usually not aggressive, fleeing rather than fighting, but if attacked, maddened, or controlled or trained, they use their long, bony "sword" as a fearsome weapon. Aquatic elves and dolphin communities often keep smaller ones as pets and guards.

The vile taers live in the coldest mountain regions, dwelling in caves and always hunting for food. They look like white-haired, greasy, shaggy cavemen, and may in fact be kin to mankind. Hair color is gray to snow white; the head is large but has almost no forehead.

  • Attack: kick, punch, and bite. Half (50%) have crude spears, thrown before closing to melee at +1 to hit and +3 to damage.
  • Stench: they ooze a fatty, foul-smelling grease. Any creature within 10 feet must save vs. breath weapon or suffer disorientation and nausea for 2-5 hours, at −2 to hit and −1 damage. The same grease helps them withstand cold, even magical cold.
  • Treasure: usually a collection of polished teeth, horns, and crude stone idols. There is a 15% chance of real treasure taken from human victims, and if so a 10% chance it includes 1 magic item, especially a weapon.

system.psionicText: Nil (immune to psionics) Attack/Defense Modes: Nil/nil
system.description:
The legendary tarrasque may be the most dreaded monster of all. When active it ravages the countryside for miles: all plants and animals are eaten or driven off, and the land it passes through becomes a barren waste that takes years to recover. It eats greedily and constantly; every living thing is food to it, though it prefers warm-blooded creatures.

  • Attacks: 2 forelimb claws; a sweeping tail lash for 2-24 points of damage; a savage bite that works like a sword of sharpness (a to-hit score of 18 or better cuts off some part of the victim, such as a limb, head, torso, etc.); and 2 thrusting horns for 1-10 points each. Because it is so large and ponderous, it can rush only once every turn.
  • Terror: the mere sight of it paralyzes creatures under 3 levels or hit dice until it is out of sight (no saving throw). Creatures of 3 or more levels or hit dice flee in panic, but those of 7 or more who save vs. paralyzation are not affected.
  • Carapace: exceptionally hard and reflective. Bolts and rays such as lightning bolts, cones of cold, and even magic missiles are useless against it: 1 in 6 reflect straight back at the caster, and the rest bounce harmlessly away.
  • Other defenses: fire of any sort has no effect. It regenerates 1 hit point per round after being damaged. Only +1 or better magic weapons can strike it.
  • Slaying it: said to be possible only by reducing it to −30 or fewer hit points and then using a wish for its death. Otherwise even the smallest piece regenerates and restores the whole monster.
  • Treasure: legend says its upper carapace, treated with acid and heated in a furnace, yields gems: 10-100 diamonds of 1000 gp base value each. The underbelly, mixed with its blood and meteoric iron, makes a metal dwarf smiths can forge into 1-4 shields of +5 magical power.
  • Activity: luckily it is active only for short periods. Usually it comes out to forage for a week or two, ravaging all but a few square miles, then finds a hidden underground lair and sleeps for 5-20 months. About once a decade it is especially active, staying out for several months, after which it sleeps 4-16 years unless disturbed. Its ratio of active to dormant time seems to be about 1:30.

Tasloi live in steamy tropical forests and are rarely seen by man. Shy and malicious, they lurk in the treetops to surprise the weak and careless. Built for life above ground, they are slow and clumsy on the ground, where they go semi-erect, but quick and nimble along tree paths.

  • Stealth: they surprise on 1-4 (1d6) and hide in shadows 75% of the time. They have infravision, suit dark jungles, and are −1 to hit in full daylight.
  • Diet: anything, but they especially like flesh, above all humans and elves.
  • Tactics: they usually attack from above, trying to capture if they can, using nets if they gain surprise. Against a watchful or prepared party, they wear it down with short, sudden attacks and retreats. If they can, they steal the enemy dead after an attack.
  • Bands: loose bands of several families. Every band of 70 or more has a chief (5 HD). Any band has a 30% chance of a shaman, who may advance up to 5th level.
  • Weapons: small shield and javelin (AC 5) 20%; club and javelin 40%; short sword and small shield (AC 5) 10%; javelin and net 15%; short sword and net 10%; javelin and lasso 5%. With a shield their AC is 5. They carry javelins and shields on their backs when traveling through the trees.
  • Lair: besides the males, there are females equal to 70% and young equal to 50%. Females fight as normal tasloi; young do not fight. The lair is 1-6 large trees with 4-24 platforms 50-100 feet up, all linked by vines and ropes. There is a 60% chance of 1-6 trained giant spiders and a 20% chance of 2-8 trained giant wasps; tasloi are said to ride wasps great distances.
  • Languages: their own, plus those of monkeys and apes. About 5% also know a pidgin Common for trading.

Description: long-legged, flat-headed humanoids who walk crouched, now and then touching their knuckles to the ground. Lustrous green skin thinly covered in coarse black hair, gold cat-like eyes, and long, grasping feet. They can often be heard at night talking in high, whispery voices.

XP for the king: V/500 + 10/hp; queen: VI/900 + 13/hp.

Giant termites live in subtropical and tropical forests and jungles with plenty of vegetation. The nest is a stone-hard mound about 100 feet across and 200-500 feet high, with many round openings 5-8 feet across near the top. These lead to vertical, diagonal, and horizontal passages and on to chambers underground.

  • Habits: nocturnal; they shun light. A group of more than 30 workers always has 3-16 soldiers with it.
  • Workers: weak mandibles; they bite for only 1-2 points of damage.
  • Soldiers: strong jaws, and they can spit an irritating fluid (like kerosene) that blinds any creature struck for 5-20 rounds unless it saves vs. poison. The fluid burns if exposed to flame or heat: 1 spit on a target, ignited, does 5-16 points of burning damage. They can spit only once per turn; range is 1", volume about 1 pint.
  • The lair: always holds 10 times the number of workers and soldiers first met, spread through the nest, plus these:
NumberTermites
5-30Workers/attendants in egg chamber
2-12Soldiers/guards in egg chamber
4-24Workers/attendants in royal chamber
2-8Soldiers/guards in royal chamber
1King (AC 5; MV 6"; HD 6+6; hp 30 or more; #AT +1 (as printed); Dmg 3-18; SA double range and quantity fluid spit possible every other round) size L
1Queen (AC 4; MV 3"; HD 8+8; hp 40 or more; #AT +1 (as printed); Dmg 5-30) size L
  • Royal and egg chambers: the king and queen are only in the royal chamber, near the bottom of the underground levels, with the egg chamber nearby holding as many eggs as there are workers and soldiers combined. If intruders enter either chamber, all regular termites (not the special attendants and guards) start moving there, while those already present fight fiercely, getting +1 to hit and to damage. This applies to workers and soldiers arriving later too.
  • Repository well: a shaft near the royal chamber leads to a well where unusable metal and mineral items are dumped. There may be incidental treasure, usually rare and of little value.
  • Enemies: their worst enemies are formians, which are bigger and smarter, hate termites, and love eating their eggs. Termites rush to defend the nest against such raiders.
  • Communication: usually by touching antennae; in a crisis, a broadcast telepathic call.

XP for the king: V/500 + 10/hp; queen: VI/900 + 13/hp.

  • Communication: usually by touching antennae; in a crisis, a broadcast telepathic call.

The dreaded thessalhydrae love dark, damp places, and are usually found in swamps, jungles, and underground lairs.

  • Fringe heads: a fringe of snake-like heads rings its vast main mouth. Each bite does 1-6 points of damage, plus another 1-6 unless the victim saves vs. poison. Each head is some 6 feet long, so many creatures can be attacked in a melee round. Each takes 12 points of damage to cut off; damage to the heads does not harm the body, and lost heads regrow in 12 days.
  • Main mouth: bites for 1-20 points, plus another 1-20 points of acid damage unless a save vs. poison succeeds.
  • Tail pincer: grabs an opponent, doing 1-12 points of damage, and drops it into the gaping central mouth in the same round.
  • Acid spit (once per day): a glob of acid saliva from the main mouth covering a 12-foot circle up to 3" away. Creatures there take 12-72 points of acid damage, half if they save vs. poison.
  • Immunity: acids of any kind, including poisonous acids, have no effect.
  • Items: things in the central mouth are usually destroyed; each owner must save vs. acid and crushing blows every round until the items are removed.
system.hpNote: 12 hit dice is the body; each fringe head takes 12 points to sever and regrows in 12 days; damage to heads does not harm the body (MMII p.119).

system.specialDefenses: Dodge missiles on roll of 9 or better
system.description:
The thri-kreen are carnivorous insect-men of deserts and dry grasslands. They live in small, dark burrows and are not social. Their warriors hunt many creatures, especially elves. These mantis warriors are strong and agile, able to leap 20 feet up and 50 feet forward.

  • Polearm: a weapon of their own design with a blade at each end, used to slash like a glaive or thrown like a spear (damage 3-8).
  • Throwing wedges: small triangles carved from a hard crystal. If they miss, they return to the thrower and can be caught and thrown again. A thri-kreen carries up to 10 and throws them up to 9" (damage 3-6).
  • Dodging: it dodges missiles on a roll of 9 or better on 1d20.
  • Unarmed: 4 clawed, arm-like limbs (damage 1-4) and a mandible bite (damage 2-5). Anyone bitten must save vs. paralyzation or be paralyzed for 2-16 rounds.

These bloated, pig-like creatures roam in herds across the layers of the Abyss. They are named for their rumbling bellow, intestinal noises, and foul breath. They live on plants and the ooze where unwholesome growths spring up, and in turn feed many other creatures there. Their flesh is rank, stringy, and disgusting to all but demons and their kind, and possibly even to them!

  • Young: 1 young for every 2 adults; the young do not attack.
  • Attacks: adults bite or make a trampling charge, which must start from 2" or farther away and does 1d4 per hit die if it hits.
  • Hit dice: roll 1d6: 1 = 4, 2 = 5, 3 = 6, etc.; at least 1 in every 5 has 9 hit dice.
  • Breath: frightened or angry, they bellow. In combat each breathes on its opponent; the breath builds to equal a fog cloud after 3 rounds. Creatures affected by the smell fight at −2 to hit. The cloud lasts 1-4 rounds.

Description: pig- or hippo-like, but with 6 longer legs and a very round, swollen-looking body. The head is low-set and cylindrical with fan-like ears, a huge mouth, small beady eyes, and no nostrils. The tail is broad, thick, flattish, and fairly short. Colors range from yellow-brown to olive, all with darker mottling and warty growths.
system.hpNote: Roll 1d6 for hit dice: 1 = 4, 2 = 5 ... 6 = 9, each +1 per die; at least 1 in every 5 has 9 hit dice (MMII p.120).

system.description: Thunderherders are distant cousins of the purple worm, but not aggressive. They travel in vast herds a few feet under the ground in desert regions, and are harmless, 3-5 feet wide and 5-10 feet long. The main dangers are the earth tremors and terrible trumpeting they make as they stampede underground. These do no real damage, but cause great confusion, knock over tents, and panic all pack animals. A single one can cause a small tremor.

Time elementals come in 2 kinds, regular and noble; figures in parentheses are for nobles. Because they exist in more than 1 time at once, they always appear as small creatures like a cloud of fiery dust or vapor.

  • Attack: a spray of fine powder; those hit take damage from cell death (aging).
  • Manifestations: a common time elemental can bring itself from other times, in effect adding 1-4 more creatures, but a hit on any 1 damages all of them. So under attack it usually brings its other selves to the present, gains several attacks that round, and vanishes into the time stream the next.
  • Time travel: it can move forward, backward, or sideways in time (1 round for each hit die), so it can usually avoid or break off contact at will. Unless the other party can also travel in time, it is then impossible to trace; those who can follow see a faint trail of haze. It can also pursue by time movement, 1" per hit die, up to a 13" or 17" movement rate, which may even put it ahead of a fleeing opponent.
  • Time spells: all time-related spells are useless within 3" of it, and none affect or reveal anything about it or its actions.
  • Spread across time: any spell or magic used against or on it has only a 1 in 10 chance of affecting it. Roll 1d10 for its current center of vulnerability, then a second 1d10; if they match, the magic works. An opponent able to move through time can find where it is most vulnerable, so that opponent’s magic works normally, though the elemental still gets a saving throw.
  • Planes: they rarely appear anywhere but the Plane of Time; elsewhere they feel discomfort and the weight of time’s forward (or other) motion relative to the plane where one of their manifestations is. They cannot be conjured, summoned, or otherwise brought into being by any standard means or known spell.

Noble time elementals have all the common powers plus these, each usable at will, once per day ("usable per round", as printed):

  • time stop (affects even common time elementals);
  • age a creature by 1-20 years, or make it younger by 1-20 years;
  • age non-living vegetable matter by 10-200 years, or mineral material by 100-2000 years;
  • move up to 4 other creatures through time (forward, backward, or sideways) randomly or to a chosen place, singly or together, if they are willing or fail to save vs. spells.

Royal time elementals: there are other, different creatures on the Plane of Time, and certain royal time elementals said to be stronger even than nobles, who rule their fellows and serve certain deities. They have 24 or 28 hit dice, do the same number of hit points of attack damage (6-24 or 7-28), and have double the number of powers. Once per day they can summon 1-4 common (70%) or 1-2 noble (30%) elementals.

The two-legged transposer looks vaguely humanoid, but has no real features, and its limbs end in sucker-like pads.

  • Attack: it lashes with its arms; the horny-ridged suckers do 1-6 points of damage.
  • Transposing field: a hit also sets up an unknown kind of field between it and the opponent struck. From then on, any damage that opponent does to the transposer harms the attacker instead and restores the same number of hit points to the transposer. A spell attack for 20 points, for example, harms the caster for 20 and restores or builds the transposer’s hit points up to its maximum of 48. Weapon attacks are likewise turned to harm the attacker and help the transposer.
  • Healing: only healing spells harm it if the caster has been struck by it; the cure damages the transposer and heals the caster instead. Opponents not bound by the field harm it normally.
  • Disguise: it uses a minor illusion, a sort of change self, to look like a human, demi-human, etc., to lure prey into melee. The illusion ends only if it flees or is slain. Special aids or disbelief can reveal the trick, but must be actively used.
system.hpNote: Its maximum is 48 hit points; damage from an opponent it has struck restores it up to that (MMII p.121).

system.description:
This plant’s deep green stalks, 5-8 feet tall, are topped by trumpet-shaped flowers of vivid orange, bright yellow, and intense red, each with its own function. Other flower color combinations are white, pale silvery-gray, pink or golden brown, chocolate brown, and russet.

  • Orange flower: shoots 2-8 tendrils, each 3 feet long, from its center. Any creature struck must save vs. the poison of the tendril’s pollen or fall into a coma-like sleep.
  • Yellow flower: sensitive rootlets locate the sleeper, and the bloom at once bends over it and trembles, shaking loose a shower of sticky enzyme that does 2-8 points of damage per round until the victim is entirely rotted away. Each flask of water poured on the victim in the same round as the damage reduces it by 1 point; total immersion in water removes the sap entirely.
  • Red flower: sinks tube-like tendrils 1 foot long into the sleeping victim, first drawing body fluids at 1-6 hit points per turn, then sucking up what remains after the enzyme has dissolved the body.

Marine trolls are a gilled form of the common troll. They live in large bodies of water and need a lot of room to hunt. Their color runs from blue-green to olive.

Freshwater trolls: scrags in fresh water are smaller than normal trolls and heavily scaled. Their claws are weaker, but their enlarged lower jaw has many small, very sharp fangs. They can attack up to 3 different opponents in a melee round. They regenerate as trolls (q.v.) do, but only when immersed in fresh water.

Saltwater trolls: scrags in seas and oceans are at least as large as ordinary trolls, with thick, heavily scaled skins. A few (10%) are smart enough to wear armor of shells and sharkskin or similar materials, for an effective AC 1. Their forelimbs are shorter and weaker than an ordinary troll’s, but they have a huge mouth full of fangs to make up for weaker talon attacks. Like freshwater scrags, they regenerate in their own element, salt water.

They can attack up to 3 different opponents in a melee round. They regenerate as trolls (q.v.) do, but only when immersed in fresh water.

A few (10%) are smart enough to wear armor of shells and sharkskin or similar materials, for an effective AC 1. Their forelimbs are shorter and weaker than an ordinary troll’s, but they have a huge mouth full of fangs to make up for weaker talon attacks. Like freshwater scrags, they regenerate in their own element, salt water.

The twilight bloom, or purple death, is a poisonous plant 8-13 feet tall with a thick, branchless, scaly trunk topped by fern-like fronds that droop a little way. Among them are cup-shaped purple flowers with silvery stamens, pointing upward. A fine, mossy mat around the base is actually its roots. The flowers give off a very attractive scent and sweet sap.

  • Poison drip: the vibrations of a creature passing under the cupped lavender blooms make them tilt gently and drip a syrupy poison. There is a 25% chance the creature is struck. If it fails to save vs. poison, it dies at once, and its decay feeds the plant’s roots.

A distant land-dwelling cousin of the sea urchin, its spiny body is often mistaken for a bush. It is a scavenger that eats almost anything edible, with a small mouth underneath and a rasping tongue that saws through armor and gathers food.

  • Defense: shy, it attacks only if a creature comes within 1". It shoots 2-12 spines (damage 1-2) per round; the victim must save vs. poison or be paralyzed for 6 turns.
  • Escape: if it must flee, it releases a dark gas cloud of 10-foot radius.
  • Senses and movement: no eyes; 2 small antennae detect any movement within 1". It has no front or back, and its 5 spindly legs rotate so it can move in any direction.
  • Pearls: now and then it eats something it cannot digest or pass, and coats it with a shiny greenish-black substance, forming "pearls" like oyster pearls worth 100-600 gp each. Very old urchins may have up to a dozen.

Ustilagor fungi look like brain-like growths with coral-like branches. They are soft and not fast by normal standards, but can scuttle and dart, which explains their fairly good armor class.

  • Attack: they flick out ribbon-like tendrils about 3 feet long. A hit does damage from alkaline fluids, and the victim must save vs. poison or take the same damage again (2-5 hp) the next round as the caustic stuff works.
  • No mind: by human standards they have no intelligence or mind, so mental attacks do not affect them (see PLAYERS HANDBOOK, p. 11, Wisdom Table, asterisked paragraph on magical attack adjustment).
  • Psionics: they do have some kind of brain, for they have psionic powers. With telempathic projection they can project one of these emotions on an individual each round: hate for an associate, distrust of an associate, fear of fungi, loathing of the area, or uncertainty, causing attack, bickering, desertion, or dithering. They use energy control to protect themselves from spell attacks and the like. They attack psionic individuals only by id insinuation (tied to the strongest basic emotions), and only a psionic blast affects them in turn.

A vagabond is a life force of unknown origin, perhaps from a far planet, a parallel universe, or an undiscovered plane. It is very rare but may be met anywhere. It occupies the form of one intelligent physical creature native to the area, apparently forming or controlling the body for its own ends. Nothing is known of its true form or society (if any).

  • Recognizing one: often obvious once you talk with it: its odd speech and behavior (never typical of the form it wears) show it does not know local customs and expectations.
  • Form: it can look like almost anything, but cannot change form once taken; its movement and other physical traits are those of the creature.
  • Behavior: very curious, often about everyday or personal details. Attacked, it uses its form to defend itself or retreat as best it can.
  • Joining a party: invited on an adventure, it usually agrees (90%), offering its form for exploring and, if needed, fighting. If the body is slain, the life force leaves, never to return.
  • Gift: if a whole adventure is completed, before leaving it enchants 1 gem for each character who went along, by way of thanks, with a variety of word of recall (3 uses per enchantment). Only the owner knows the 1-segment phrase that activates it.
  • Immunities: all forms of mental attack or control, except psionics.
system.hpNote: As the form it occupies (MMII p.123).

system.description:
These horrible monsters are said to have been spawned in Tarterus and loosed on the Prime Material Plane to cause havoc. They look like hideous flying heads crowned with writhing tentacles, come out at dusk, and are gone by dawn. They lair in caves, caverns, and deep underground holes, and have both infravision and ultravision.

  • Light: they hate it, attacking and putting out torches or smashing lanterns. They shun brighter light, and daylight blinds them.
  • Bite: most feared because its damage can be permanent. For each bite the victim must save vs. poison; on a failure the hit points lost (1-4) are gone for good and can be restored only by a wish.
  • Treasure: incidental only; valuables of past victims may be in the litter of the lair.

system.xp: 1 HD = III/53 + 1/hp; 2 HD = III/81 + 2/hp; 3 HD = III/120 + 3/hp; 4 HD = IV/175 + 4/hp; 5 HD = IV/245 + 5/hp; 6 HD = V/425 + 6/hp
system.description:
Vegepygmies are plant creatures of low intelligence. They form regional bands and live by scavenging and hunting. They eat meat (and carrion) no matter what its condition.

  • Camouflage: color and size vary, usually matching their surroundings. Where they match the background they blend in, surprising 50% of the time.
  • Hit dice and size: 1-4 hit dice, leaders more. A force is 1 hit die 50%, 2 hit dice 25%, 3 hit dice 15%, and 4 hit dice 10%. A 1 hit die vegepygmy is 2 feet tall, plus half a foot for each hit die over 1.
  • Leaders: for every 50 there is 1 subchief of 5 hit dice with 2-5 bodyguards of 3 hit dice each. Every band has a leader of 6 hit dice with 2-8 bodyguards of 4 hit dice each.
  • Defenses: piercing weapons such as arrows and spears do only 1 point of damage. Electrical attacks do no damage; fire and cold do normal damage. They are immune to all charm/enchantment spells except those that affect plants, and always get a saving throw against enchantment, even where one is not normally given.
  • Lairs: usually in warm places underground, some in dark forests, near their main food supply, which they defend in an organized way. They live well alongside other plant life. There is a 40% chance of 1-3 shriekers guarding the lair (members of the band can pass them unnoticed) and a 70% chance of russet mold nearby.
  • Reproduction: by russet mold or by budding from their bodies.
  • Communication: no spoken language, but they can cry out; they talk mainly by a code of chest slaps and thumps.
  • Thornies: they live with dog-like creatures: AC 3, MV 15", HD 4, hp 21-30, #AT 1, Dmg 2-5 (plus 3-12 ripping damage from their thorny growths in close combat), animal intelligence, man-sized.

Description: short, two-legged creatures with sharp, thorn-like claws. Shoulders, bellies, and limbs are fringed with leaf-like tendrils, and the head has a topknot of small leaves.

The verme is the largest of fish, usually living in great rivers, though some go into salt water. It prefers warm water with plenty of food: fish, reptiles, cattle, humans, or almost anything else. It is long, flattish underneath, and wider than it is high, so it can lie on the bottom and swim in fairly shallow water.

  • Armor: its heavily scaled, very bony head is AC 3; the body is less protected.
  • Swallowing: it swallows prey whole, even as large as a water buffalo; any hit swallows prey not more than 12 feet tall, doing 3d8+4 damage in the process. Swallowed creatures take 2-16 more points per round and are dissolved in 6 rounds. Its stomach may hold indigestible items such as metal, gems, crystal, etc.
  • Boats: when hungry and hunting it can upset vessels up to small galley size.
  • Defenses: its thick, slimy scales make edged weapons useless: only 1 point of damage per blow. Fire-based attacks do half damage, unless they strike inside the mouth or somewhere inside the body, in which case damage is +1 per die.

Description: much like a giant catfish, but with large scales and many needle-like teeth. Pale yellow underneath, the flanks shading from dark brown to a mottled green and brown back.

Humans call vilstraks marl muggers or tunnel thugs. Their stony bodies give them excellent protection and the uncanny ability to merge with earth or stone, making them 75% undetectable even at only 20 feet.

  • Attack: 2 club-like blows with its fists.
  • Lair: usually a hollow in earth or stone reachable only by beings that can pass through solid stone or packed soil. Not being very bright, they sometimes (5%) choose a den that can be found and broken into, where plunderers will find the treasures these greedy creatures carried in.

Vulchlings are bird-like creatures that look like vultures with vaguely human features. They prefer desolate or underground lairs and sometimes keep company with harpies or even type I demons. They roost in trees or on ledges and swoop down on unwary prey with talons extended, then hop in to attack with their sharp beaks. A lair holds 0-9 eggs.

These carrion eaters live in temperate to tropical regions. Their eyesight is at least as good as any falcon, hawk, or eagle, so they stay very high up, searching the land below.

  • Feeding: when they see a creature moving erratically, crippled, or fallen, they swoop lower to see if it is near death or dead, and eat helpless or dead creatures.
  • Driving them off: ordinary vultures move out of reach of a victim able to strike at them and wait for it to weaken. Giant ones must actually be hit (a successful to-hit roll) to drive them off to a safe distance.
  • In battle: where vultures are present, they appear 7-12 rounds after a creature falls, whether unconscious, killed, or magically asleep or held. If no combatants are within 20 feet of the fallen, they land and peck at the victim, 1-6 attacking each round.
  • Game: game that is removed quickly and kept near active, obviously healthy beings does not attract them.

These carrion eaters live in temperate to tropical regions. Their eyesight is at least as good as any falcon, hawk, or eagle, so they stay very high up, searching the land below.

  • Feeding: when they see a creature moving erratically, crippled, or fallen, they swoop lower to see if it is near death or dead, and eat helpless or dead creatures.
  • Driving them off: ordinary vultures move out of reach of a victim able to strike at them and wait for it to weaken. Giant ones must actually be hit (a successful to-hit roll) to drive them off to a safe distance.
  • In battle: where vultures are present, they appear 7-12 rounds after a creature falls, whether unconscious, killed, or magically asleep or held. If no combatants are within 20 feet of the fallen, they land and peck at the victim, 1-6 attacking each round.
  • Game: game that is removed quickly and kept near active, obviously healthy beings does not attract them.

Weasels and their kin, such as mink, ferrets, and stoats, are common predators. Their armor class comes from small size, darting movement, and speed. They do not attack unless cornered. Some are hunted for their valued fur. Ferrets can be caught young and trained to hunt small burrowing game.

The webbird is not really a bird; it may be some kind of feathered insect or arachnid. It lives in semitropical lands, usually at the edges of woods so it can hunt the open ground nearby. It eats small flying creatures.

  • Attack: when large warm-blooded creatures come into sight, a flock takes to the air, gathers, and makes low passes over the victims’ heads. Each webbird can shoot a sticky, flammable strand of web 7-12 feet long once per round. Roll 1d6 and add 1 for every 6 webbirds in the flock; the area attacked is 12 feet by 12 feet:
Die scoreResult
1-3Ineffective attack
4-61 creature ensnared for 2-8 rounds
7-102-5 creatures ensnared for 2-5 rounds
11 and upEntire area covered with webs, and all therein are held fast for 2-5 rounds
  • Escaping: strength 17 shortens the time held by 1 round, and 18 (with or without exceptional strength) by 2. Alcohol dissolves the strands; 1 flask of wine frees 1 man-sized creature.
  • Eggs: once a victim is held, 1-4 webbirds land on it, and next round push their chest tubes into exposed flesh and inject 2-8 eggs. Grubs hatch in 3-6 turns and each eats into the host for 1 point of damage per round (per grub), eventually killing it. Young webbirds emerge from the corpse within 7 turns of death. The pain is excruciating. A cure disease spell kills the grubs.
  • Fire: they shun flame. Someone with a torch is safe; they avoid him or her and attack unprotected creatures.
  • Crushing: a webbird can be caught in the hand (a successful to-hit roll) and crushed on the spot, but it always gives its killer a dying bite (1 hit point).

Description: looks like a raven-sized bird without a beak, with long-feathered wings and a long, spiky tail. A close look shows a slit mouth with hard, sharp ridges for biting and a drooping chest tube about 4 inches long. Feathers are metallic gray with greenish hues at wingtips and tail; the belly is bright gray, shading to light green near the tail.

Wemics are large lion-centaurs that roam temperate grasslands and savannas hunting antelope and similar herd animals. They are intelligent, use fire, are said to be excellent trackers and guides, and speak their own language and Common.

  • Senses: surprised only on a 1.
  • Combat: claws and a weapon. They can leap 10 feet up and 30 feet forward.
  • Males: carry javelins and a stone club or short sword, often with tough leather shields (AC 5).
  • Females: fight without weapons, clawing, at AC 7, and get +2 to hit if their young are attacked. The young do not fight.
  • Prides: 4-16 males, 2-24 females, and 1-12 young. 3-30 prides band into a tribe led by a chief (AC 5, HD 6+4, Dmg 1-6/1-6 + weapon +1). Sometimes 2d4 tribes form a clan or nation led by a king (AC 3, HD 9, Dmg 1-8/1-8 + weapon +2) with 2-8 chieftain bodyguards.
  • Witch doctor: 70% chance with any tribe (7th level cleric/4th level magic-user maximums).

The black willow is a mobile, intelligent tree of evil nature. It lives where normal willows grow but gets only part of its food from sun, air, water, and earth: it is a meat-eater, especially fond of elves, gnomes, and humans.

  • Disguise: it can shape its trunk and limbs to look like any kind of normal willow, so a creature is 90% unlikely to recognize it. Sometimes it has a smooth trunk and broad, inviting limbs; other times safe-looking hollows at the base or high on the trunk. Treants spot one at once, but even druids cannot without magic (such as locate plants).
  • Attack: usually lashing, whip-like branches, but it has 2 special attacks, one generally used first.
  • Sleep aura: when a creature climbs out on a safe-looking limb, it makes an aura of drowsiness in a 20-foot radius, putting tired creatures into natural sleep (no saving throw). A hole opens beneath, and 1 or more victims are taken into the hollow limb, which tilts to slide them into the trunk.
  • Trunk trap: the safe-looking openings in the trunk also close to trap victims in its digestive cavity, coated with sticky, nonflammable sap. Digestive sap oozes up from the roots, filling the 8-foot cavity at 1 foot per 10 rounds. The acid juice does 1-4 points of damage per round until death. At −12 or more hit points the victim is digested and cannot be resurrected.
  • Fighting from inside: only short, sharp weapons can be used in the cramped space, doing at most 1 point of normal damage per round, plus magic and strength bonuses. Rescue usually must come from outside.
  • Regeneration: 1 point per turn.
  • Treasure: sometimes buried under the tree with bones and other indigestible matter, if victims had treasure the weak acid could not digest and if the tree has stayed in one place for weeks.

This weird plant monster lurks in undergrowth or grassy meadows, creeping slowly about on its 7 root tentacles, which it also uses for feeding and to catch live prey. Its 2 or 3 eyestalks are long enough to give it excellent, wide-angle vision.

  • Body and limbs: the body (stump) can take 9 hit dice of damage. Its limbs can be broken or cut off without permanent harm, regrowing in 1-4 weeks. Root tentacles take 19-22 hit points each and eyestalks 13-16.
  • Attack: it lures prey within 12 feet, then strikes and grabs with 1-3 gnarled root tentacles. A hit does 1-4 points of damage and entangles the victim, who is pulled to the mouth next round for another 1-4 points plus a sure bite for 7-12 more, unless the victim breaks free of the root or roots.
  • Breaking free: breaking a root by strength needs an unhindered grip, so a held creature cannot break the root, but it may break free. That needs 13 or greater strength, 5% per point. At 18 strength the chance is 30% +1% per 1% of exceptional strength, so 18/70 strength has 100% (as printed). Only creatures with exceptional strength can break a root tentacle.
  • Surprise: 90% likely to attack by surprise. It looks like a tree stump, and can grow a lure like a small furry creature that "looks" at approaching prey and then "freezes" so as to be "unnoticed".

Description: a grayish-brown tree stump 2-3 feet across. Eyestalks 10-15 feet long, brown near the base and green at the tips, with pinkish or violet flower-like eyes. Roots 9-12 feet long. The vertical mouth in the trunk has jagged teeth and thick, black lips; shut, it looks like an old scar on an ordinary stump.
system.hpNote: The stump takes 9 hit dice of damage; root tentacles take 19-22 and eyestalks 13-16 each, regrowing in 1-4 weeks. It has 2 or 3 eyestalks: ignore the third if it has 2 (MMII p.127).

system.specialDefenses: Iron or +1 or better weapon to hit
system.description:
The hated and feared wolfwere lives in out-of-the-way places and is the bane of humans and demi-humans alike, because it can take the form of a man or woman of considerable charisma. In its true shape or as a human it slyly hunts, kills, and eats its favorite prey: men, halflings, elves, etc.

  • Pack: it usually (75%) runs with a pack of normal wolves (30%) or worgs (70%).
  • Disguise: against strong prey it slips back to its lair, dresses as a human, and approaches as a pilgrim, minstrel, tinker, or similar wanderer, often carrying a stringed instrument so its crooning raises no suspicion.
  • Attacks: powerful jaws with terrible bites. It can also half-change, gaining human-like arms and legs to use a human weapon, and still bite in this form.
  • Song: worst of all. Listeners who fail a save vs. spells become lethargic, as if slowed, for 5-8 rounds, and this cannot be countered once it takes effect.
  • Defenses: hit only by cold-wrought iron weapons or magic of +1 or better.
  • Enemies: wolfweres and werewolves hate each other. Wolfweres are disgusted by wolvesbane and avoid it when they can.

These insect-like predators live across most of the Plane of Shadows, more commonly in forests. They seek warm-blooded prey but hesitate to attack humans. For the adult stage, see "Gloomwing".

  • Mandibles: powerful jaws dripping a highly caustic acid from glands behind the many-faceted eyes. Anyone struck must save vs. poison at −3 or take double damage from the bite.
  • Bristles: stiff, poisonous (to mammals) bristles cover the head and forebody. Anyone striking there with an open hand or similar attack (claw, bite, cause wounds spell, etc.) is at once filled with bristle filaments, taking 1-4 (1d4) points of damage, and must save vs. poison or be paralyzed. Unless given neutralize poison or slow poison within 1-4 rounds, the contact is fatal.
  • Armor helps: those striking with a weapon are protected by armor. Multiply the attacker’s armor class (without shield and dexterity bonuses) by 10 for a percentage; contact happens on that number or lower on percentile dice. There are fewer bristles on the head, so reduce the chance by 20% there. For example, a character in plate and shield has a 30% chance (AC 2 plus 1 for ignoring the shield, times 10), dropping to 10% if aiming at the head.

Description: huge, partly bare caterpillars. The front is covered with dull black bristles; the rear is a wet, sickening gray. The many-faceted eyes glimmer in the half-light of the Plane of Shadows, the only warning of their presence. Small black legs let them move fast. Huge pearly mandibles flank the great mouth; these tusks are beautiful cut into sheets and inlaid (like mother-of-pearl), worth 1000-3000 gp per set.

This giant cousin of the centipede is an aggressive predator and scavenger. Its burrows, 2 feet across, honeycomb the walls and ceilings of caves and dungeons. It feeds on and lays its eggs in carrion, dragging corpses back to its lair, and waits near its hidden burrow entrance for prey to pass. Its nest may hold treasure dragged in with a corpse.

  • Attack: it lunges from its tunnel and seizes prey in its mandibles at +2 to hit.
  • Chewing through armor: a hit does no damage until its teeth tear through the victim’s armor: 1 round for leather, 2 for chain mail, 3 for plate mail. After that it bites automatically for 2-16 points of damage per round.
  • Retreat: if it takes 15 or more points of fire damage, or loses more than 60% of its hit points, it lets go and retreats into its burrow, not attacking again unless cornered.

system.specialDefenses: +1 or better weapon to hit; see below
system.description:
Xag-ya come from the Positive Material Plane and xeg-yi from the Negative Material Plane. They are much alike, mirror images of each other. Both are spherical with many radiating, tentacle-like growths; xag-ya are silver and fiery with glowing golden eyes, xeg-yi black and lifeless with dull metallic orbs.

  • Xag-ya touch: a surge like a lightning bolt that sets highly flammable materials (parchment, cloth, wood, etc.) alight.
  • Xag-ya bolt (every other round): a bolt equal to its touch at a single target up to 10 feet away. It heats metal objects to glowing. Magic metal items do not heat if their owners save vs. lightning (base 11 for hard metal, 16 for soft, with pluses to the die for magic). Heated metal must be dropped and worn metal taken off; each segment of contact does 1-4 points of damage.
  • Xeg-yi touch: cell death, a mild life energy drain, and aging and rotting of the same materials a xag-ya burns. It sends matching tendrils of negative current that chill metal and do damage. Normal metal, and magic metal that fails its save, loses its magical properties; whatever fails against the negative current shatters or corrodes. (Same saving throw as against a xag-ya.)
  • Death burst: slaying either releases a burst of energy or negative force in a 10-foot radius, doing double damage (14-24) to all within; saves are made as if a bolt had touched them.
  • Meeting: if a xag-ya and xeg-yi ever meet, they rush together and destroy each other in a huge explosion (30-foot radius) doing 28-48 points of damage (4d6+24).

Harming them:

  • Only magic weapons affect them. Magic that creates cold affects xag-ya; magic that creates heat affects xeg-yi. Both are subject to disintegrate and magic missile.
  • Negation and absorption work against a xag-ya’s attack; a mace of disruption and rod of cancellation work against a xeg-yi’s attack without harm to the devices.
  • A shield spell stops the attack of either. A circle of protection (spell, magic circle, thaumaturgic triangle, or pentagram) repels both.
  • All other magic has no effect, except these, which can slay either or send it back to its own plane: abjure, alter reality, banishment, dismissal, dispel magic (treated as magic of a level equal to twice the creature’s hit dice), holy (unholy) word, limited wish, plane shift, wish.

Guardians: they are often used to guard magic, snared by magical summons and linked to an object. If the object is torn, broken, or opened without properly cancelling the link, the creature appears and attacks everything within 3" of it.

Xaren are relatives of the xorn. They live on the Elemental Plane of Earth but like to travel to the Prime Material Plane to feed. Their favorite metals are iron, copper, silver, gold, and electrum, in that order.

  • Magic metal: each plus on an item eaten gives 1 hit point permanently (+1 to +5 for eating a shield, for example), but total hit points can never exceed 45. Items without pluses neither help nor harm unless aligned to harm neutral creatures. They still crave magic metal, knowing how it helps their health.
  • Feeding: they blend with rocky surroundings and are very likely to surprise others there. They snack on metal, even ore, smelling ore at 20 feet and magic metal at 40 feet. They eat little: 5-8 pounds of metal satisfies one for 1-4 days.
  • Begging: they speak a bizarre tongue (telepathy or tongues helps understand it) and come up looking for a handout. If they smell magic metal that is not offered, they become very aggravated and are 80% likely to attack; not offering ordinary metal brings an attack 40% of the time.
  • Defenses: fire and cold (even magical) do not harm them; lightning does half or no damage. Move earth, flesh to rock, and dig kill them instantly. Rock to mud lowers their AC to 10 in 1-4 rounds. Sharp weapons do half damage; blunt weapons do full damage.
  • Biting weapons: attacked with a magic weapon, a xaren is 40% likely to try to bite it (treat the weapon as AC −2). A bite destroys the weapon utterly unless its owner saves vs. crushing blow (no bonus).
  • Movement: they can go to the Elemental Plane of Earth at will, and move through solid rock at 9" per round after taking 1 full round to adjust their molecules.
  • Treasure: those living on the Prime Material Plane are usually near treasure or ore. They hoard treasure for emergencies, eating it only if no other metal is at hand: 40% for 2-200 of each coin type except platinum; 20% for 1-8 gems (10 gp base value); 10% for 1-2 magic items not made of metal, worth under 10,000 gp.
  • Lair: may be a room inside solid rock, since they burrow at 3" per round. If so (70% likely), it is not deep (only 10 feet or so). A xaren losing a fight flees to its lair and, if found there, escapes to the Elemental Plane of Earth.

system.specialDefenses: Silver or magic weapon to hit
system.description:
The hideous yeth hounds live only in the wildest, most remote places. They lair in underground dens until the clean sunlight fades and they can come out to hunt. They eat any warm-blooded prey but much prefer demi-humans, brownies, and the like.

  • Baying: a ghastly sound heard a mile or more away. Creatures within 9" must save vs. spells or flee in panic, usually to be pulled down and gnawed to death by the pack.
  • Defenses: struck only by silver or magic weapons, and only the magical pluses do damage: a +1 long sword does 1 point, a +2 dagger 2 points, a +3 spear 3 points, etc. Silver weapons do 1 point because of their metal.
  • Masters: they can fly by magic and enjoy serving night hags, evil humans, and the like, so they are often found working with some sort of evil huntsmen. Those who hunt with them are not subject to fear from the baying.

Description: huge dull black dogs with almost human-looking heads, horn-like ears, and eyes glowing cherry red.

Yochlol usually have no clear form at all: they are misty columns of gas that form pseudopods as needed, noticed only by their vile smells and a hazy smudge in the air. They are common in the Abyss and very rare elsewhere. "If they do not take mates" (as printed), they have an effective armor class of −10. Yochlol are a type of demon and are affected by whatever affects demons.

  • Gaseous: they cannot stay immaterial and attack physically, but in gas form their touch equals a stinking cloud spell. In this form only a +1 or better weapon can hit one. A stinking cloud spell heals it for 3-12 points. A gust of wind does 6-36 points of damage unless its magic resistance stops the spell. A wind walk spell destroys one yochlol (no magic resistance check); if the cleric could normally take 2 other persons along, 2 yochlol may be destroyed. Either way the cleric must touch the victims.
  • Materialized: to do physical damage it must materialize, becoming AC 10. It can take 3 forms:
    • Amorphous column with 8 pseudopods (its natural form): it uses psionics or strikes with the pseudopods, each blow doing 5-8 points of damage, its strength being in effect 18/50.
    • Giant spider: as a giant spider in all but armor class (10) and psionics.
    • Beautiful human or elf: it uses its psionics, plus abilities available only in this form such as weapon attacks, as a 6th-level fighter. It can use weapons and magic items usable by clerics and fighters equally well. It may wear armor, but must then become gaseous before changing to spider or amorphous form, since the armor would injure those forms.
  • Changing form: it can change from one form to another within a single round. A gaseous yochlol can materialize in the same round as its stinking cloud attack and attack again (in a way suited to its new form) at the end of the round; or in amorphous form it can make several attacks, then turn into a spider at the end of the round to climb into webs to escape next round.
  • Psionics: cell adjustment (only in humanoid form), domination, aura alteration, and probability travel.
system.hpNote: Printed “6 (1d10)”. The book does not explain the “(1d10)”; reading it as 10-sided hit dice is likely but not stated.

system.psionicText: 150 Attack/Defense Modes: B, D/F, I, J
system.description:
The yuan-ti live in tropical jungles. They are a degenerate, corrupt race that was once human. All are devout demon worshippers with a high regard for every kind of reptile. Dark, unknown practices have fouled their blood, and they produce monstrosities. There are 3 types: purebloods, halfbreeds, and abominations.

  • Purebloods: the weakest, with only 6 hit dice. Human-looking except for small differences such as scaly hands, a forked tongue, or a somewhat reptilian look; they pass as human 80% of the time. They usually handle dealings with the outside world and may travel far and wide to do so.
  • Halfbreeds: 7-8 hit dice, and very distinctive: part of the body is a snake’s, the rest human. Roll once or twice on the table below, or the DM may choose. Ignore combinations that seem impossible or unworkable; the DM may also invent other snake-human results.
d6Halfbreed feature
1Snake head
2Torso can bend and move like a snake’s
3No legs, torso ends in a snake’s tail
4Has snakes instead of arms
5Body is covered by scales
6Snake tail is growing from backside
  • Halfbreed attacks: a snake head bites for 1-10 points of damage, snake-headed arms bite for 1-6, and a tail constricts for 1-4. Otherwise they use weapons as normal humans. All snake parts are AC 0.
  • Abominations: the strongest, all with 9 hit dice. Often mistaken for nagas and other snake creatures, they are either totally snake-like or have only 1 human feature, such as a head or arms. Their bite (unless from a human head) does 1-10 points of damage.
  • Movement: those with human legs move 12" per turn; those with snake bodies 9" per turn, and can coil around pillars and the like.
  • Spells (human-headed yuan-ti, once per day each): cause fear, darkness in a 15-foot radius, snake charm, sticks to snakes, neutralize poison, suggestion, and polymorph other.
  • Languages: their own, and speech with any snake or snake-like monster. Those with human heads also speak Chaotic and Common.

system.specialDefenses: +1 or better magic weapon to hit, see below
system.description:
Juju zombies are made by magic-users who drain all life levels from humans or man-sized humanoids with an energy drain spell (q.v.). They are "programmed" as regular zombies are, but are better in every way.

  • Abilities: better armor class; they move quickly (even under water, since they do not breathe), climb like 6th-level thieves, and attack with great force as 6 hit dice monsters. They can throw weapons or shoot a bow or crossbow.
  • Weapons: existing partly on the Negative Material Plane, they can be hit only by +1 or better magic weapons. Being undead, they take only half damage from piercing or blunt weapons; only cleaving weapons do normal damage (axes, broad, bastard, or two-handed swords, bardiches, halberds, voulges, and similar weapons).
  • Immunities: all magic affecting the mind (illusion, charms, holds, etc.), poison, electricity, and magic missile, death, and cold spells. Fire has half normal effect; acid and holy water have full effect.
  • Turning: as a spectre.

Description: like an ordinary zombie, but its flesh is less rotted, gray, leathery, and hard. A hateful light burns in its eyes, for it knows what it has become and wants to destroy living things.

Monster zombies are the animated corpses of huge humanoid monsters such as bugbears, giants, etc., usually made and controlled by evil clerics or magic-users. They can obey simple commands or follow instructions a few words long.

  • Combat: slow, so they strike last in melee, and they attack until destroyed.
  • Defenses: blunt weapons do only half damage. Immune to charm, cold, death magic, hold, and sleep.
  • Turning: as ghasts.
  • Holy water: normal damage, 2-8 points per vial that strikes.

This meat-eating beast likes human and demi-human flesh. When first met its armor class and damage are poor, but it can absorb the natural armor class of its surroundings in 1 round: earth AC 7; wood AC 5; metal AC 3; stone AC 0.

  • Absorbed armor: lasts 10 rounds and also gives a damage bonus equal to its original armor class 10 minus the new armor class.
  • Stealing protection: when it hits an opponent it can absorb the armor class and defensive bonuses of 1 random protective item (armor, shield, ring of protection, etc.), turning the item to dust (no save). If this would make its armor class worse, the item is still destroyed but nothing is absorbed.
  • Example: attacked in a cave, it absorbs stone on the 1st round: AC 0 and a damage bonus of 10 − 0 = 10. Next round it hits and absorbs its opponent’s shield +2: AC −2 and damage bonus +12. On the 3rd round it hits the opponent’s plate mail (AC 3), which turns to dust without changing its armor class or damage.

Zygoms are small fungus growths, each a short, thin stem with an egg-shaped cap. One or 2 dozen are joined by a root structure into a single shared creature, a zygom. They can live in earth, but prefer to infest living flesh and feed on the host’s blood and tissue.

  • Infestation: usually on the head, neck, and back (spine). It controls the host through brain and nerve links, so the host moves, attacks, and defends as the zygoms direct. It kills the host in 1-8 weeks, depending on its size and constitution, and stays until the whole body is eaten, then moves on. Typical hosts are giant ants, giant rats, osquips, and now and then small humanoids.
  • Glue: whenever a colony comes into rough contact with a creature, there is a 1 in 6 chance the pale blue "milk" of a broken cap sticks fast to it. It is extremely sticky, gluing things together for 2-5 days before it dries and crumbles. Glued to flesh, zygom spores infect the creature and start growing by the time the glue powders, letting the zygoms infest and control the host. Only a cure disease removes the infestation. The glue can be embarrassing in other ways too, sticking weapons to targets, creatures to creatures, etc.
  • Mind: their fungus intelligence is totally alien to humans, so no mind-affecting magic (beguiling, charming, dominating, holding, hypnotizing, etc.) affects them.
system.hpNote: Printed “3 (host’s - see below)”: an infested host is controlled with its own hit points (MMII p.132).
